papers.abstract: Does readily available lifestyle information improve machine-learning prediction of hypertension beyond routine demographic and anthropometric data? On NHANES 2017-March 2020, five model families (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Bagged Decision Trees, and XGBoost) were evaluated with fold-local preprocessing and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Adding physical activity, alcohol use, smoking, and sleep information showed no consistent detectable improvement in held-out discrimination: every paired ROC-AUC confidence interval included zero, including under a stricter measured-blood-pressure phenotype and without synthetic oversampling. Mean cross-model SHAP rank agreement fell from 0.873 to 0.806 over all encoded columns, but this decline was largely attenuated over the 19 baseline columns shared by both arms (0.873 vs. 0.863), and likewise under both robustness checks; attribution-agreement comparisons across feature sets of different sizes therefore require a matched comparison space. In exploratory analysis of untreated adults (measured-blood-pressure outcome), all five models showed small positive differences, two with unadjusted intervals excluding zero, meriting confirmation. These results do not imply that lifestyle factors are clinically unimportant; within this cohort, the evaluated lifestyle block added little incremental discrimination beyond an already-informative baseline.

papers.title: Finding Low-Energy States of the Bernasconi Model via Simulated Transverse-Field Quantum Dynamics
papers.abstract: The Low-Autocorrelation Binary Sequence (LABS) problem, the ground-state problem of the Bernasconi model, has a rugged landscape with deep, isolated local minima. We study real-time transverse-field dynamics initialized in these minima as a means of reaching lower-energy configurations. Using GPU statevector simulation for N = 20-30 spins, we compare the escape probability per verified quantum sample with the success rate per energy evaluation of steepest-descent kicks, random restarts and tabu search. Using the same field and sampling window across all system sizes, we find that, relative to the best classical baseline, the sampler achieves a factor of 11.9-35.2 for the deepest traps and 13.4-27.2 for the next energy tier. These ratios describe a constant-factor improvement in sample efficiency over the sizes studied. At the adopted field, broad Hamming-space spreading coexists with a strong preference for low-energy states. This regime follows a sharp increase in displacement as the field is raised. To connect this behaviour to the landscape, a short-time expansion relates the onset of escape to target distance and intermediate energies. Bounds on isotropic spin flips and on the free transverse mixer quantify the role of the Bernasconi potential in the observed transfer. At N = 28, the ground-state probability at t = 30 exceeds a canonical cost prediction fitted to the same mean energy by a factor of about 1.9. The cost of generating each quantum sample is assessed separately through a hardware estimate, which places a direct circuit implementation two to three orders of magnitude beyond present processor capabilities.

papers.title: Inelastic confinement-induced resonances in multiwell potentials
papers.abstract: Recently, resonance features associated with multiwell effects have been reported in a fascinating experiment conducted with an ultracold-atom quantum simulator [Y. K. Lee, H. Lin, and W. Ketterle, Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 213001 (2023)]. The results were explained as a consequence of superexchange, which determines the spin dynamics in a singly-occupied Mott insulator, by allowing for the virtual population of two particles on the same site. In this work, a complementary interpretation of the resonance features is provided based on inelastic confinement-induced resonances, manifested as avoided crossings in the two-particle spectrum, showing excellent agreement with the experimental results. The comparison of the results of the single- and double-well descriptions of the optical trapping potential confirms the multiwell origin of the experimental features. However, the double-well model is already shown to be sufficient for providing an explanation of the apparent symmetry violation that occurs within single-well models. Furthermore, certain limitations of the harmonic approximation are discussed.

papers.title: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.

papers.title: NetBreaker: Benchmarking Network Dismantling across Objectives, Scales, and Toplogoies
papers.abstract: Network dismantling seeks to fragment a network with as few node removals as possible, which is widely applied in vulnerability analysis, epidemic containment, and infrastructure protection. Although learning-based methods have become increasingly prominent, their progress remains difficult to assess because existing studies differ in method coverage, datasets, evaluation criteria, and experimental protocols. Thus, we introduce NetBreaker, a comprehensive benchmark designed for the learning era of network dismantling. NetBreaker organizes 30 methods (18 non-learning and 12 learning-based) under a common taxonomy and evaluates them on 185 networks from eight unified domains, ranging from 14 to 1.69 million nodes. To enable fair comparison, heterogeneous method outputs are converted into node removal sequences and assessed under a unified execution protocol. The evaluation covers four complementary dimensions: target-based effectiveness, trajectory-based effectiveness, structural diagnostics, and applicability & computational efficiency. Extensive experiments show that current learningbased methods do not consistently outperform strong non-learning approaches, while exposing substantial differences in effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency across network conditions and evaluation perspectives. NetBreaker provides a reproducible basis for measuring progress and developing reliable, scalable, and computationally efficient network dismantling methods.

papers.title: Where Mixture Recognition Fails: An Ingredient-Level Audit of Unseen Combinations in SmellNet
papers.abstract: An electronic nose must name every ingredient of a mixture, including combinations it has never measured. SmellNet, a public benchmark for this task, scores ingredients with a hit rate that is told how many each sample contains. We audit what this protocol hides. We hold out ingredient combinations from the SmellNet training data, evaluate four architectures (MLP, CNN, LSTM and a Transformer encoder) without revealing the ingredient count, and repeat the evaluation once on the official unseen split. Under the count-informed protocol, 90-96% of mixtures receive an ingredient that is absent, on our folds and on the official split alike. On our folds, every model identifies one ingredient reliably but the second rarely, and it completes the pair with a familiar training partner about twice as often as chance. On the official split, even the first-ranked ingredient is correct in only 29-46% of binary mixtures, often because a frequent training ingredient that is absent from every test pair is ranked first, and on its combinations that are truly absent from training no model names both ingredients in more than 1.2% of them. The failures fall on the same ingredients for every architecture, and a frequency correction only moves errors between ingredients. Mixture recognition is therefore limited by ingredients the models cannot separate and by a preference for frequent ingredients, not by the architecture, and it should be evaluated with set-level errors and without oracle cardinality.

papers.title: Predicting local electric field in Al$_x$Ga$_{1-x}$N p-i-n photodiodes using exciton Franz-Keldysh photocurrent spectroscopy
papers.abstract: In AlGaN p-i-n photodiodes, reverse bias redshifts and broadens the sub-bandgap photocurrent responsivity through the eXciton Franz-Keldysh (XFK) effect, and this spectral line shape encodes the local electric field inside the device. Fitting the photocurrent spectra of two such photodiodes, with 5% and 40% Al, to an XFK absorption model at each bias yields the local voltage, $V_l$, a single parameter that sets the line shape and uniquely determines the electric-field profile inside the device. In both devices, $V_l$ varies linearly with the applied bias ($R^2 = 0.994$ and $0.998$) but changes far more slowly than the bias itself, revealing a strong local reduction of the electric field that points to non-uniform electrostatics. The slopes show that only 12.4% of the applied bias in the 5% Al device, and 45.8% in the 40% Al device, drops across the junction at the probed location. Extrapolated to zero bias, $V_l$ gives built-in voltages of 3.39 and 4.29 V, within 0.02 V of the 3.41 and 4.28 V obtained from technology computer-aided design (TCAD) simulation, which validates the extracted local voltages at equilibrium. These results extend sub-bandgap photocurrent spectroscopy to AlGaN devices as an optical probe of local electrostatics, relevant to ultraviolet photodetectors and high-voltage electronics.

papers.title: Optional Traps: An Empirical Study of LLM Agents Against Credential Deception and Alert-Driven Revocation
papers.abstract: Deception (honeypots, decoys and canary credentials) rests on a simple premise: legitimate users never touch a fake asset, so any touch is a high-confidence signal. We ask whether that premise holds when the attacker is a large language model (LLM) agent, and what deception contributes once ordinary hardening is in place. We built an isolated, hash-chained lab around a mock Records API and report four studies. (1) In an exploratory run, a local 9.7B-parameter model ignored every optional decoy, read a genuinely leaked service key from a debug endpoint and exported the protected records in both static and adaptive deception modes. (2) After removing the leak, planting a canary credential in its place and revoking the offending client, a frozen 60-session study with a 4B-parameter model found export success of 20/20 at baseline, 0/20 with hardening alone and 0/20 with hardening plus deception (exact paired McNemar p = 1.9e-6 baseline vs. defended; p = 1 hardened vs. defended). Deception added detection and per-client revocation in 19 of 20 defended sessions, but no measurable prevention beyond hardening. (3) On Google Cloud, a real OpenCanary login alert was authenticated, signed and turned into revocation of the attacking client; the first denied export followed within an observed upper bound of 303 ms, a separate legitimate client completed 100/100 requests, and all 14 control checks passed. (4) In multi-agent swarm engagements, agents that used the canary were revoked 39-59 s after the bait was served without affecting siblings, but one model-driven legitimate agent also took the bait, a false-positive risk specific to LLM clients. Against LLM agents, traps must sit on the attacker's path rather than beside it, closing real weaknesses does the preventive work, and deception's measurable value is fast, attributable detection. All results are lab-scale and are not a production claim.

papers.title: Initial Conditions Dictate Gas-Stellar Counter-Rotation in Galaxies
papers.abstract: We present a physical origin of gas-stellar counter-rotation in galaxies. Scale-dependent partitions of tidal torques from cosmic primordial perturbations source angular momentum for distinct baryonic components. This scale dependence maps to radial hierarchy in Lagrangian space clustering: stellar components, assembled at earlier times from the inner protohalo, retain persistent memory of small-scale tidal torques, whereas gas, accreted later from outer Lagrangian regions, is governed by large-scale perturbations and can develop counter-rotation. This mechanism is observationally testable and offers a direct probe of the hierarchical cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm. Unlike conventional late-time scenarios that only explain the existence of counter-rotation, our framework further predicts its component-resolved direction, enabling component-resolved angular momentum to serve as a new probe of primordial density perturbations and improving cosmological initial condition reconstruction.

papers.title: Bayesian Time-Varying Spectral Estimation for LISA with P-Splines
papers.abstract: We model the evolutionary spectrum of a slowly time-varying process by a linear combination of products of time- and frequency-dependent B-splines, placing a Gaussian tensor-product penalty prior on the coefficients. The posterior distribution is obtained by updating the prior using a Whittle-type likelihood approximation of the Wilson-Daubechies-Meyer time-frequency coefficients. Separate regularisation in time and frequency allows non-stationary spectral structure to be inferred. An adaptive coarse-grained likelihood reduces the computational cost while preserving fine resolution around sharp spectral features. We first validate the method using repeated simulations of a locally stationary process with known spectrum, showing lower reconstruction errors and narrower posterior intervals as the sample size increases. We then apply it to a year-long simulated LISA data set with stationary instrumental single link spectra, an evolving time-delay interferometry (TDI) response, and a modulated Galactic foreground. We compare a flexible total power spectral density (PSD) model with models incorporating progressively stronger physical information and examine both continuous and gapped observations. Allowing time variation substantially improves reconstruction relative to a stationary model, while incorporating physical information about the TDI response further improves recovery, particularly near its moving spectral features. The results illustrate the trade-off between spectral flexibility, physical assumptions, and posterior uncertainty in non-stationary LISA noise estimation.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses.

papers.title: Repairing actuator schedules under graph constraints
papers.abstract: We consider a discrete-time linear system in which each actuator is assigned to one time slot. A graph $H$ records which pairs of actuators cannot share a slot. We seek to remove conflicts by exchanging actuators between slots, while preserving all tail reachability spaces. These spaces describe the terminal corrections available from each time slot onward. We give a sufficient condition based on the number of exchanges that preserve the required bases. The condition guarantees repair from every compatible starting schedule. Two bounds for checking it use failed basis tests and dependent column selections. Each accepted exchange reduces the conflict count, so the procedure uses at most as many exchanges as there are initial conflicts. An explicit family with unequal rank increments admits repair when $3N>4Δ(H)+4$, where $Δ(H)$ is the largest number of forbidden partners of any actuator. We also give a family of two-slot examples with only one forbidden partner per actuator and two initial conflicts. The basis constraints force every strict improvement to move arbitrarily many actuators, although one exchange suffices without those constraints. A second example has a connected conflict graph and one initial conflict.

papers.title: Complete Hypergraph States as a Resource for Robust Quantum Metrology
papers.abstract: Hypergraph states extend graph states by incorporating many-body interactions via multi-controlled-$Z$ gates, but their metrological advantages and design principles remain elusive. We develop an analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information (QFI) of complete weighted hypergraphs with respect to the collective-spin generators $J_x$ and $J_y$, reducing to three finite binomial averages requiring $O(n|K|)$ arithmetic for a set of hyperedge orders $K$. At the entangling phase $ϕ=π$, order-optimized $J_x$ sensing approaches the Heisenberg limit (HL), while $J_y$ oscillates between the HL and half the HL at large total number of qubits, $n$. We derive the quadratic and linear coefficients of the QFI under erasure and dephasing noise, showing that complete hypergraph states retain Heisenberg scaling for finite erased particles and dephasing probability $p<0.5$ in the asymptotic system size limit. For $J_y$ sensing, computational basis measurement, or, more simply, using Hamming weight detection, is sufficient to saturate the QFI under noiseless conditions and retain Heisenberg scaling under both noises. These results suggest that complete hypergraphs are a robust resource for practical metrological sensing tasks.

papers.title: Spreads Don't Price a Rival Market Maker's Information
papers.abstract: When one market maker becomes better informed, do its competitors widen their bid-ask spreads? Adverse-selection reasoning suggests that they should, because the better-informed maker avoids toxic order flow and leaves more of it to the others, and the closest model of competition with an informed dealer predicts more conservative quotes by the uninformed dealers. We study this question in a stochastic quoting game in which one maker receives a private signal of varying precision about a persistent state that drives order flow. Strategies are learned with independent reinforcement learning, which we benchmark against an exact dynamic-programming solution of the single-agent case. In none of the configurations we examine does the average spread of the uninformed makers increase with the rival's precision. Where competition for order flow is weak, the slope of their spread in precision is statistically equivalent to zero within half an action tick; where competition is strong, their spread tightens. The informed maker's own spread tightens markedly in every configuration and serves as a positive control. These results hold with two, three and four makers, across an eightfold variation in the depth of the background liquidity, with a background quote that reprices after toxic fills, and under price-time priority. Our measurements point to a competitive trade-off. In the model the total toxicity of the flow does not depend on any maker's information. A better-informed maker avoids more of it, and where this leaves more toxic flow to its competitors, it also quotes more tightly, so that a wider quote would cost them more order flow than it would save in adverse selection. The uninformed makers adjust the skew of their quotes and their inventory instead, and the rival's information changes the distribution of profits across makers while quoted spreads remain nearly unchanged.

papers.title: An all-steps-at-once algorithm for time-domain wave propagation in heterogeneous and unbounded media
papers.abstract: We propose, analyze, and implement a convolution quadrature (CQ) algorithm for transient acoustic waves in an unbounded medium consisting of a heterogeneous domain embedded in free space, where the wave speed may be spatially variable and discontinuous. Multistep CQ, applied to the time-domain solution operator, reduces the evolution problem to a family of Helmholtz problems with damped complex frequencies, which can be solved independently in parallel, all time steps at once. The frequency problems are discretized by an overlapping coupling of finite elements (FEM) on a polygonal/polyhedral domain containing the inhomogeneity, and boundary elements (BEM) on a smooth curve enclosed by that domain, in the region where the medium is homogeneous, which accounts exactly for the unbounded exterior. Neither discretization needs to conform to the geometry of the heterogeneous domain, nor to each other. For the resulting FEM--BEM coupling we prove bounds for the solution operators of the transformed problems that are explicit in the Laplace parameter and the wave speed. These bounds yield convergence of the time discretization for A-stable multistep schemes. We also prove explicit estimates on the exponential decay of the transformed solutions away from the heterogeneity, which show that the correction provided by the BEM part is small but relevant, and cheap to compute: a few GMRES iterations suffice, and the correction is needed only over a fixed range of weakly damped frequencies, beyond which it becomes negligible and can be dropped. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates in time and space and explore iterative (multigrid) methods for the interior FEM problems.

papers.title: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly $3\times$ speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.

papers.title: On Representational and Functional Alignment of Training Data Attribution Methods for Language Models
papers.abstract: Existing approaches to training data attribution derive influence estimates from different sources of information, including gradients, model-internal states, and surface-level similarity. However, comparisons between attribution methods remain incomplete, often relying on indirect evaluations through downstream task performance. In this work, we introduce a framework for directly comparing methods along three dimensions: functional alignment, which measures correlation between full attribution vectors; representational alignment, which captures structural similarity of the representations underlying attribution; and cross-method predictability, which evaluates agreement on local pairwise ranking decisions. We observe strong representational and moderate functional alignment within paradigms. Alignment across paradigms is low and task-dependent, yet stable across models. Our results suggest that the similar downstream performance observed across paradigms in prior work can be attributed to agreement on the relative importance of documents, rather than to agreement on rankings of the full training data.

papers.title: Generate, Align, and Restore: MLLM-Empowered Diffusion for Generalizable Low-light Image Enhancement
papers.abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is essential to numerous vision applications operating under adverse illumination. Despite substantial advances, real-world nighttime enhancement remains challenging due to the scarcity of strictly aligned day-night pairs and complex degradations involving extreme darkness and heterogeneous artificial light sources, leading to fragile generalization. To overcome these challenges, we propose MrLIE (MLLM-empowered reference Low-light Image Enhancement), a novel reference-based unsupervised LLIE framework that synergizes the generative and reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with conditional diffusion. MrLIE employs the MLLM as a high-fidelity reference synthesizer and diagnostic critic, iteratively generating, diagnosing, and correcting normal-light references directly from degraded nighttime observations. Based on this, our method governs the enhancement process through two complementary mechanisms, in which a confidence offset module rectifies spatial-geometric inconsistencies for reference reliability and a structure-anchored injection scheme harmonizes aligned reference cues, low-light structural constraints, and ControlNet additive anchoring during the denoising process. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that MrLIE achieves superior perceptual quality, natural appearance, and robust generalization.

papers.title: LC-ISP Benchmark: Learning Advanced ISP with Live and Capture Streams
papers.abstract: High-quality paired RAW-to-sRGB datasets are essential for data-driven ISP, yet existing datasets often rely on cross-device collection, causing misalignment and failing to faithfully reflect real capture conditions. We therefore introduce LC-ISP, a large-scale benchmark built from the intrinsic gap between a camera's live preview and offline capture streams. LC-ISP contains 53.9k spatially aligned groups, each comprising live RAW/live sRGB and multi-frame fused RGB/capture sRGB, and covers day, night, indoor, outdoor, and HDR scenes. It also provides capture-stream intermediates for modular supervision. We further develop a compact two-stage baseline that uses these intermediates as auxiliary targets. Under a 2.5-GFLOP budget for 448$\times$448 RAW inputs, it outperforms the strongest single-frame baseline by over 2 dB PSNR while improving texture, denoising, and color reproduction. LC-ISP supports realistic benchmarking, the design of supervision strategies, and the development of lightweight ISP models.

papers.title: Fourier Crosstalk and Leakage Correction for Binary-Encoded Fourier Single-Pixel Imaging
papers.abstract: Digital micromirror devices enable high-speed Fourier single-pixel imaging (Fourier-SPI), but their binary modulation introduces quantization errors that degrade the reconstructed image quality. In particular, each binarized Fourier probe contains non-target Fourier components, thereby distorting the corresponding Fourier-domain measurement. This Letter presents a Fourier domain correction framework that characterizes these errors using the Fourier-domain response matrix of the decoded binary Fourier patterns. Accordingly, a response-matrix-based Fourier-SPI measurement model is established by partitioning the matrix into components associated with the sampled and unsampled frequencies, thereby decomposing the quantization error into sampled-frequency crosstalk and unsampled-frequency leakage. This model established a generalized correction framework, termed Fourier Crosstalk and Leakage Correction (FCLC), alongside two simplified methods: Fourier Sampled-Frequency Crosstalk Correction (FSCC) and Fourier DC Crosstalk Correction (FDCC). FSCC is implemented via an inversion-free Richardson-type iteration, whereas FDCC admits a closed-form solution. Numerical simulations and experiments across multiple binary encoding strategies reveal that the proposed framework improves reconstruction fidelity without modifying the binary patterns or acquisition process.

papers.title: Sensing with OFDM Signals: How Do the Constellations Affect the Sensing Accuracy?
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how communication constellations affect joint range-velocity estimation with data-bearing orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) signals. To this end, starting from the continuous-time sensing process, we derive a discrete observation model and specify its validity conditions. For multiple targets with unknown delays, Doppler shifts, and complex gains, the complete Fisher information matrix (FIM) admits a structural factorization separating deterministic channel derivatives from random symbol-energy weights. This structure yields a Jensen-type lower bound on the average conditional Cramer-Rao bound (CRB), which is attained exactly by constant-modulus constellations. Single-target closed-form expressions further reveal the dependence of the bounds on the transmitted energy distribution and physical OFDM parameters. We also formulate two-dimensional fast Fourier transform (FFT), concentrated maximum-likelihood (ML), and sliding-subarray multiple signal classification (MUSIC) processing under the derived observation model. Numerical results support the theoretical optimality of constant-modulus constellations but also show that the CRB gap between phase-shift keying (PSK) and quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) becomes negligible when the numbers of subcarriers and OFDM symbols are considerably large. The performance of ML estimation closely approaches the derived bounds, which confirms the effectiveness of the theoretical analysis. FFT processing exhibits grid-induced error floors. In the considered scenarios, MUSIC provides lower estimation errors than FFT and exhibits a more pronounced constellation dependence.

papers.title: Hadwiger-Debrunner numbers from rainbow Turán numbers and beyond
papers.abstract: The Hadwiger-Debrunner number $\operatorname{HD}_d(p,q)$ is defined as the maximum piercing number over all finite families of compact convex sets in $\mathbb R^d$ in which among every $p$ sets, some $q$ have non-empty intersection. We develop three complementary constructions that improve lower bounds for Hadwiger-Debrunner numbers. For any fixed $q>d\ge 2$, a randomly sparsified family of hyperplanes, analyzed using hypergraph containers, yields $\operatorname{HD}_d(p,q)\ge p^{(d+q-2)/(q-1)+o(1)}$ as $p\rightarrow\infty$. To deduce further bounds, we establish a transfer argument from upper bounds on the sizes of sufficiently general-positioned subsets of high-dimensional integer grids to lower bounds for Hadwiger-Debrunner numbers. Two methodologies are adopted to derive the former: one connects rainbow Turán theory and general-positioned grid sets, and the other uses full spark linear reduction of tuples with bounded-size preimages. As a combinatorial ingredient, we describe the rainbow Turán behavior under suspension operations, which may be of independent interest.

papers.title: Hardware-Friendly Plug-and-Play MVDR Beamforming for Microphone Arrays: Algorithm, Prototype, and System-Level Feasibility
papers.abstract: Beamforming has been widely recognized for its spatial filtering capability in speech signal processing, enabling effective interference rejection and signal enhancement. The performance of adaptive beamforming methods, e.g., the conventional minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR) beamforming, often deteriorate significantly in complex and dynamic acoustic environments. Part of the reason is that such conventional beamforming ignores the intrinsic characteristics of speech. To address this issue, this paper proposes Plug-and-Play Minimum Variance Distortionless Response (PnP-MVDR) algorithm, which integrates data-driven speech prior information into the MVDR framework to enhance robustness against non-stationary noise while maintaining its interpretability. The PnP-MVDR framework supports joint interaction of signal processing and deep learning methods and is designed to be compatible with modern DSP-NPU architectures, making it hardware-friendly for potential edge deployment. Beyond the algorithmic innovation, we have developed a complete microphone beamforming system to validate practical feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms traditional and deep learning-based baselines, establishing PnP-MVDR as an effective and deployable solution for edge audio scenarios.

papers.title: Rethinking KV Caching for LLM Decode: Free-Space Optical KV Regeneration for Reduction of Memory Traffic
papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) decoding repeatedly reads the historical key-value (KV) cache, making multi-head attention (MHA) memory-bandwidth-bound. Caching layer-input activations instead halves historical-cache storage and traffic, but requires regenerating KV from each cached activation. On digital accelerators such as GPUs, this regeneration takes far longer than fetching the activation from HBM. The KV regeneration overhead outweighs the savings from reduced memory traffic, shifting decode attention from a memory bottleneck to a compute bottleneck. We present OptiDecode, a hybrid optoelectronic decode-attention accelerator that regenerates historical KV using free-space optics and computes attention digitally. Projection weights remain resident on optical tiles, exploiting reuse across historical tokens for high-throughput optical regeneration. Scaling to large models introduces two challenges. First, distributing weights across tiles requires sending the same activations to every head group, while each readout die produces only partial KV. Activation replay shares one set of electrical-to-optical converters across head groups without costly broadcast. In-situ attention avoids transferring partial KV from readout dies to reducers by computing on them locally and exchanging only partial scores, probabilities, and partial outputs. Second, processing an activation chunk through all dependent stages takes longer than one activation-fetch interval. Chunk pipelining overlaps successive chunks so that OptiDecode sustains the HBM activation-fetch rate. OptiDecode demonstrates 1.92-1.99x decode-attention speedup over an ideal GPU KV-read baseline at equal peak HBM bandwidth (A100-B200), for 32K-token contexts across evaluated 30B-175B MHA models, approaching the 2x upper bound from halving historical memory traffic.

papers.title: Matroid Parity Meets Vertex Splitting
papers.abstract: A vertex split replaces a vertex by two non-adjacent descendants and partitions its incident edges between them. We study exclusive $\ell$-shallow splitting, where each original vertex has at most $\ell+1$ descendants, with the aim of obtaining a forest, a pseudoforest, or a cluster graph. We consider two natural objectives: minimizing the total number of split operations and minimizing the number of original vertices that are split. Our main conceptual contribution is a connection between vertex splitting and matroid parity. For both forests and pseudoforests, we give a characterization of feasible splitting sequences that leads, via weighted linear matroid parity, to polynomial-time algorithms for minimizing the number of split vertices when $\ell=2$. These algorithms are complemented by NP-hardness for every fixed $\ell\ge3$; for pseudoforests, hardness holds even on graphs of maximum degree four. The total number of split operations behaves differently: for both sparse target classes, this objective is polynomial-time solvable for every $\ell$, using matroid intersection. For cluster graphs, both objectives admit linear-time algorithms when $\ell=1$ and are NP-hard for every fixed $\ell\ge2$. Together, these results identify how the target class, the local splitting bound, and the choice of objective determine the complexity of vertex splitting.

papers.title: $α$--$α$ Correlations in Excited Clustering Nuclei Across the Solid-Liquid Transition
papers.abstract: We investigate the structural evolution of $α$-cluster matter using a microscopic transport model for four $α$-conjugate collision systems, including $^{12}\text{C}+^{12}\text{C}$, $^{16}\text{O}+^{12}\text{C}$, $^{28}\text{Si}+^{12}\text{C}$, and $^{40}\text{Ca}+^{12}\text{C}$ at incident energies ranging from 2.0 to 7.0~MeV/u. The $α$-cluster structure of an excited nucleus undergoes a solid-liquid phase transition with increasing incident energy. Whether it proceeds by the dissociation of individual clusters or by the collapse of their spatial organization remains unexplored, as does the question of whether any characteristic $α$--$α$ correlation survives. The one-body density $ρ(\mathbf{r})$, the standard clustering diagnostic, cannot by itself settle this question, since it neither distinguishes a genuine cluster configuration from a density fluctuation nor reveals the sparse residual clusters masked by the surrounding nucleon medium. We therefore construct the exclusive $α$--$α$ two-body spatial correlation function from the $α$-cluster centroids to isolate the $α$ clusters. In all four systems the $α$--$α$ correlation exhibits two peaks, a nearest-neighbor one and a next-nearest-neighbor inter-cluster one. Both peak positions increase with system size. Over the energy range studied, which spans this transition, the mean number of $α$ clusters per event falls steeply while the $α$--$α$ correlation persists and the inter-cluster distances change only slightly. The individual clusters therefore dissociate rather than lose their spatial organization.

papers.title: ReCALM: A Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism for Distributed Continual Service Construction
papers.abstract: Crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising paradigm for constructing AI services by harnessing the collective capabilities of distributed workers. As consumers' demands continually evolve, service models must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned information. However, due to the inherited reliance on gradients for backpropagation, existing approaches typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual model updates on heterogeneous data. Recent studies have introduced analytic learning, a gradient-free paradigm that achieves invariance through recursive closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, existing analytic methods are typically constrained by single-layer linear networks, which tend to suffer from underfitting due to their inability to perform deep representation learning. To address this issue, we propose ReCALM, a Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism that achieves deep nonlinear invariance for distributed continual service construction. Inspired by the success of ResNet, we develop gradient-free residual blocks for ReCALM with closed-form solutions. To implement distributed continual training for ReCALM, we further devise a cross-recursive strategy via least squares. Both theoretical and experimental analyses verify ReCALM's dual superiority in heterogeneity invariance and deep representation. With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85%-9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline, while reducing computational costs by over 94% compared with gradient-based baselines.

papers.title: Beyond Clumsy Agentic Tool Calling: How Cueing and Spotting Make the Difference
papers.abstract: LLM-based task-oriented agents depend on tools to interact with their environments, but may overlook execution feedback, repeat ineffective calls, or persist with unproductive strategies. These behaviors can hinder agents' ability to use tools autonomously and sustain task progress. We characterize tool-use symptoms at two temporal granularities: local clumsy tool-use behaviors and tool-use detours spanning multiple interactions. Towards greater autonomy in tool use, we present ToolPulse, an online middleware supporting autonomous tool use through cueing and spotting. ToolPulse tracks execution state and temporal interaction patterns, monitoring proposed calls before dispatch and inspecting execution feedback prior to the agent resumes reasoning. It combines state-based rules, semantic sequence analysis, and interaction-feature similarity to identify intervention opportunities and provide verbal reminders, structured feedback, or context-specific advice from auxiliary models. Our process-oriented evaluation distinguishes trigger validity, behavioral cessation, and substantive correction alongside task outcomes and resource costs. Using SWE-agent with three backbone models, we evaluate 1,350 trajectories on 90 Python, C++, and Java bug-fix tasks, comparing unassisted execution with four assistance strategies. Substantive responses follow 61.6-90.9% of valid triggers for tool-use detours. Concise reminders achieve the highest observed aggregate substantive-response rate; more elaborate assistance offers symptom-dependent benefits and can be less effective. Aggregate repair outcomes remain close to baseline, with token savings in selected settings. These findings support proactive runtime assistance for autonomous tool use. The gap between behavioral adjustment and aggregate repair gains calls for careful decisions on intervention timing and assistance strategy in autonomous agents.

papers.title: HospitalBench: Diagnosing Where and Why Embodied Agents Fail on Long Hospital Task Chains
papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.

papers.title: B-OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs
papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has recently attracted interest because it provides dense teacher guidance without a separate, often larger teacher model. However, OPSD conditions its teacher on ground-truth solutions, which limits its use when such solutions are unavailable. We propose On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs (B-OPSD). Using a prompt template, the initial model or a saved student checkpoint generates a problem brief from the question alone. The prompt asks for relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls, but not a final answer or a complete solution. A frozen teacher uses the brief as privileged context to guide the current student's on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching. B-OPSD uses no ground-truth solutions during training. Results on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 show that both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD at each of three Qwen3 model sizes. Code is available at https://github.com/ZevineXu/B-OPSD

papers.title: Distributed Shaping of Robot Swarms Through Spatial Moments of Arbitrary Order
papers.abstract: This paper shapes a swarm into a target pattern, such as a figure taken from an image, by controlling its spatial moments. The image is sampled into a reference configuration whose centroid and covariance set the position and principal spreads of the formation, while its higher-order moments, expressed in covariance-normalized (whitened) coordinates, encode the remaining shape. In contrast with geometric formation control, which prescribes distances, bearings, or relative positions between specific agents, this specification concerns the swarm as a whole and assigns no agent to a particular place. The key mechanism is orthogonalization in the swarm's own empirical inner product: projecting negative-gradient velocities onto the complement of low-degree polynomials sampled at the agents makes every higher-order correction preserve all lower-order moments exactly. The resulting hierarchical controller has lower triangular error dynamics and converges locally exponentially for any positive gains, so orders can be added without undoing those already achieved. A joint alternative regulates the higher moments together through a regularized Gauss--Newton step while preserving the centroid and covariance dynamics. We give bounds on the number of agents and sufficient conditions for regularity. Both controllers admit a distributed implementation that uses only relative positions and neighbor communication and retains local exponential convergence when estimation is sufficiently fast. In a distributed simulation on a sparse graph, 350 agents form an airplane from an unstructured swarm through moments up to order ten; the hierarchy reaches the full specification, while the joint law approaches it with smaller velocities.

papers.title: DLR variational principle for the one-dimensional log-gas and another proof of existence of Sine-beta
papers.abstract: We show that every stationary solution of the Dobrushin--Lanford--Ruelle (DLR) equations for the one-dimensional log-gas with a quantitative control on its number variance minimizes the free energy functional. This yields a DLR variational principle for this continuous long-range system. Moreover, we show that any limit point of the finite-volume log-gases is stationary and satisfies this condition. This allows us to give a new, physical proof of the existence of a microscopic limit for the Gaussian Beta Ensembles, known as the Sine-beta point process.

papers.title: Arginine metabolism drives tumor immune escape by shaping an immunosuppressive microenvironment
papers.abstract: The tumor microenvironment evolves through the ``elimination-equilibrium-escape'' paradigm, yet the quantitative mechanisms by which metabolic reprogramming contributes to immune evasion remain unclear. We develop a mathematical model of tumor-immune interactions to investigate how arginine metabolism shapes an immunosuppressive microenvironment. We establish the positivity and boundedness of solutions and analyze the existence and stability of equilibrium states. The model is calibrated using tumor growth data from three mouse cohorts and reproduces tumor growth patterns under distinct immune conditions. The calibrated model predicts faster tumor growth in immunocompetent mice than in immunodeficient controls, with macrophage dynamics accounting for this difference. It further predicts that arginine administration promotes tumor progression by enhancing macrophage polarization and weakening T cell-mediated tumor control. To account for interindividual heterogeneity, we develop the TVInfABC algorithm to generate a virtual mouse cohort. Moreover, our analysis indicates that tumor-associated macrophages can promote transitions from immunologically ``hot'' to ``cold'' states. Systematic pharmacodynamic simulations further uncover a synergy between arginine depletion (anti-ARG1) and immune checkpoint blockade (anti-PD-1/PD-L1). These results provide a mathematical basis for studying metabolic-immune interactions and for evaluating mechanism-based combination therapies.

papers.title: Entropy-Based and Quadratic Conditional Innovation Metrics for Informed Dynamic Scheduling of Belief-Propagation Decoding for LDPC Codes
papers.abstract: We propose two enhanced conditional innovation (CI) metrics for informed dynamic scheduling (IDS) in belief-propagation (BP) decoding of LDPC codes. The CI-based residual BP (CIRBP) algorithm uses the CI metric to guide the selection of the variable node (VN) to be updated and has been shown to outperform several existing IDS-based BP decoders, especially at the early decoding stage. However, the original CI metric uses only the absolute difference between the current and precomputed posterior probabilities and does not separately account for the reliability associated with each probability. By reformulating the CI metric relative to the decision boundary, we separate each posterior probability into its decision side and a linear-distance term reflecting reliability. Replacing the latter with the binary entropy complement yields the proposed entropy-based CI (E-CI) metric. Moreover, the proposed quadratic CI (Q-CI) metric is derived from the leading quadratic term in the local expansion of the entropy complement, avoiding the logarithmic operations required for direct E-CI evaluation. We apply both proposed metrics to the CIRBP decoder and its node-wise variant. Numerical results show that the proposed metrics generally provide lower frame error rates than the original CI metric, with their relative advantages depending on the code and decoding procedure.

papers.title: Multidimensional mixed Bohr radii for Banach space valued holomorphic functions
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce and study a generalized notion of multidimensional mixed Bohr radii for holomorphic functions defined on the unit ball of the finite-dimensional Minkowski sequence space with values in complex Banach spaces. We first prove that the multidimensional mixed Bohr radius is positive for every non-null bounded linear operator whose norm is sufficiently small relative to the scaling parameter. We then determine the exact asymptotic behavior of the multidimensional mixed Bohr radius for infinite-dimensional Banach spaces of finite cotype and we obtain analogous bounds for spaces without finite cotype. Finally, for concave Banach lattices and summing operators, we prove lower bounds that involve a logarithmic factor. These results connect classical scalar Bohr phenomena with operator-valued and Banach space valued settings, and highlight how the geometry of the spaces and the mapping properties of the operator influence coefficient estimates and their dependence on dimension. Several examples illustrate the consistency of our results with the classical Bohr radius and the sharp Defant--Frerick asymptotics.

papers.title: Small Harnesses, Default Checks, Limited Coverage: Bounded Model Checking in Practice
papers.abstract: The growing use of AI to generate software and verification artifacts has increased the need for automated systems that provide reliable software assurance. Bounded model checking (BMC) offers a practical foundation for such systems by automatically checking correctness and security properties directly on software. However, effective verification requires choices about properties, input assumptions, function models, and execution bounds that influence the guarantees obtained. Little systematic evidence exists on how practitioners make these choices, limiting the empirical foundation for developing automated verification systems. We present an empirical study of BMC practices in open-source C and Rust projects using CBMC and Kani. Through LLM-assisted open coding, static analysis, and artifact execution, we characterize verification properties, artifact complexity, and verification outcomes. Our findings reveal diverse verification objectives and generally small harnesses, but also property-specification errors and extensive use of execution bounds and environment models. Most artifacts complete verification quickly and achieve high coverage within their scope, while repository-level coverage decreases with project size. Our findings and annotated dataset provide empirical baselines for verification automation and motivate improved techniques for property validation, harness generation, and scaling verification breadth.

papers.title: Lipschitz bounds and gradient continuity for the Trudinger equation
papers.abstract: We establish local spatial Lipschitz and gradient Hölder estimates for general nonnegative weak solutions to Trudinger's equation $\partial_t u^{p-1}=Δ_pu$, $p>1$. The estimates are uniform across the zero set. The proofs combine Bernstein-type estimates for power transformations, smooth approximation, and comparison with exponential barriers near the zero set.

papers.title: Quantum Dynamics of Dynamics
papers.abstract: Quantum channels (in discrete time) and Gorini--Kossakowski--Sudarshan--Lindblad (GKSL) master equations (in continuous time) are the central tools of open quantum systems, but they rest on memoryless approximations (Born, Markov, secular) that fail in many physically relevant settings, most notably non-Markovian dynamics. There, tracking the state alone is insufficient: interventions at intermediate times disturb the environment, so multi-time correlations carry physical information that the state evolution cannot capture. The framework of higher-order quantum operations addresses this by treating controllable operations as \textit{inputs} to a process that maps operations to operations, so that the primitive object is a quantum \textit{dynamics} rather than a quantum \textit{state}. Here, we derive the most general continuous-time, CP-divisible evolution of such an object, the \textit{quantum comb master equation} (QCME), which governs the quantum ``dynamics of dynamics''. Its GKSL-like generator includes encoder--decoder correlation terms coupling distinct temporal interventions. A generalized Born--Markov coarse-graining derivation identifies microscopic conditions for this structure. The QCME yields time-local evolution equations for two-time correlators beyond reduced-state dynamics and extends to more times. We show correlations between Schr"odinger- and Heisenberg-picture evolutions inaccessible to independent GKSL equations, describe quantum-channel evolution motivated by process tomography, and obtain time-local equations for linear response functions and OTOCs under environmental influences.

papers.title: Read Boundaries in Agent Memory: Consistency, Completeness, and Repair
papers.abstract: Agent-memory services assemble evidence through several reads across connections or stores. An update between those reads can pair an assertion with source content from another revision. We protect the complete recall, including enrichment and materialization, and evaluate the resulting evidence and service behavior in Hindsight and Cognee. A 600-run Cognee study compares unprotected recall, a repeated recall, a read/write lock, and optimistic epoch validation under default incremental updates and full rebuilds. At approximately 20 recalls/s, unprotected default updates yield 199 conflicting responses among 12,010 scheduled recalls with spaced writes and 284 among 12,010 with bursts. The lock and epoch validation each deliver complete, compatible evidence for all 24,020 default-update recalls. With default bursts, epoch validation reduces update p95 by 109 ms while adding 290 ms to recall p95 relative to the lock. A separate 160-run incremental-failure study distinguishes mixed revisions from complete new derived content whose canonical source record remains old. Both protected policies refuse service after failure; the first default retry restores all 80 fault runs through native full-rebuild fallback. In Hindsight, a shared PostgreSQL snapshot removes the mismatch in ten controlled pairs, with recall p95 rising from 19 ms to 29 ms. These results identify the read boundary needed for coherent evidence and the publication and recovery conditions governing service after an update fails.

papers.title: Femtosecond Free-Space Time-Frequency Transfer at km/s Relative Motion with Doppler Compensation
papers.abstract: A global optical clock network holds great promise for a wide range of applications, including international metrology--particularly the redefinition of the ``second''--as well as navigation, geoscience, and fundamental physics. Satellite-based high-precision time-frequency dissemination is essential for realizing such a network. Despite remarkable progress in ground-based free-space simulations over high-loss channels, the Doppler effect arising from satellite motion has remained an unsolved barrier. Here we demonstrate femtosecond two-way time-frequency transfer over a 113-km free-space link under simulated Doppler shifts of up to 1.55 km/s. To overcome the Doppler barrier, we first reproduce satellite-like Doppler shifts of up to 1.55 km/s on the ground by locking a frequency comb to a broadly tunable laser. We then correct the resulting disturbances with two complementary techniques: a dual-channel sampling architecture that compensates for optical dispersion and radio frequency (RF) nonlinearity while eliminating Nyquist dead zones, and an iterative interferogram reconstruction algorithm that removes Doppler-induced distortion. After correction, residual systematic errors are within $\pm10$ fs over the full 1.55 km/s range. Using simulated medium earth orbit (MEO) and geosynchronous orbit (GSO) satellite trajectories, we achieve fractional frequency instability of $3.9\times10^{-19}$ at 4,600 s and $3.6\times10^{-19}$ at 23,600 s, respectively. This extends the operational velocity range by nearly two orders of magnitude beyond previous free-space demonstrations, removing the last major technical barrier to a global femtosecond-precision satellite-based time-frequency link.

papers.title: Half-factorial generating sets and the realization of Dedekind class groups
papers.abstract: We prove a cardinality obstruction to realizing an abelian group as the ideal class group of a half-factorial Dedekind domain. If an abelian $p$-group $P$ satisfies $\bigcap_{r\ge1}p^rP=0$ and admits a half-factorial generating subset, then $|P|\le\max\{\aleph_0,|P/pP|\}$. The proof separates generators of equal order by finite quotients. Its group-theoretic ingredient is a direct summand generated by selected members of an arbitrary finite generating set. The torsion subgroup of $\prod_{j\ge1}\mathbb{Z}/p^j\mathbb{Z}$ is uncountable and $p$-adically separated, but has countable quotient modulo $p$; hence it has no half-factorial generating subset. This gives a negative answer to the universal half-factorial Dedekind realization problem for every prime. Pure subgroups give counterexamples of every uncountable cardinality at most the continuum, so the least cardinality of a counterexample is $\aleph_1$. We also study free-kernel lifting, order-preserving lifts across torsion kernels, character-compatible generators, and the failure of compatibility under unions and contraction. These results distinguish global realizability from half-factoriality on bounded subgroups and from integrality of cross numbers.

papers.title: dit.xpu : Taming DiT Sparse Inference on Mobile SoCs
papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) enable on-device image generation and editing but incur high attention costs at high resolutions. Existing sparse attention reduces computation, yet dynamic sparsity introduces preprocessing and irregular data accesses that poorly fit mobile NPUs. We present DiT.XPU, a sparse DiT inference framework for heterogeneous mobile SoCs. DiT.XPU combines tile-aligned sparse attention with anchor-based error compensation by exploiting slowly varying dense-sparse output residuals across denoising steps. Heterogeneous XPU collaboration overlaps NPU dense attention with GPU sparse calibration, while mask-guided dataflow reduces data transfers and layout conversion by overlapping data movement with computation. Across five DiT models on two Snapdragon smartphones, DiT.XPU achieves up to 1.56x end-to-end denoising speedup over the Hexagon-NPU backend and 11.5x attention-kernel speedup over the fastest alternative, while preserving generation quality close to dense attention. Code is available at https://github.com/IF-LAB-PKU/dit.xpu.

papers.title: Auditory-Feedback-Conditioned Flow TTS for Implicit Lombard Adaptation
papers.abstract: Conventional text-to-speech (TTS) systems can lose intelligibility in noise environments because they cannot adapt to environmental changes. However, humans tend to increase their vocal efforts in noisy environments, a phenomenon known as the Lombard effect. Building on an auditory-feedback Lombard TTS, we investigate whether a pretrained Flow-based TTS can learn acoustic adaptation directly from auditory feedback without explicit prosodic control. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) feedback and automatic speech recognition (ASR) feedback are extracted from the noise-corrupted waveforms and injected into the Flow-matching condition for utterance refinement and causal block-level updates. We assess feedback benefits across prompting and noise conditions using plain/Lombard prompting, prompt-switching controls, and paired-finetuning. Experiments show that while finetuning provides strong robustness under in-domain conditions, auditory feedback yields additional cue-dependent benefits that generalize to unseen noise. Moreover, stronger power/F0 tracking alone does not guarantee better speech intelligibility or quality.

papers.title: Thermal-energy relaxation in chiral quantum Hall edge mode
papers.abstract: We study the nonequilibrium state generated by a real Ohmic contact (ROC) in the charge-fractionalization regime. We then investigate its thermal-energy relaxation along a quantum Hall edge mediated by a fictitious Ohmic contact (FOC) with large capacitance and perfect coupling to the edge. For cold Ohmic contacts, the electron distribution function and current noise are fully described by their equilibrium forms and the corresponding Fermi-Dirac distribution. In contrast, in the case of hot Ohmic contacts, strong thermalization effects do not drive the outgoing state into complete equilibrium. Both the distribution function and the noise retain signatures of the initial nonequilibrium state and therefore cannot be characterized solely by the effective contact temperature, contrary to common assumptions.

papers.title: Brunn-Minkowski inequalities for Riesz capacity in all dimensions
papers.abstract: We prove the Brunn--Minkowski inequality for Riesz $p$-capacity on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ when $n-1<p<n$, extending the known endpoint $p=n-1$. For sets of positive capacity, equality holds if and only if they are convex and positively homothetic. The inequality remains conjectural for $n-2<p<n-1$, when $n\ge2$. Known isodiametric counterexamples rule out a general extension to negative $p$, even for convex planar sets.

papers.title: A unified cross-scale framework for the dynamic Waddington landscape
papers.abstract: The Waddington epigenetic landscape is a foundational concept in developmental biology, yet its quantitative formulations remain largely disconnected from the population dynamics that originally motivated the metaphor. Existing approaches typically describe either intracellular gene-regulatory dynamics or population-level cell kinetics, but rarely both within a unified framework. Here, we develop a unified PDE-integral framework that couples stochastic gene-regulatory dynamics with probability-conserving population renewal, yielding a dynamic Waddington landscape $U(\vec{x}, t) = -\log f(\vec{x}, t)$ defined directly from the evolving epigenetic probability density $f(\vec{x}, t)$. Rigorous mathematical analysis of this framework establishes its well-posedness and provides conditions for the existence and uniqueness of stationary solutions. Application to canonical gene regulatory circuits shows that proliferation is not merely a determinant of population size, but an active regulator of landscape topology. Population renewal reshapes attractor stability and transition barriers in a circuit-dependent manner, generating transient plasticity in some regulatory architectures while stabilizing progenitor states in others. Under highly proliferative conditions, these interactions further produce oscillatory ``breathing'' landscapes. Together, these results establish population renewal as an integral component of cell-fate regulation and extend the Waddington landscape from a static description of intracellular dynamics to a predictive multiscale framework linking gene regulation, cell-state dynamics, and tissue homeostasis.

papers.title: Independent Sets in $C_4$-Free Planar Graphs: Sharp Claw-Free Bounds and Structural Reductions
papers.abstract: For every claw-free $C_4$-free planar graph, we prove the sharp weighted bound $α_w(G)\ge (10/31)\sum_v w(v)$, equivalently $χ_f(G)\le31/10$. The proof uses a line-graph representation and the matching polytope; the exceptional small roots are excluded analytically by planar duality and degree-four neighborhood analysis in triangulations. We also prove that, in every $2$-connected $C_4$-free graph of minimum degree at least four, an independent selection of claw centers leaves a compatible subgraph of noncenters with fractional chromatic number at most three; planarity is not required. We apply these results to the conjecture $α(G)\ge5|V(G)|/16$. A minimum-order counterexample without degree-three vertices has at least forty-nine vertices. When all degree-three components of a minimum counterexample are triangle trees, we derive exact boundary states and a joint matching formula. We identify the remaining deficiency estimate and the additional component types that must be addressed to extend this approach. The general conjecture remains open.

papers.title: Many faces of integer semidefinite programming
papers.abstract: We first establish several properties of integer positive semidefinite matrices, extending known results for binary and ternary positive semidefinite matrices. We then show how to reformulate an integer quadratic program (IQP) as an equivalent integer semidefinite program (ISDP). We distinguish three cases, namely IQPs with two, three, or more than three distinct integer values, and provide several ISDPs for each case. Each reformulation yields either a binary ISDP, a ternary ISDP, or a rescaled version of one of these. The results show that ternary SDP formulations for problems with three distinct integer values provide SDP relaxations with fewer constraints and, in the case of equally spaced integers, also smaller matrix variables than binary-based SDP relaxations. For quadratic problems whose variables can take more than three distinct integer values, one can choose among three formulations based on the size of their matrix variables, the number of constraints, and the strength of the resulting SDP relaxations. We also show how to reformulate a mixed-integer QP as a mixed-integer SDP.

papers.title: Bringing coherent closer to compute: coherent-lite multidimensional on-chip interconnect beyond 100 terabits per second
papers.abstract: The continued scaling of artificial intelligence (AI) demands optical interconnects that deliver higher bandwidth density within stringent electrical-bandwidth and energy budgets. Coherent optics offers a route beyond the per-lane bandwidth constraints of intensity-modulation direct-detection links, yet its receiver complexity and power overhead have largely confined its use to longer reaches. Here we bring coherent optics closer to compute by demonstrating a coherent-lite multidimensional on-chip interconnect that combines wavelength- and mode-division multiplexing with self-homodyne detection. The architecture co-transmits the local oscillator (LO) and parallel data channels within a single silicon waveguide, using polarization-division routing to preserve LO purity and support high-order modulation. Based on this principle, we develop an inverse-designed dual-polarization mode multiplexer that provides over 37 dB inter-polarization isolation across the C band in an $8 \times 6~μ$m$^2$ footprint, enabling millimetre-scale on-chip multimode routing. Without power-intensive digital carrier recovery, the architecture delivers a single-wavelength line rate of 2 Tb s$^{-1}$ and scales to an aggregate line rate of 103.96 Tb s$^{-1}$ across four modes and 100 wavelengths, using formats up to 64-ary quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM). These results extend on-chip coherent interconnects into the hundred-terabit-per-second regime, offering a scalable route to bandwidth-dense optical connectivity for next-generation computing systems.

papers.title: KaleidoKV: Rearranging Evidence for Efficient KV Cache Reuse in Offline RAG Inference
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) augments large language models (LLMs) on question-answering (QA) tasks with retrieved evidence at inference time. Related questions in an offline batch often retrieve overlapping evidence, but prefix caching reuses key-value (KV) states only for identical token prefixes, making reuse dependent on evidence order. Although all questions and evidence are known before execution, existing reordering methods commit to early grouping decisions and can miss sharing opportunities that require several requests to move together. Evaluating alternative layouts can incur planning costs that offset inference savings, while concurrent requests may still recompute shared prefixes before their KV states become available. To address these challenges, we propose KaleidoKV, a framework that plans evidence orders across the batch and controls when requests enter the engine while preserving each request's evidence set and content. Joint layout planning revises formed groups through coordinated request moves and keeps a move only if it lowers planned prefill, the computation required when each shared prefix is computed once. A global prefix index selects evidence orders by locating reusable prefixes and evaluates each move incrementally from only the affected request paths. Prefix-ready admission tracks nested prefix dependencies, delaying requests whose shared prefixes are still being computed while allowing independent requests to proceed. Experiments on four QA workloads and four LLMs show that KaleidoKV achieves the highest throughput and lowest mean time to first token in all 16 settings, with approximately 1.24-1.75x the throughput of the strongest baseline, including planning time. With Llama-3.1-8B under the default configuration, actual prefill stays within 0.5% of planned prefill across all four workloads.

papers.title: Exploration as Feedback in Model Predictive Path Integral Control
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how exploration affects closed-loop stability in model predictive path integral (MPPI) control. With a warm start, MPPI optimizes a control sequence by sampling candidates around the previous solution, and their covariance, the exploration covariance, is typically tuned to balance solution quality and computational cost. Small exploration is attractive because most samples then contribute to the solution, and existing stability analyses treat reduced exploration only as a bias toward the previous solution. Whether insufficient exploration can destabilize the closed loop has therefore remained open. We show that, for linear quadratic (LQ) problems with infinitely many samples, the exploration covariance also determines the feedback gain, i.e., how strongly MPPI updates the previous solution in response to the current state. With small exploration at a fixed temperature, MPPI nearly repeats the previous solution and fails to stabilize an exponentially unstable plant. Because a single covariance governs both exploration and feedback, stability and sample efficiency are in structural conflict: stabilization requires large exploration, which leaves few samples that contribute to the solution. To resolve this conflict, we propose Stabilizing Subspace MPPI (SS-MPPI), which computes the control inputs required for stabilization and samples only the rest. For LQ problems, SS-MPPI remains stable with small exploration and is thus sample-efficient. Simulations of an inverted pendulum and a quadruped robot confirm the analysis, showing that MPPI fails under small exploration, whereas SS-MPPI remains stable even with few samples.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning for Nonstationary Robot Dynamics
papers.abstract: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.

papers.title: Learning Graph-Conditioned Predictors in Weight Space
papers.abstract: The same node attributes can imply different labels in different structural contexts. Yet fast graphless models typically treat topology as additional evidence supplied to a globally shared predictor. This assumes that structure augments the available information, rather than determining how node attributes should be interpreted. We introduce SCOPE (Structure-COnditioned PrEdictor), in which a small generator maps each node's cached structural fingerprint to coefficients over a shared low-rank basis, producing a context-specific update to a global weight matrix. The base predictor, basis, and generator remain shared across all nodes, while the resulting transformation adapts how attributes are processed in each relational environment. Once fingerprints are cached, inference requires only a forward pass and no online message passing. This design combines context-specific specialization with global parameter sharing, compact low-rank adaptation, and message-passing-free inference. On two large OGB node-classification graphs, conditioning the weights with raw positional signals yields clear gains over supplying the same signals through input concatenation. Further results under a structure-transductive held-out-node protocol and in teacher-free graph classification show that the mechanism extends beyond a particular distillation setting. These findings establish graph structure not only as predictive evidence, but as context that determines the predictor used to interpret that evidence.

papers.title: Classification problems for diassociative and dendriform algebras: a survey
papers.abstract: Diassociative algebras (associative dialgebras) and dendriform algebras are vector spaces with two binary operations, introduced by J.-L. Loday in the study of Leibniz algebras; their operads are Koszul dual to each other. We survey the classification problem for these two classes, including the Zinbiel algebras, the commutative dendriform algebras, which are Koszul dual to Leibniz algebras.
