Building on this analysis, we rethink four aspects of authorization: plan selection shapes permission requirements; contextual information can inform decisions without itself granting authority; restrictions must retain their meaning across system interfaces; and authorization must be reassessed as workflows evolve. These insights motivate open challenges and future directions for mechanism design and benchmark construction. In particular, evaluation should examine both observed agent behavior and the unauthorized effects that remain enabled. Our analysis connects existing mechanisms to the requirements for preserving authorization throughout an agent workflow.

papers.title: APOLLO-Timing: Annealed Phase - Orbit Lattice Linking across Observations for Binary Pulsar Timing
papers.abstract: Sparse observations of binary pulsars can leave the orbit and the pulse count across observing gaps uncertain. We present APOLLO-Timing, a Bayesian phase-orbit lattice method that fits timing parameters together with integer pulse offsets between observing sessions. To validate candidate phase connections, we refit the timing model at fixed pulse numbers using the Python pulsar timing package PINT. We demonstrate the method on PSR J1912-1215, discovered in the CRAFTS survey. A preliminary Keplerian fit to variations in the apparent spin period and its derivative did not phase-connect 96 times of arrival (TOAs) spanning 1438.07 days in 23 sessions. Starting from its position, spin frequency $F_0$, and first time derivative $F_1$ estimated in that fit, with dispersion measure fixed, APOLLO-Timing recovers the orbit and a unique best-supported phase-connected solution without supplied orbital parameters. A repeat full-data blind search recovers the same pulse counts in 914.0 s, including the final fit. Setting the initial $F_1$ to zero in the 17-, 18-, and 19-session subsets also recovers the reference path. The solution gives $P_b=17.526$ days, $x=23.448$ light-seconds, $e=2.65\times10^{-5}$, $χ^2=188.01$, and a weighted rms residual of $5.08\,μ\mathrm{s}$. For a pulsar mass of $1.4\,M_\odot$ and inclination of $60^\circ$, the inferred companion mass is $0.67\,M_\odot$, favoring a CO/ONeMg white dwarf.

papers.title: How many sorted projections determine any n points in k dimensions?
papers.abstract: Let $d_1,\dots,d_m$ be directions in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ge 2$. A multiset $X$ of $n$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ projects to the $m$ multisets of numbers $\{\{x\cdot d_j : x\in X\}\}$, or equivalently to the $m$ sorted lists of these numbers. How many directions are needed for these projections to determine every multiset of $n$ points? Two simple bounds are known in every dimension: more than $(k-1)\log_2 n$ directions are always needed, and $(k-1)n+1$ directions in general position always suffice. In the plane much more is known: Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron showed that almost every choice of $O(\log n \log\log n)$ directions suffices. Whether anything similar holds in higher dimensions was left open by Dym, Wellershoff, Tsoukanis, Levy and Balan. We observe that two lemmas of Hair and Sahai, proved for list recovery of random linear codes, answer that question, and by tightening their argument we show that in every dimension almost every choice of $(4k-2)\ln(2n)\ln(k\log_2 2n)+k+1$ directions suffices. For $k\le 10$ this beats the linear bound once $n$ is larger than about 100: for example, 144 directions suffice for multisets of 1000 points in the plane, and an exact computation lowers this to 133. Letting some of the random blocks in their argument fail removes a factor $\log k$: almost every choice of $O(k\log n\log\log n)$ directions suffices, uniformly in $k$ and $n$. We also show that $2k-1$ directions never determine three points, so that the logarithmic lower bound is not tight; that every $m$ directions in the plane fail on some pair of multisets of size $O(1.65^m)$, improving the bound $O(1.80^m)$ of Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron; and that for each $k$, $m$ and $n$, either almost every choice of $m$ directions works or almost none does.

papers.title: Local Whittle estimation for distributional time series: A regularization framework in Bayes Hilbert space
papers.abstract: We study local Whittle estimation of long memory in density-valued time series in Bayes Hilbert space. The centered log-ratio (clr) transformation maps densities to a linear Hilbert space, allowing analysis using standard Hilbert space methods. When densities are reconstructed from finite samples, however, small absolute estimation errors can remain large relative to the true density in low-density tails. Taking logarithms can amplify this noise and introduce systematic distortions that affect memory estimation. We develop a framework for regularizing estimated densities before transformation to improve finite-sample performance while preserving the latent memory target. Using the clr representation, we apply local Whittle estimation to principal component scores along an estimated leading direction of the long-run covariance operator. The framework is based on local Whittle admissibility, defined by uniform asymptotic equivalence between the feasible and latent-score criteria. We separate density-estimation error from the population perturbation induced by regularization and give sufficient admissibility conditions based on density-estimation rates and the temporal dependence of the error components. Under suitable regularity assumptions, these conditions yield consistency for the latent memory parameter. We study additional tail smoothing, a vanishing density floor, and their combination. Monte Carlo experiments show that these procedures can reduce finite-sample bias relative to unregularized kernel density reconstruction. An application to daily distributions of intraday EUR/USD exchange rate returns illustrates the methodology.

papers.title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
papers.abstract: Dantzig--Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying constraint families, and each candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, as in classical lot-sizing, network-design, and facility-location formulations. We prove that when an evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, methods that observe only bounds need of order $k^w$ evaluations to find a hidden group of $w$ families in the worst case. A prediction missing $e$ members reduces this to $Θ(k^e)$ through a staged search that need not know $e$. The orders extend to several groups, prices, and growing evaluation costs. We study two predictors: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, which vanishes on groups whose families share no variable, and language models reading the model, verified by the staged search in JointDW. Such groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and in all 59 benchmark instances. Given the coefficients of constructed models with up to 16 families, one language model names a true group first in 249 of 252 answers. On the benchmark instances, decompositions chosen by language models from the text solve faster than those of GCG's detector.

papers.title: A General Theory of Dynamic Mechanism Design: Joint Optimization of Contracting, Information-Production Technology, and Disclosure
papers.abstract: We develop a general theory of dynamic mechanism design that jointly optimizes contracting, information-production technology, and disclosure across a broad class of economic environments with general allocation constraints. Hidden actions, endogenous information acquisition, learning, and disclosure interact through dynamic incentives. We accommodate correlated private information, interdependent preferences, and potentially infinite-dimensional allocations. We introduce joint perfect Bayesian equilibrium, establish the Dynamic Revelation Principle, and recursively characterize incentive compatibility. Under private values with informational interdependence, we characterize joint incentives through choice obedience, reporting-envelope first-order conditions, and global integral monotonicity. We derive an exact dynamic information-rent identity, dynamic revenue equivalence, and dynamic virtual surplus. Comparing first-best, two second-best, and third-best contracts distinguishes information rents, hidden-action implementation costs, and direct information-production expenditures, revealing nonadditive interactions of either sign and branched outcomes. Applications show Milgrom-Weber revenue-ranking reversal with endogenous acquisition, no efficient first-price equilibrium under Gaussian signals, and absent, interior, or full financial-contract disclosure.

papers.title: Toward an Optimal Configuration for Tree Species Classification from Bark Images: A Leakage-Safe Ablation Study
papers.abstract: Identifying tree species from bark photographs matters for forest inventory and the wood-processing industry, yet the design choices behind deep-learning approaches have not been studied systematically, and some reported results may be inflated by images of the same trunk appearing in both training and test sets. We present a systematic ablation on BarkNet 1.0 (20 species) under a tree-level, leakage-safe five-fold cross-validation, using ConvNeXt-V2 backbones with attention-based multiple instance learning (AMIL). We vary patch size, aggregation strategy, training regime, backbone capacity, the whole-image baseline, and test-time bag size, and we measure leakage directly with a matched image-level split. Per-patch accuracy rises with patch size (75.2% at 160 px to 89.3% at 512 px), and image-level accuracy plateaus near 94.9% at 512 px. AMIL exceeds majority voting by at most 0.7 pp; soft voting and mean pooling do no better than hard voting, so the gain comes from the learned attention weights and vanishes at 512 px, where attention is near-uniform. Backbone capacity changes accuracy by less than a point, and two-stage training gives no advantage. Whole-image classification (91.9%) trails patch aggregation, and accuracy saturates around 64 patches per image. Under an image-level split, the same configuration reaches 99.9% (+5.0 pp) and the whole-image baseline 99.2% (+7.3 pp), an inflation as large as the entire effect of patch size that also erases the differences between design choices. We recommend patches as large as possible while leaving enough to aggregate (about 512 px here), a nano backbone, and tree-level splits for bark benchmarks.

papers.title: Search for the 229Pa Parity Doublet via Internal-Conversion Spectroscopy at FRIB
papers.abstract: The radioisotope $^{229}$Pa is predicted to possess a nearly degenerate ground-state parity doublet. Previous $γ$-ray and conversion-electron spectroscopy suggests a splitting of $ΔE = (60\pm 50)~\mathrm{eV}$, although the doublet's existence remains unconfirmed. Such a small splitting would give $^{229}$Pa an exceptionally large enhancement of symmetry-violating nuclear properties. However, the splitting, and with it the sensitivity of $^{229}$Pa to CP-violating physics, remains uncertain by orders of magnitude. We propose an experiment to measure this splitting with sub-eV precision within a few days of measurement time by using delayed-coincidence internal-conversion spectroscopy of $^{229}$Pa ions produced by the electron-capture decay of $^{229}$U$^{+}$ ions stored in a Penning trap at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams (FRIB). This measurement would provide the key nuclear-structure input needed to establish $^{229}$Pa as a leading candidate for next-generation atomic and molecular electric-dipole-moment (EDM) experiments.

papers.title: Kerr metric perturbations in Lorenz gauge via numerical relativity methods
papers.abstract: Gravitational self-force calculations are needed to accurately describe the motion of a small body in a spinning (Kerr) black hole spacetime, which is vital to predict gravitational wave signals from asymmetric-mass compact binaries. Accurate calculations for the upcoming LISA mission require a minimum of second perturbative order in the mass ratio, which has thus far only been achieved for nonspinning (Schwarzschild) black holes due to nonlinear complexities of the Einstein equations. In this work, we calculate Kerr metric perturbations with a new computational approach based on numerical relativity methods, extending recent scalar self-force results to full general relativity. We formulate the perturbative Lorenz-gauge Einstein equations in terms of azimuthal $m$-modes in the frequency domain and solve the resulting elliptic partial differential equations using a spectral discontinuous Galerkin discretization, adaptive mesh refinement, and preconditioned iterative solvers. With our new method, we achieve exponentially convergent first-order gravitational self-force calculations for circular equatorial orbits in Kerr spacetime up to spin $|a|/M=0.998$ (the Thorne limit). Our framework is designed to carry over to second order by delivering accurate and well-behaved first-order data for nonlinear source construction, and as a solver for the second-order metric perturbations themselves.

papers.title: Ensembles of Random Partition-Based Models under Covariate Shift
papers.abstract: Distribution shifts, including covariate shifts, are ubiquitous in real-world applications of machine learning. Empirical evidence suggests that, across a variety of models with and without downstream adaptation, ensembles tend to be more robust to covariate shift than single models. We extend the theory of covariate shift severity from single models to ensembles, providing theoretical justification for the empirical trends. We introduce new discrepancy measures of covariate shift severity to control the risk of partition-based kernel estimators. We then show that with sufficient ensemble size, these models can achieve minimax-optimal risk convergence rates under covariate shift. Our results suggest that modelers can expect to need larger ensemble sizes for more severe covariate shifts.

papers.title: Geometric Obstructions and Sharp Genus Dependence in LCD Scalings
papers.abstract: We study the least pole order of a rational function whose nonzero evaluations scale a prescribed code to a Euclidean LCD code. A residue-one differential yields an obstruction for odd-dimensional one-point AG codes in characteristic two: for $C=C_L(D,aQ)$ with $0\le a<n$ and odd dimension, the threshold is at least $n+2g-a-1$. The obstruction uses alternating Gram matrices and does not require the scaled code to be self-orthogonal. For the dimension-three codes $C_L(D,(r+1)Q)$ on Hermitian curves over $\F_{r^2}$, $r=2^e\ge4$, we obtain \[ n+2g-r-2\leτ_D(C;Q)\le n+2g-3. \] Consequently the leading genus contribution is asymptotically sharp even in dimension three. On the elliptic curve $y^2+y=x^3$ over $\F_4$, we prove the exact dimension-three threshold $6$ by an explicit multiplier. For repetition codes on the Hermitian family, the threshold equals the general interpolation bound $n+2g-1$. The upper bounds use information sets and hold for $q>3k$, and for $q>2k$ in characteristic two.

papers.title: Solar extreme-ultraviolet waves and other associated solar activities
papers.abstract: Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) waves are large-scale, tsunami like disturbances on the solar surface associated with eruptive phenomena such as solar flares, filament eruptions, and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). Because their strong correlation with major solar eruptions, we present here a comprehensive statistical study of EUV waves and their connections to Moreton waves, CMEs, solar flares, type II radio bursts, and solar energetic particle (SEP) events during Solar Cycle 25 (December 2019-December 2025). This study utilizes EUV data from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly onboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory and coronagraph data from the Large Angle and Spectrometric Coronagraph onboard Solar and Heliospheric Observatory. Our analysis reveals that 12.3% of the observed EUV waves are associated with Moreton waves, 95% with CMEs, 92.7% associated with flares, 44.3% with metric type II radio bursts, and 11.8% with SEPs. While nearly all EUV waves are linked to CMEs, their association with solar flares varies significantly, ranging from weak B-class events to major X-class flares. Furthermore, the majority of Moreton waves correlate with large- or medium-class flares, with only a small fraction associated with weaker C-class flares. Our findings may contribute to a better understanding of space weather events and, potentially, to their forecasting.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Finite-Sum Nonconvex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization with Exact Proximal Oracles
papers.abstract: Finite-sum nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax problems arise in adversarial training and distributionally robust learning. Known lower bounds for these problems cover only linear-span algorithms, zero-respecting algorithms, or a restricted proximal protocol. This leaves open whether unrestricted adaptivity or exact component proximal steps, which return global saddle points of regularized component problems, can improve the polynomial complexity. We show that they cannot. Consider $n\ge2$ components with joint mean-squared smoothness $L$ and condition number $κ\ge1$, and a starting point with primal gap at most $Δ$ and joint gradient norm at most $\sqrt{2LΔ}$. For $\varepsilon^2/(LΔ)$ below a universal constant, every randomized adaptive algorithm with exact component values, gradients, and proximal responses requires at least $Ω(n+\min\{\sqrt n\,κ,n^{3/4}\sqrtκ\}LΔ/\varepsilon^2)$ expected component queries in the worst case to find an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of the value function. A method that uses only component gradients attains this rate up to a factor $\log^2(2+κ)$, including its initialization cost. Zhou (arXiv:2610.04944) concurrently proves the same rate for zero-respecting first-order methods. For large condition numbers, our hard instances link primal stages through dual paths whose edges belong to random components, and with high probability a proximal query to a component reveals a path only up to the first edge owned by another component.

papers.title: Statistical approach of random packing of polydisperse hyperspheres: with application to binomial and lognormal size distributions
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the packing fraction of polydisperse similar hyperspheres with a discrete binomial and continuous lognormal particle size distribution. First, a closed form expression is derived of a mix consisting of multiple discrete particles in D-dimensional Euclidean space R^D with small size differences. A recently developed analytical model for binary packings with small size ratio u is used, here applying it to the statistically probable particle pairs in the multi-sized mix. The new model is subsequently applied to discretely sized particles with a binomial number distribution and a constant size ratio u between each subsequent particle size. By taking the limit of u -> 1 and an infinite number of particles sizes, the binomial particle distribution is transformed into a continuous lognormal distribution. The resulting expression for the packing fraction can be solved in closed form, resulting in an original expression for the packing fraction of mixtures of hyperparticles with a lognormal distribution. This explicit expression is governed by the standard deviation, the Euclidean dimension D, and the monosized packing fraction of the considered particle shape. For a number of particle shapes and their packing modes (from looser to denser) the scaled expression is thoroughly compared with data reported in the literature. They concern packed particles with small standard deviations and in Euclidean dimensions D = 2 and 3, and good agreement is found. For large standard deviations the scaled packing fraction approaches a limiting value, which appears not to depend on the Euclidean dimension. Based on the insight, a closed form expression is put forward for the packing fraction that matches the small standard deviation solution, and the large standard deviation asymptote, so covering arbitrary standard deviations, Euclidean dimensions, particle types, and their mode of packing.

papers.title: Surrogate Models for Stochastic Al-Cu Phase-Field Solidification
papers.abstract: Phase-field models resolve microstructural evolution during rapid alloy solidification, but their computational cost limits long trajectories, stochastic ensembles, and studies across process conditions. We compare a deterministic U-Net with conditional flow matching (Flow), conditional diffusion (EDM), and a variance-preserving denoising diffusion bridge (VP-DDBM) for two-dimensional Al-Cu solidification. Given the current phase, concentration, and prescribed temperature fields, each model predicts the subsequent state and is applied autoregressively. At two thermal gradients outside the training range, we compare surrogate rollouts spanning \(48{,}000\) phase-field Euler steps with five phase-field futures generated from a common restart at each gradient. With two network evaluations per transition, Flow achieves the lowest time-averaged fair continuous ranked probability score among the generative surrogates for mean phase, mean Cu concentration, interface length, and leading-tip position at both gradients. Flow also reproduces the cellular morphology and retains sharp solid--liquid interfaces. It generates a single future approximately \(107\times\) faster than the phase-field solver on the reported hardware, showing potential for faster process-condition screening and ensemble-based microstructure studies.

papers.title: Strain-Glass Dynamics in the Superionic Conductor Na3PS4
papers.abstract: Ionic conduction in solid-state electrolytes is conventionally described as cations migrating through a static host lattice. Yet the fastest conductors are often the most disordered, and how disorder shapes mesoscale transport remains unresolved. Using Bragg X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy on a micrometer-sized ball-milled Na3PS4 particle, we find that the host is not static. The cubic phase behaves as a strain glass of three degenerate tetragonal variants whose domain walls move under residual milling stress, crossing over irreversibly to thermally activated dynamics on annealing. Rearrangements occur as scale-free avalanches, as in ferroelastic martensites but without external driving, while the tetragonal polymorph shows none of these features and relaxes fifty times more slowly. These dynamics evolve on timescales comparable to ionic diffusion across the particle. This work introduces a probe of dynamics in locally frustrated solid electrolytes, revealing that mechanochemical synthesis yields not merely a metastable polymorph, but a stress-driven strain glass.

papers.title: Studentized inference in randomized experiments when a few units dominate the outcome variation
papers.abstract: In completely randomized experiments with heavy-tailed outcomes, a few units can carry a share of the residual variation that does not vanish as the number of units grows. In this setting, we study the studentized difference in means and Lin's regression-adjusted estimator under a design-based framework. The studentized statistic has a nonnormal limit in general. Populations with the same marginal distributions of potential outcomes can have different limits, as the limit depends on how the two potential outcomes of each dominant unit are paired. When the outcome errors are drawn from a heavy-tailed law, the limit is random and, outside a degenerate case, varies with the population. Under balanced allocation, the conventional Wald interval has an explicit asymptotic coverage floor. At the nominal level of $0.95$, the floor is about $0.42$ for every population and about $0.84$ when the two potential residuals of each unit are equal. Both floors are close to the best possible, and without balanced allocation, the coverage can fall to the smaller of the proportions of treated and control units.

papers.title: Higher-order many-sorted categorial algebras via generalized hep-derivors
papers.abstract: Higher-order many-sorted categorial algebras are many-sorted algebras whose carriers are strict higher-order categories and whose operations are higher-order functors. They admit a homogeneous and a heterogeneous presentation, both by partial algebras whose operation domains are given by existence equations. To relate these presentations and their dimensions, we introduce generalized hep-derivors between hierarchical equationally partial signatures. A generalized hep-derivor selects carriers by existence equations in one variable and interprets operation symbols by terms, with operation domains evaluated recursively in the transformed algebra. Every generalized hep-derivor induces a functor between categories of many-sorted partial algebras. The values of this functor satisfy the domain conditions wherever their operations are defined, and we characterize when the operations are defined exactly where these conditions hold. The functor induced by a composite receives a natural inclusion from the composite of the induced functors; this inclusion, which can be strict, makes the induced functors a normal lax indexed category. In finite dimensions, generalized hep-derivors realize graduation and unification as an equivalence between the homogeneous and heterogeneous presentations, and discretization as a left adjoint to truncation. In dimension $ω$, we reconstruct the categories of $ω$-categorial algebras as projective limits of their finite-dimensional truncations and obtain unification by a quotient construction; we also establish algebraic squares and compatibility with change of signature. Finally, for nonempty sets of sorts, we show that the finite-dimension condition in the homogeneous $ω$-presentation is not axiomatizable by quasi-existence equations on its fixed signature.

papers.title: Zeta functions of quasi-split reductive algebraic groups over local fields
papers.abstract: We calculate zeta functions of quasi-split reductive algebraic groups over local fields using the classification of Tits and prove a functional equation. We give explicit exam- ples of these zeta functions for non-split unitary and orthogonal groups.

papers.title: On the Convergence of Vanilla Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise and Index Sampling
papers.abstract: Understanding how stochastic gradient noise affects the convergence of Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) is an important problem in stochastic optimization, particularly when the noise exhibits heavy-tailed behavior. In this paper, we investigate the convergence of vanilla Adam in both the expected risk and the empirical risk minimization, focusing on the effects of heavy-tailed noise and its relationship to index sampling. For the expected risk minimization, we establish convergence guarantees under Hölder smoothness and bounded $\mathfrak{p}$-th moment assumptions, allowing stochastic gradient noise with infinite variance. Our analysis provides explicit upper bounds on the expected squared gradient norm and shows that the iteration-dependent convergence term decays more slowly as $\mathfrak{p}$ decreases. For the empirical risk minimization, we establish asymptotic and non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and demonstrate that heavy-tailed population noise can deteriorate convergence bounds through dataset-dependent constants as the dataset size increases. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings on the effects of heavy-tailed noise.

papers.title: TRIO: Task Refinement with Individual Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Despite the remarkable progress, current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory due to inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our TRIO is to equip three well-designed agents with an iterative refinement paradigm by aligning their individual optimization objectives. Specifically, we first expand ambiguous queries with a query extension agent and quantify the reward based on the improved answer quality, which can be utilized to refine our agent for higher expansion efficiency. To enhance the retrieval quality, we include a unanimity voting to annotate the expanded query as insufficient or sufficient, and their generative outcomes are utilized as ground truth to optimize the judge agent. To further improve evidence utilization and answer accuracy, an answer agent is optimized with dynamic matching-based rewards with curriculum learning for final outputs. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed TRIO in comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingtaoren/TRIO.

papers.title: IssueLighter: An Issue Type-Aware LLM Agent for Issue Report Validity Assessment
papers.abstract: Invalid issue reports are prevalent in open source software (OSS) projects, imposing substantial burdens on maintainers who already face a high risk of burnout. Prior research has primarily focused on identifying invalid reports for specific issue categories (e.g., bug and wontfix), leaving the broader landscape of OSS issue types largely unexplored and limiting the generalizability of existing approaches. Moreover, existing methods provide little support for explaining or validating their predictions, reducing their practical usefulness for maintainers. With the rise of LLM-based agents, it remains unclear whether a comprehensive understanding of the causes of invalidity across all issue types can improve validity assessment performance while producing well-grounded rationales. To this end, we first manually annotated the validity status of 520 issue reports from three OSS projects, i.e., pandas, scikit-learn, and mypy, resulting in 257 invalid reports and 263 valid ones. Then, we conducted a thematic analysis on these invalid reports and identified 13 causes of invalidity that are closely specific to issue types. Based on these insights, we propose IssueLighter, an agent-based framework with a type-aware validity assessment strategy that dynamically executes commands. Experimental results show that IssueLighter consistently and substantially outperforms all baseline methods, with an average F1 improvement of over 20 percentage points. Ablation studies confirm that both the type-aware strategy and the taxonomy of causes of invalidity contribute to the performance gains. Qualitative analysis further demonstrates that IssueLighter generates rationales grounded in accurately identified causes of invalidity and supported by evidence. Moreover, leveraging these rationales, we challenged maintainers' original decisions in four disputed cases, and all received approval.

papers.title: OctreeSplat: Hierarchical Octree-Guided Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods typically regress pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives, often causing excessive overlap and artifacts, while inaccuracies in predicted camera poses can lead to misalignment in novel-view synthesis (NVS). We present VoxelTTO, a feed-forward framework for reconstructing geometrically accurate 3DGS from an arbitrary number of images and optional camera parameters. VoxelTTO aggregates dense image features into global voxels and decodes Gaussians from voxel features, breaking the pixel-to-Gaussian correspondence. To exploit known camera parameters while keeping the pretrained visual foundation model (VFM) parameters frozen, we introduce test-time optimization (TTO) that adapts lightweight LoRA modules using pose supervision. We further replace vanilla 3DGS rasterization with stochastic solid volume rendering during training and inference, improving geometric fidelity. Training updates only the voxel-aligned Gaussian reconstruction modules, requiring 80 GPU hours. Experiments on Replica, Tanks and Temples, RE10K, and DTU demonstrate improved RGB-D NVS and camera-pose alignment relative to prior methods.

papers.title: Herding or Racing? Decomposing Cross-Account Order-Flow Persistence in On-Chain Markets
papers.abstract: Most of the autocorrelation in trade signs on decentralized exchanges comes from pairs of trades sent by different wallets. For Uniswap v3, this has been read as herding dominating order splitting -- the reverse of what equity markets show. We show that this herding share mixes two quantities: the probability $p$ that consecutive orders come from the same account, which is small when thousands of wallets are trading, and the ratio $κ$ of cross-account to same-account sign correlation. For any $p$, $κ$ equals one under the public-signal benchmark of Tóth et al. and zero under independent order splitting. On Uniswap v3 USDC-WETH (one week each in 2023 and 2024), the herding share is 0.65-0.86, but $κ$ is only 0.05-0.10. On a fully on-chain EVM limit order book, the herding share is similar (0.61-0.87), but $κ$ is 0.72-0.76; among Uniswap swaps above USD 100k, it is 0.34-0.52. Where $κ$ is high, cross-account co-movement is mostly a race for the price on a centralized exchange. It is concentrated in orders a few blocks apart, and a cross-fitted gradient-boosted filter that sees only Binance data removes about three quarters or more of it. This race flow accounts for most of the losses of liquidity providers. We recommend reporting $κ$ alongside the herding share and modeling on-chain order flow as splitting traders plus arbitrageurs who respond to the centralized-exchange price.

papers.title: Sharp Hausdorff--Young inequalities for solvable and semisimple Lie groups
papers.abstract: In this paper, we obtain the sharp constants for Hausdorff--Young inequalities on simply connected, completely solvable Lie groups, and connected real semisimple Lie groups with finite center.

papers.title: SGR-OPSD: Learning from Subgoal Plans with Graph-Regularized Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: OPSD provides dense supervision for agentic reinforcement learning through privileged information feedback. However, existing privileged information often lacks explicit task-progression planning, while teacher-student log-probability gaps reflect shifts in model preference rather than true task progress. To address these limitations, we propose Subgoal-Guided Graph-Regularized OPSD (SGR-OPSD), a framework that combines subgoal supervision with interaction-derived evidence for turn-level credit assignment. Specifically, SGR-OPSD uses LLM-generated subgoal plans to provide dense action-level guidance, converting them into advantage weights via a constrained, KL-regularized objective. To ground credit in observed outcomes, we construct a Subgoal Progress Graph that estimates empirical returns from sampled transition frequencies. The graph compares empirical action returns against the state average to derive preferences that calibrate the teacher's credit weights. Evaluated on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA across two model scales (Qwen2.5-3B and 7B), SGR-OPSD consistently outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, improving success rates over GRPO by up to 7.6 percentage points and reaching 85.8% on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablation studies confirm that subgoal guidance and graph-based weight calibration are key to these performance gains.

papers.title: Autonomous steady-state quantum magic under local noise
papers.abstract: We determine the local reset cost of sustaining quantum magic under continuous depolarization. Static spin interactions convert reset-induced polarization into nonstabilizer correlations. For interactions involving at most $k$ spins and local coherent strength $J$, the optimal strong-noise threshold obeys $K_{\rm on}^{(k)}/γ=Θ_k[(γ/J)^{1/(k-1)}]$, where $γ$ is the noise rate and $K$ the reset cap. The exponent is uniform in device size, and the two-body leading coefficient is $1/(2\sqrt{2})$. The hierarchy follows from a coherent transition competing with simultaneous local defects. In weak noise, population amplification across growing devices lets the normalized onset cost vanish with static two-body interactions. Entropy balance separately constrains the size and total reset rate required for a fixed global resource. Explicit two-, three-, and four-body dynamics generate magic from free inputs and converge to a unique mixed steady state. A physical two-body construction connects this stationary resource to its coherent budget, control precision, and preparation time.

papers.title: Wang's log-Harnack inequality for Markov chains and its applications
papers.abstract: We consider irreducible reversible Markov chains whose nonzero off-diagonal transition probabilities are bounded below by $\varepsilon>0$ and whose reversible measure satisfies $m_-\le m(x)\leκm_-$. Under the Bakry--Émery curvature condition $\mathrm{CD}(K,\infty)$, with $K\in\mathbb{R}$, we establish Wang's log-Harnack inequality $$ P_t(\log f)(x)\le\log P_tf(y) +\frac{C\mathrm{dist}(x,y)^2}{\int_0^t e^{2Ks}\mathrm{d} s}, $$ for bounded positive $f$ bounded away from zero and all $x,y\in V$, where $C$ is a constant dependent only on $\varepsilon$. Building upon this inequality, we prove volume doubling property, which extends the work of Guo-Huang-Huang to general weighted setting. We further prove a sharp volume growth and Li-Yau gradient estimates under $\mathrm{CD}(0,\infty)$ .

papers.title: Singular Tracking of Fractional Brownian Motion under Proportional Costs
papers.abstract: We study the tracking of fractional Brownian motion by adapted controls of finite variation, with quadratic loss and proportional adjustment costs. Let $B^H$ be standard fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H\in(0,1)$. We write $V_λ(T;a,b,σ)$ for the optimal expected cost of tracking $σB^H$ over a horizon $T>0$, where $σ>0$ is the target amplitude, $a>0$ weights the quadratic loss, and $λb$ is the cost per unit of adjustment, with $λ,b>0$. We prove \[V_λ(T;a,b,σ)\underset{λ\to0}{\sim}κ_HT a^{(1-H)/(1+H)}(λb)^{2H/(1+H)}σ^{2/(1+H)}. \] Here $κ_H>0$ is the long-run optimal cost per unit time in the normalized problem $a=b=σ=λ=1$. Observing the entire past does not change $κ_H$. For the normalized problem with full past information, a horizon $L>0$ and a terminal adjustment to the target, the difference between its value and $κ_H L$ is bounded uniformly in $L$. This estimate also yields continuity of $κ_H$ in $H$. In the Brownian case, $κ_{1/2}=\frac12(\frac32)^{2/3}$. We extend the asymptotic formula to nonstationary targets under a coupling condition on local paths and their observation filtrations. We verify this condition for Gaussian Volterra targets under Brownian observation. All asymptotically optimal controls have the same leading-order split between tracking and adjustment costs. We also give primal and dual bounds on $κ_H$. For $H<1/2$, we construct approximations based on exponential sums with positive weights and quantify their error as the horizon grows.

papers.title: What reviewers call a Long Method is a length: A pre-registered test of coupling divergence as a god-unit signal, and what it settled instead
papers.abstract: A companion study found that a complexity outlier rule shows where complexity concentrates but cannot tell a god unit from a complex algorithm. This paper pre-registered a test of one way to tell them apart: weight a unit's complexity by its coupling divergence, the data it hands on minus the data it receives, so that a leaf is set aside. Coupling was measured by resolving every call in 520 MLCQ repositories, 500 fresh Java repositories and 73 Qualitas Corpus systems. The claim fails: the primary, the pooled MCC of the weighted form minus complexity alone against MLCQ's human Blob, is -0.041 [-0.130, +0.054], no difference resolved and underpowered, and the resolved readings go against it. What the data settle is at method level. What MLCQ's reviewers call a Long Method is an absolute length: a constant of 26 lines or more, chosen on the explore half, reaches MCC 0.777 on the confirm half, +0.080 [+0.016, +0.145] over the best per-repository form; every reviewer with ten or more positives, on their non-leaf reviews, has a best cutoff between 17 and 34 lines; and nothing measured inside a method, its calls, variables, data flow or the cost of cutting it, refines the constant. The constant is a limit of human reading. The next form of the construct is the cost of bringing a long method under it, which is where the construct meets architecture.

papers.title: Zero-shot evaluation of open vision-language models as System 1 decision models on radiology tasks
papers.abstract: Purpose: To compare two multimodal System 1 decision models (Clef 27B, d1 3B) with three generative vision-language models read out zero-shot from a single answer token (Qwen3.8-27B, which is Clef's backbone; Gemma 4 31B; MedGemma 1.5 4B) on seven radiology tasks. Methods: All models ran locally on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The System 1 models returned a probability for each option in one pass; for the generative models, probabilities were read from the log-probabilities of the option letters. Tasks covered chest CT and radiograph reports (CT-RATE, PadChest), device MR safety records (GUDID), tubes and lines on chest radiographs (RANZCR CLiP), chest CT volumes (CT-RATE), brain MRI motion (MR-ART) and MRI sequence (BraTS 2021), 4,435 cases in total. The primary endpoint was AUROC with bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: All five models retrieved report findings well (AUROC 0.93-0.99). Clef ranked higher than its backbone on CT volumes (0.749 vs 0.668) and tube and line radiographs (0.812 vs 0.766) and lower on motion (0.625 vs 0.709), but it changed decisions more than ranking: it identified 90 of 100 FLAIR volumes, a class its backbone never chose, and cut calibration error on CT volumes from 0.436 to 0.072. d1 was within 0.04 of Clef on reports while using 3 to 9 times less energy per request, but was weak on images. Gemma 4 31B ranked device MR safety best (0.854) and MedGemma 1.5 4B ranked motion best (0.821), yet MedGemma was at chance on MRI sequences and answered "severe" for 93% of motion scans. Conclusion: A single-token readout turns open generative models from several families into usable decision models without retraining, but no model was best on every task and each had task-specific answer biases, so models and decision thresholds should be chosen on local cases.

papers.title: Write Facts the Way Models Read Them: Lifting the Two-Hop Curse
papers.abstract: A language model that learns a new fact by fine-tuning can repeat it but cannot reason with it: taught that a person is a citizen of a new country, it still cannot say, without chain-of-thought, who the head of state of that person's country is. This two-hop curse is widely treated as a reasoning deficit, and the strongest knowledge editors answer it with synthesized reasoning data. We show that the reasoning is intact and the writing is wrong. Fine-tuning writes a new fact as an answer to be said, whereas the second hop reads the bridge ("that person's country") as an entity, from the middle layers on: patching the model's own representation of the entity into the bridge at those layers largely restores the second hop, yet after fine-tuning the bridge there is no closer to the new entity than before the edit. We therefore propose read-equivalent writing (Legible): one loss term makes the bridge phrase, at the layer where the second hop finishes reading it, match the model's own reading of the new entity, and keeps the same relation's other subjects unchanged. Phrases and targets come from the edited model itself, and no multi-hop training data is used. Across Qwen2.5, Llama-3 and Qwen3, Legible (I) composes learned facts more often than the model composes its own knowledge, on MQuAKE's two-hop-curse questions; (II) reaches 1.8-2.6x the bridge accuracy of CaKE, whose reasoning data composes no better than plain fine-tuning, and has the best average over composition, accuracy and locality against four families of writers; and (III) lifts the curse on RippleEdits, on the benchmark of Balesni et al., who named the curse, and at 14B.

papers.title: The classification of Fano contact manifolds revisited
papers.abstract: We present an account of the classification of Fano contact manifolds based on the proof of OpenAI and the solution of LeBrun-Salamon conjecture by Hu, Liu and Wan. The proof combines their constructions with earlier results on contact lines, with some simplifications.

papers.title: Ab Initio strain-dependent vibrational analysis of different silicene structures for 2D devices
papers.abstract: We report first-principles phonon dynamics studies in isotropically strained mono-layer silicene films of various topologies by density functional theory and density functional perturbation theory methods. The strain introduced in the sheets are of both tensile and compressive nature and its effect on the thermal transport properties are analysed using the Boltzmann Transport Equation (BTE) reported. We performed electronic and vibrational analysis of each silicene topology and concluded that hhk-silicene is a potential candidate for next generation electro-thermal devices due its molecular stability, bulk-Si like bandgap and tolerable thermal performance that can be engineered by strain. The novel hhk-silicene topology offers excellent thermal and electronic capabilities that are sensitive to strain along with the band gap following a near-linear monotonically decreasing trend making it suitable for strain-tronics applications.

papers.title: Nonlinear Physics and Self-Organized Criticality in Astrophysics
papers.abstract: Since standard photon statistics is not applicable to nonlinear physics processes, it is of utmost importance to properly include the nonlinearity in astrophysical instabilities and emission processes. Bak et al.~(1987) postulated sandpile avalanches and called the underlying principle ``self-organized criticality'' (SOC), but its definition remained ambiguous and controversial. Here we discuss the nonlinear physics of six basic SOC definitions, such as: (i) phase transitions, (ii) fractal structures, (iii) power laws, (iv) SOC contingency, (v) exponential growth, and (vi) diffusive decay. Statistics of SOC events or avalanche processes can be inferred from their size distributions, or from their spatio-temporal evolution, described with the logistic equation. Here we quantify each nonlinear process in terms of quantitative scaling laws.

papers.title: The Golden Quadruple: Four Reals Whose Differences Form a Geometric Progression, Rigidity of the Golden Ratio, and a Bohr Almost Periodic Cosine Sum
papers.abstract: Let $φ=(1+\sqrt5)/2$. The set $\{0,φ,φ^2,φ^3\}$ is classical (Euclid, Elements XIII.8): by $φ^2=φ+1$ its six pairwise differences take the values $1,φ,φ^2,φ^3$, with multiplicities $1,2,2,1$. We write it as the golden quadruple $S=(F, F-a, F-b, F-a-b)$, $a=φu$, $b=φ^2u$, $F>a+b$, and study its extremal and rigidity properties. No five distinct reals have all their positive differences in $\{uφ^n:n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$; this follows from a result of Lenstra (1977), and we give a self-contained proof. We give an elementary proof of uniqueness: every four-element set with this property is a translate of $uφ^m\{0,φ,φ^2,φ^3\}$ for some $m\in\mathbb{Z}$, and if all its differences lie in $\{u,φu,φ^2u,φ^3u\}$ it is a translate of $S$. Among all $x>1$, only $x=φ$ admits a four-point set of reals whose set of distinct differences is $\{c,cx,cx^2,cx^3\}$. For the analogous quadruple with base $x\neqφ$ the failure is measured by two closure residues, which along Fibonacci quotients equal $\pm u/\mathrm{Fib}_n^2$ and $\pm \mathrm{Fib}_{n+1}u/\mathrm{Fib}_n^3$. The cosine sum $C_S(t)=\sum\cos(2πd t)$ over the six differences equals $8\cos^2(πa t)\cos^2(πb t)-2$; it is not periodic but is Bohr almost periodic, with explicit almost periods $τ_n=\mathrm{Fib}_n/u$, and we determine the two-term asymptotics $\sup_t|C_S(t+τ_n)-C_S(t)|=6\sqrt3 πφ^{-n}-2\sqrt3 π^3φ^{-3n}+O(φ^{-5n})$, with optimal constants; the inclusion length of the $\varepsilon$-almost periods is of order $1/\varepsilon$. For a scale $K>0$ the golden ladder $ν_n=Kφ^{-n}$ realises the construction with differences $ν_{200},\dots,ν_{203}$; we evaluate it for $K=\sqrt{c^5/(Gh)}$. All proofs are elementary and self-contained.

papers.title: Non-intrusive appliance state detection in unseen homes using classical machine learning
papers.abstract: Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) infers, from the aggregate signal of a single smart meter, when each appliance in a home is ON or OFF, offering significant potential to enhance energy efficiency. Classical machine-learning detectors report F1 scores (the harmonic mean of precision and recall) from 0.53 to 0.98, but the causes of this spread are unseparated, so it is unclear which design choices matter. Real-world deployments, however, require detectors that work in houses never seen during training, whereas most studies test on houses used for training. To address this challenge, we propose a factorial analysis of variance design that separates the effects of classifier, feature set and class-imbalance strategy across five appliances (270 configurations), and a leave-house-out protocol with house-grouped model selection. Unlike studies that vary one factor at a time or pool houses, the approach attributes performance to each factor and measures it on unseen homes. Extensive experiments on REFIT, a public dataset of 20 UK households, show that the appliance explains 38 percent of F1 variance, the feature set 13 percent, the classifier 8 percent and the imbalance strategy 2 percent. Pooled testing overstates support-weighted F1 (0.548 versus 0.447 in unseen houses), class weighting gains grow from 32 percent to 69 percent, and feature engineering gives the same 52 percent gain in both protocols. House-grouped selection raises F1 for three of five appliances, by up to 0.110, and a convolutional neural network scores 0.450 (0.496 calibrated) against 0.447 for classical models. The findings guide appliance-level monitoring in smart-metering and energy-management systems.

papers.title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
papers.abstract: Decision-making in humans and AI involves multiple cognitive abilities. System One decision models produce fast, structured choices. Their cognitive strengths and limitations, however, remain poorly understood. We introduce S1CogBench, a benchmark of 24 established cognitive tasks and 27 evaluation modes, evaluating seven open models and the API model Jev. It combines human-response prediction, autonomous execution, and controlled task manipulations to reveal strengths and failures that aggregate scores miss. We find distinct behavioral profiles across the evaluated models. In these models, strong performance on some learning tasks coexists with failures to gather information or adapt to feedback, while high accuracy does not guarantee human-like responses to changing task demands. Shared readout controls show that model rankings depend partly on how choices are extracted. Separate latency comparisons with generative language models show that long responses are much slower than direct decisions, whereas matched one-token generation adds little overhead. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments. It provides a common empirical basis for identifying their capabilities and limitations before integrating them into automated decision systems.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin
papers.abstract: Attribution graphs predict sparse autoencoder (SAE) ablations to first order on the active features, but a TopK SAE passes only its k largest preactivations, so small changes often swap active features. On five public TopK SAEs, zeroing one feature changes the active set of the next layer's SAE in 74% to 89% of cases. Our margin graph adds the first order change to every downstream preactivation, then selects the k largest again. On Pythia-70M the margin graph cuts the median error of predicted activations, relative to their exact change, from the attribution graph's 0.739 to 0.121, 84% lower. Exact recomputation of 48 interventions runs 3.5 times faster than the margin graph on our GPU. Patched into Pythia-70M with the clean reconstruction error, the margin graph's activations predict the change in the subject verb agreement logit difference with 1.95 times the attribution graph's mean error, on interventions above a fixed floor. Between seeds of our SAEs, which share one auxiliary loss coefficient, sparse feature maps recover 85% of a graph's squared norm on active features but 47% with each graph masked to its own, 38 percentage points less. Unmasking the inactive tenth nearest the TopK threshold recovers 73% of the masking loss, against 11% for a random tenth, so the margin to that threshold decides how ablations change activations and what graphs carry between seeds.

papers.title: Quasi-polynomial valuations of lattice polytopes
papers.abstract: We prove that for any valuation $φ$ of lattice polytopes in ${\mathbb R}^m$, which is quasi-polynomial with respect to ${\mathbb Z}^m$-translations, and any lattice polytope $P$, the function $φ(nP)$ is quasi-polynomial in $n$.

papers.title: Software Change Request in AI-Synthesized Software Evolution
papers.abstract: Mobile app stores are a rich source of user feedback containing many change requests, bug reports, improvement suggestions, etc., relevant to the post-deployment modification of software. However, it is challenging to manually translate this free format data to actionable change requests (SCRs). This review presents studies that have applied rule-based techniques, traditional ML approaches, topic modelling, hybrid approaches, and a few deep learning approaches. The data sets used range from small annotated sets to millions of reviews. However, there is inconsistency in the names, availability, annotation guidelines and sampling methods used across different studies. Many studies use Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF, while Naïve Bayes, Support Vector Machines, Decision Trees and Random Forest are frequently applied. Precision, Recall and F1-scores are commonly used for evaluation; however, results and experiments are not easily comparable. Some tools have been developed such as SURF, ARDoc, ChangeAdvisor, ALERTme, AUREA, DIVER, ACRM and KEFE to partially automate the classification, summarization, topic detection and traceability. This review shows that there is still a lack of consistency in the data sets used, reproducible annotation, generalization across languages and domains, contextual modelling, interpretability and integration with maintenance activities. This review provides a consolidated view and taxonomy to provide a research agenda to support more reliable AI enabled software evolution.

papers.title: Two moments suffice for Bessel approximation: conditioned differences, contingency tables, and probabilistic divide-and-conquer
papers.abstract: We develop Stein's method, with explicit constants throughout, for the discrete Bessel distribution: the law of a Poisson variable given its difference from an independent Poisson variable. The Bessel family is characterized by a birth-death operator with quadratic death rate $n(n+k)$ and as the exact fixed-point set of a centered quadratic-bias transform, and we prove a dependency expansion of Arratia-Goldstein-Gordon type: two joint moments of a column array control the total-variation distance from the conditioned row sum to a matched Bessel law. Applied to the row-constrained Fisher-Yates ensemble on $2\times c$ contingency tables -- independent Bernoulli or capped-Poisson entries conditioned on the row-sum difference, column sums free -- this yields a limit theorem -- which upgrades to the entire conditioned table at the same two-moment error -- a completely explicit enumeration estimate, and an exact divide-and-conquer sampler with certified acceptance. The entire apparatus -- operator, expansion, enumeration, sampler -- generalizes to $r\times c$ tables, where conditioning on all successive row differences produces a hyper-Bessel law. Verification scripts are included as ancillary files.

papers.title: Quantum 3xplorer: AI-Native Engine for Next-Generation Quantum Materials Modeling
papers.abstract: Quantum-mechanical approaches, such as density functional theory (DFT), underpin much of modern computational materials science and are the primary source of data for AI-driven discovery. Yet the established electronic-structure codes today represent decades-old software architectures, making new physical models slow and costly to implement, validate, and deploy on emerging hardware. We present Quantum 3xplorer (Q3, pronounced "Quantum Explorer"), an AI-native quantum simulation engine written from scratch by AI coding agents under the direction and supervision of domain scientists. As a first and demanding validation case, we implement plane-wave pseudopotential DFT end to end: norm-conserving, ultrasoft, and projector-augmented-wave formalisms, spin polarization, DFT+U, and dispersion corrections, together with forces, stresses, structural relaxation, and electronic-structure analysis. Q3 reproduces established reference implementations, runs faster on a single core in representative benchmarks, and scales across GPU-accelerated supercomputers. It was developed in weeks rather than years. Its layered, physics-first architecture separates abstract quantum-mechanical concepts from their numerical representations, making its framework extendable beyond plane waves to other basis sets and levels of theory. Its inputs and outputs follow structured, schema-validated data standards, making every result AI-ready. Q3 is open source under Apache 2.0 and built to be reused, extended, and improved by the research community. Q3 points to a paradigm shift in how computational quantum science is done. Scientists define the physics, formulate the models, and set the criteria for validation; AI agents write, test, and optimize the code. The decades-long path from a new theory to a trusted, high-performance implementation can thus collapse to days, significantly accelerating scientific discovery.

papers.title: 3SUM Made Simpler (Without Matrix Multiplication), $k$-SUM Hypothesis Refuted for Odd $k$, and Real 3SUM/APSP Derandomized
papers.abstract: Recently, a truly subquadratic algorithm for the 3SUM problem and a truly subcubic algorithm for the all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) problem were found by Anthropic, as reported by Alman and Vassilevska Williams (2026). These algorithms relied on a new subroutine for rectangular matrix multiplication with selected output entries, which was obtained by modifying known matrix multiplication techniques of Schönhage (1981) and Coppersmith (1982). 1. We present a different truly subquadratic randomized algorithm for 3SUM for integer inputs. It completely avoids the use of matrix multiplication but instead modifies known dynamic programming algorithms for subset convolution and the zeta transform, which rely only on simple subtraction tricks via inclusion--exclusion (and does not even require fast Fourier transform), and so is conceptually easier to understand (the whole solution is about 5 pages long). 2. Following a similar approach, we obtain a randomized algorithm for $k$-SUM for integer inputs for odd constant $k$ in $O(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil-\varepsilon_k})$ time for some constant $\varepsilon_k>0$, disproving the $k$-SUM Hypothesis for all odd $k$. 3. Existing reductions from 3SUM and APSP to selected-entries rectangular matrix multiplication were randomized in the case of real-valued input. We present new deterministic reductions, yielding a truly subquadratic deterministic algorithm for Real 3SUM and a truly subcubic deterministic algorithm for Real APSP.

papers.title: TwinPast: Benchmarking Historical Evidence Use in Streaming Video Understanding with Evidence Contrastive Video Pairs
papers.abstract: High accuracy on streaming video benchmarks does not show that a model uses visual history. Auditing OVO-Bench and StreamingBench, we find that recent frames alone suffice for 32% of sampled historical-task questions, and that the question and options alone also yield many correct answers. We introduce TwinPast, a benchmark of 350 human-reviewed video pairs spanning five historical tasks. The two videos in a pair share the recent video context, question, and ordered options, and differ in earlier events and therefore in the correct answer. Each video is evaluated independently and PairAcc requires both answers to be correct, so an answer determined by the shared inputs cannot solve a pair. Masking the annotated critical evidence lowers PairAcc from as high as 91% to at most 19%, whereas equal-area masking elsewhere changes it by at most 3.4 points. The strongest streaming system reaches 49% PairAcc, while general-purpose MLLMs given each complete video reach 67-91%, leaving substantial headroom. Streaming systems fail mainly by giving both histories the same answer. They give different valid answers on at most 57% of pairs, while the general-purpose MLLMs do so on 79-94%. Case studies further show wrong answers when the deciding evidence is still available at the final query.

papers.title: Matching Workloads to Blackwell: Power-Resolved Benchmarking of NVIDIA B200 and B300 across HPC and AI Workloads
papers.abstract: We evaluate NVIDIA B200 and B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPUs on two independent eight-GPU clusters, spanning computer-vision inference and training, LLM inference with Llama-3-8B and 70B~\cite{llama3}, and six production HPC codes. The B300 is not a uniform successor to the B200: it trails by up to 5.6$\times$ on convolutional inference, 8$\times$ on 3D vision transformer training, 24--27\% on 70B LLM throughput, and 16$\times$ on double-precision Quantum ESPRESSO. We resolve the convolutional deficit using per-GPU board power rather than throughput alone: on the affected workloads the B300 draws only 36--53\% of its 1100\,W envelope, whereas on ViT-Large, which it wins, both parts saturate at 95--97\% of TDP. Because our harness keeps inputs resident in device memory, a host-side data pipeline is excluded by construction, localizing the cause to per-kernel cost. Two B300 nodes of identical silicon differ by 2.1$\times$ in time-to-first-token solely from a development vLLM build. We give per-workload procurement guidance.

papers.title: Fooling Relying Parties of the EUDI Wallet Architecture: Credential Pooling Attacks and CRESTA, a Standard-Compliant Countermeasure
papers.abstract: The European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet will let millions of EU citizens prove who they are and what they are entitled to, disclosing only what is needed. Many services need several credentials at once, such as an identity card and a university degree, so combined presentations are essential. We present credential pooling attacks on relying parties of the EUDI Wallet reference architecture. Colluding users, each holding some credentials in their own wallet, cooperate through a proxy that acts as a single synthetic user and presents all the requested credentials, although no single user holds them all. Every signature is genuine and computed by certified hardware, and nothing is extracted or forged. We ran the attack against the European Commission's reference implementation, also on two Android phones. The attack would fail if all credentials of a user carried the same public key, but colluding relying parties could then link all presentations of that user. For this reason, the Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF) requires a fresh key for each credential and recommends batches of single-use copies, each with its own key: precisely what makes pooling possible. One might think that preventing pooling requires giving up unlinkability or adopting non-standard cryptography, such as zero-knowledge proofs. We show that this is not the case: we present CRESTA (CREdential STApling), an efficient countermeasure that uses only standard cryptography and credential formats and preserves unlinkability. In CRESTA, an ordinary issuer checks at issuance that a set of keys was generated in the same secure hardware, and certifies it in a binding attestation: a standard credential whose attributes can be selectively disclosed. CRESTA works entirely within the EUDI Wallet framework and costs a relying party one additional signature verification per presentation.

papers.title: Veloxity: Towards Memory-Safe UAV Embedded Firmware using the Rust Programming Language
papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed increased momentum towards memory-safe programming languages for safety-critical systems. Memory-safe languages can eliminate entire classes of common software errors that have historically required extensive analysis and expenditure to avoid. Nevertheless, memory-safe language adoption in aerospace remains fragmented and incomplete, particularly for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Recent Rust UAV projects either run only in simulation, are closed source, or have not been integrated with an established autonomy ecosystem and tested against existing C/C++ firmware. To address this gap, we present Veloxity: an open-source embedded UAV autopilot written in the memory-safe Rust programming language. Veloxity lowers the barrier to using memory-safe languages within modern ecosystems by providing a minimal, modular foundation for autonomous UAVs. We compare Veloxity to equivalent autopilots written in C++ in simulation, with hardware testbenches, and via outdoor waypoint-following flight tests, demonstrating functional parity with improved performance. These results indicate that modern memory-safe languages are a viable option for reliable and performant firmware for autonomous aerospace systems.

papers.title: Consensus Within, Competition Between: Decentralized LLM Teams for Perimeter Defense
papers.abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multi-agent teams raises a fundamental architectural question: whether task allocation should be centralized in a single LLM controller or distributed across autonomous LLM agents, particularly when communication is unreliable. In a deliberately simplified perimeter-defense simulation against LLM-controlled intruders, we compared a central commander, an auction-based consensus team and independent agents under five network conditions. Breach rates were 15% for the consensus team, 32% for the commander and 29% for independent agents. Burst message loss, falsified reports and limited radio range raised the commander's breach rate by 10 to 18 percentage points (pp), whereas the consensus team's changed by at most 5. In the consensus team, giving a low-cost LLM more authority over the bid computation raised its breach rate by 38 pp. With birds and civilian drones in airspace, we added an image for each to the input text state. Only the near-frontier model treated them apart from intruders. Intruders disguised as existing taxidermy bird drones were mistaken for birds by both low-cost and near-frontier LLMs, being dropped from pursuit in 59-61% of near-frontier decisions (1-16% before). However, a one-sentence forewarning in the prompt lowered it to 0-25%. We find that the LLM team with a dedicated external conflict-resolution protocol had the fewest breaches. The code is available at https://github.com/the-kas-lab/consensus-within-competition-between.

papers.title: Quantum-Walk Inspired Spectral Metrics for Evaluating QAOA Mixers
papers.abstract: QAOA mixers play an important role in enabling exploration of the exponentially large solution space of binary optimization problems. However, the choice of mixer Hamiltonian is typically guided by convention and implementation or circuit constraints, rather than by a graph-topology-aware criterion. In this work, inspired by quantum-walk mixing theory, we propose two complementary spectral heuristics for characterizing QAOA mixer topologies. The first is the normalized minimum eigenvalue separation of the mixer Hamiltonian $H_M$, while the second is the long-time averaged minimum eigenvalue separation of the mixer unitary $U_M(β)=e^{-iβH_M}$. Both quantities are invariant under any positive rescaling of the mixer Hamiltonian and provide Hamiltonian- and unitary-level characterizations of the mixer's spectral structure. We use them as heuristic indicators of the mixer dynamics relevant to amplitude redistribution during QAOA evolution. We derive exact expressions and asymptotic bounds for the complete graph, hypercube, cycle, and balanced 2-D torus, revealing a broad spectral separation between the studied topology classes. We then compare these separations with empirical QAOA performance. For random permutation-invariant cost Hamiltonians, the observed performance ordering is broadly consistent with the spectral characterization. In contrast, for structured 1-D and 2-D Ising QUBOs, this ordering breaks down, indicating that mixer-cost alignment can become important. These results illustrate both the usefulness and the limitations of topology-level, cost-agnostic spectral heuristics for QAOA mixer selection.

papers.title: Transport in spinful non-Hermitian gauge lattices
papers.abstract: We extend the generalized transfer-matrix method introduced in [H. Ghaemi-Dizicheh, Phys.\ Rev.\ B \textbf{107}, 125155 (2023)] to one-dimensional spinful non-Hermitian tight-binding lattices with matrix-valued Abelian and non-Abelian gauge couplings. We derive a minimal channel-resolved transfer matrix and identify its eigenvalues with the generalized Bloch factors. The same transfer matrix determines the periodic- and open-boundary spectra, generalized Brillouin zone, skin localization, and finite-sample scattering conditions. In the Abelian limit, the model separates into fixed spin sectors, yielding exact spectral results and closed finite-length transport expressions in terms of Chebyshev polynomials. These results reveal bipolar spin-dependent skin localization and distinguish the reciprocal hopping scale, which governs poles, zeros, and reflectionlessness, from the directed-amplification factor controlling transmission asymmetry, transparency, and invisibility. For non-Abelian gauge fields, noncommuting link matrices coherently mix the spin sectors, such that four transfer eigenmodes jointly determine the non-Bloch spectrum and transport eigenchannels. We show that this mixing produces spin-hybridized lasing and coherent-perfect-absorption channels, Zeeman-tunable lasing thresholds, and direction-dependent reflectionless transport accompanied by pronounced spin conversion. The resulting boundary-condition criteria describe lasing, coherent perfect absorption, reflectionlessness, transparency, and invisibility, while identifying spin polarization and conversion as experimentally accessible signatures that distinguish Abelian from non-Abelian non-Hermitian transport.

papers.title: Matrix Nearness Problems Revisited
papers.abstract: Given a nonempty set of matrices $\mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathbb{C}^{m \times n}$ and a matrix $A \not\in\mathcal{E}$, a matrix nearness problem (or matrix distance problem) consists in finding a matrix in $\mathcal{E}$ that is closest to $A$, in some norm, as well as the corresponding distance. This article is a survey of matrix nearness problems and of numerical algorithms for their solution. We pay special attention to modern related topics, such as Riemannian optimization and pseudospectra, that were not discussed in depth in previous reviews about this topic. Besides collecting known facts, we also prove some foundational results that, at least in the present form, we could not locate in the literature.

papers.title: Dynamical relations on $\mathbb{P}^1$, higher bifurcations, and arithmetic bigness
papers.abstract: In this article, we study algebraic relations among rational maps on $\mathbb{P}^1$ and among their preperiodic points. Working over $\mathbb{C}$, we characterize algebraic families of positive-dimensional varieties in $(\mathbb{P}^1)^N$ and tuples of maps $(f_1, \ldots, f_N)$ for which the subvariety is dynamically special for a Zariski-dense set of parameters. Moreover, outside of well-understood Lattès phenomena, we show that all families of maps and subvarieties that bifurcate are maximally bifurcating; that is, we show that a positive bifurcation (1,1)-current implies positivity of the associated bifurcation measure on the parameter space. Working over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, we characterize arithmetic and geometric potential bigness for the canonical line bundle associated to families of endomorphisms of $(\mathbb{P}^1)^N$ when restricted to the subvarieties. As consequences, we obtain uniform bounds for the periods and preperiods of relations among non-exceptional maps, and we show uniform bounds on the geometry of preperiodic points satisfying these relations. Over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, our results yield corresponding uniform bounds for points and subvarieties satisfying a height gap.

papers.title: Cheap Retrieval and Observation Credit Assignment from One Quantity: The Value of Information
papers.abstract: Memory in reinforcement learning raises two problems. Attention finds the relevant item by scoring the whole store, which is costly for robots under latency and energy limits. When a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must cross the whole sequence. We argue that both are governed by one quantity, the value of information, and propose to estimate it from archived rollouts. We show that, read at the observation, it yields a lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action. This bound floors the action's TD target and credits the observation that earned it. Read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. This work-in-progress submission does not yet test this algorithm. Still, a pilot retrieval system learns to approximate an optimization problem introduced by the proposed algorithm.

papers.title: Avoid-or-Compress Words for Reachable Images Missing Four or Five States
papers.abstract: Given a set of states $S$ and a nonempty proper subset $A\subset S$, an avoid-or-compress word either omits a state of $A$ from the image of $S$ or reduces the size of that image. We determine the largest possible length of a shortest such word when $S$ is a reachable image missing four or five states. For strongly connected synchronizing automata, the answers are $\min(n-|A|,11)$ and $\min(n-|A|,14)$, respectively, and both are attained over a binary alphabet. The lower bounds follow from uniform constructions. For the upper bounds, short-pair graphs and the linear span of short images reduce the problem to finitely many configurations. A computer-assisted classification eliminates these configurations except for one complete bipartite graph, which is excluded by a combinatorial argument.

papers.title: LinQuant: Functional Invariances for Low-Precision Linear Recurrences
papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are emerging as practical alternatives to softmax attention in large language models, appearing in both standalone and hybrid architectures. However, despite their rapid emergence, low-precision inference remains much less developed for these models than for softmax attention. During prefill, chunkwise-parallel algorithms cast much of the recurrence as dense matrix multiplications, suggesting a natural path to low-precision execution. Simply quantizing these operations in their native form, however, can be fragile. In this work, we identify functional invariances that preserve the full-precision computation while making the operands more amenable to quantization. Building on this observation, we introduce LinQuant, a framework for low-precision recurrent prefill based on seven such invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescalings, and alternative placements of recurrent decay and write factors. We derive when these transformations remain valid across common recurrence families spanning linear, gated, and delta-rule updates, and show that they provide complementary degrees of freedom for improving low-precision accuracy. We implement these transformations in INT8 and INT4 kernels and evaluate them on the recurrences of Nemotron-H, Qwen3.5, and Kimi Linear, recovering most of the accuracy lost to quantization while accelerating recurrent prefill. We also augment SSDi8, an existing low-precision prefill pipeline for Mamba-2, improving perplexity at matched prefill latency on pretrained Mamba-2 and Nemotron-H models. Altogether, these results demonstrate the practical utility of invariance-based quantization for recurrent models.

papers.title: Actuator-Aware Observer Inputs for Cascade ADRC of Quadrotors Under Rotor Lag, Measurement Delay and Sensor Noise
papers.abstract: In sampled cascade linear active disturbance rejection control (LADRC) of quadrotors, the extended-state observer is usually driven by the instantaneous command, although the delayed measurement reflects an earlier, rotor-filtered acceleration. This simulation and software-in-the-loop (SITL) study examines actuator-aware (AA) observer inputs: the altitude and attitude observers use the limited virtual input filtered by a rotor-lag model and aligned with the measurement delay, and the horizontal observers use the acceleration reconstructed from the measured attitude. Fixed gains are selected on the sampled model under sensitivity and step-response requirements and covariance-based ceilings on the noise-induced control increment, including the path from position noise to the inner loop. In 30 paired set-point trials, the two AA designs reach position root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 19.2 and 16.9~mm, versus 65.5~mm for a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller tuned under the same requirements, with lower rotor-command increments. Ablations attribute the improvement to the rotor-lag model and the measured-attitude input; delay alignment is negligible at the nominal 5-ms delay. PX4 SITL runs reproduce these results within 2~mm. Behind the PX4 state estimator, the white-noise ceilings no longer describe the loop. After redesign with an identified estimation-error model, one AA design reduces the set-point RMSE from 59.1 to 44.0~mm with a 15\% lower quantized rotor-command increment, whereas the half-gain variant is worse than the PID. With fixed gains, the AA designs tolerate less unmodelled rotor lag and delay than the PID. Hardware validation remains future work.

papers.title: Topology of Wannierizable Insulators
papers.abstract: We study the freedom in choosing Wannier centers and the associated symmetry representations in noninteracting Wannierizable insulators.
