We compare Wyckoff deformations of atomic configurations with symmetry-preserving adiabatic deformations of occupied states, both with and without adding common occupied atomic orbitals. Explicit examples show that stable Wyckoff equivalence and adiabatic equivalence at fixed filling do not imply each other. In spinless $Fm'm'm'$, an Euler class distinguishes stably Wyckoff-equivalent configurations. In spinless $P\overline1'$, adiabatically equivalent configurations remain distinct under stable Wyckoff deformations. We also classify when stable Wyckoff and stable adiabatic equivalence coincide. They agree in two or fewer dimensions and in three-dimensional spinful systems. For three-dimensional spinless systems, Chern insulator pumps give additional equivalences in 134 magnetic space groups. These groups preserve spacetime orientation and have a point whose site-symmetry group contains $222$, $\overline1'$, or $\overline4'$.

papers.title: ParaTTT: Parallelizing Test-Time Training Layers with Deep Memories
papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) layers replace the linear fast-weight memory of modern recurrent architectures with a small neural network trained online by gradient descent. This nonlinear memory is more expressive than the linear memories of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, but is difficult to parallelize: existing implementations such as TTT-MLP rely on sequential, block-wise weight updates that run several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences. Their block-wise execution only approximates the token-by-token online recurrence, whereas linear recurrences admit an exact chunkwise-parallel evaluation. We introduce ParaTTT (PTTT), an algorithm for parallelizing arbitrarily deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining estimates of the inner-loop gradient trajectory. Each refinement consists of three chunkwise-parallel passes: a forward pass that evaluates the resulting feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass that computes the readout trajectory and its feature gradients, and a backward pass that propagates these gradients into a new estimate. The exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration. Training and prefill approximate this recurrence with a finite number of iterations, while decoding applies the exact token-by-token update without refinement. We prove geometric convergence for a two-layer variant under sufficient contraction conditions. With two refinement steps at 4K context, PTTT evaluates the inner-loop trajectory $32\times$ faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, while the full 340M model trains $4.9\times$ faster. Models trained at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 and remain competitive with same-size Transformers on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with better recall than the linear recurrences.

papers.title: Skeleton Coding: Program Structure as Control for AI Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents are typically provided end-to-end behavioral specifications that the code they produce should satisfy, such as tests and input-output examples. How many such specifications must users provide, and which ones, for the agent to implement a program that fulfills their intent? We argue that this cannot be determined a priori, because it depends on the structure of the implementation, which is left to the agent to decide. An agent first commits to a structure - that is, a decomposition into data types, modules, and functions - which fixes a class of candidate programs; behavioral specifications then select a program within that class. A set of tests that suffices for one structure may leave another underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples. Since the structure is chosen by the agent, users cannot ensure their specification is complete without reverse-engineering such structure from thousands of lines of generated code. To address this issue, we introduce Skeleton Coding, a process in which humans jointly specify the structure in high-level, code-like format, alongside behavioral specifications for the desired outcome. Theoretically, we model AI-assisted coding as a control problem, and show that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests users must supply to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. Empirically, across four models and three benchmarks, the best-performing skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. Even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27%. Skeletons also narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while lowering implementation cost by 15-26x, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.

papers.title: Nijenhuis Lie $n$-algebras
papers.abstract: We introduce a homotopical framework for Nijenhuis operators on semistrict Lie $n$-algebras ($n$-term $L_\infty$-algebras) for every $n \ge 1$ and, more generally, on arbitrary $L_\infty$-algebras. A Nijenhuis operator is defined as a family $N = (N_q)_{q \ge 1}$ of multilinear maps, with $N_1$ linear, realizing an $L_\infty$-morphism from an $N$-twisted copy of the structure to the original one. We prove that this condition is equivalent to the vanishing, at every arity $m$, of the $m$-th Nijenhuis torsion up to a correction term $Λ^N_m$ formed by higher-component substitutions, and we provide a closed combinatorial formula for $Λ^N_m$ as a sum over set partitions. Along the way, we show that the arity-$k$ Nijenhuis torsion factors canonically as a composite of $k$ commuting elementary slot deformations. The resulting objects form a category $\mathbf{NijLie}_n$; we establish that $\mathbf{NijLie}_m$ embeds as the full subcategory of $\mathbf{NijLie}_n$ on objects concentrated in the bottom $m$ degrees for all $m \le n$. These levels assemble into a tower whose first three stages are classical Nijenhuis Lie algebras, the Nijenhuis Lie $2$-algebras of Das, and the newly introduced Nijenhuis Lie $3$-algebras. We characterize the strict and skeletal objects at every level, introduce $n$-term representations up to homotopy of a Nijenhuis Lie algebra, and prove that the semidirect product construction establishes an equivalence between the category of such representations and split abelian $\mathbf{NijLie}_n$-extensions. Finally, two corrections to published level-three identities are documented, and all component identities up to arity five are verified via computer algebra.

papers.title: Computing GR(1) Assume-Guarantee Contracts
papers.abstract: Assume-guarantee contracts provide a set of algebraic operations that enable the efficient compositional design and analysis of complex engineering systems. The explicit computation of these operations at component interfaces is currently supported only for some logics lacking a notion of time. This paper develops theory and algorithms to compute these operations when the contracts are expressed in the GR(1) modulo theory. The key challenge is the computation of two quantifier elimination problems for temporal formulas. We develop context-aided variable elimination procedures on GR(1)-modulo formulas, establish their soundness, characterize subproblem-wise optimal solutions within an admissible class of formulas, and use the procedures to compute contract operations, including composition and quotient. We implement the resulting framework in Pacti, automating compositional reasoning over GR(1) contracts. Finally, we demonstrate the framework on an automated emergency-braking case study, where we compute system-level contracts and expose compatibility conditions arising from the interaction of component specifications. Experiments on synthetic families show that the cost is governed by the number of eliminated variables and liveness conjuncts, and a comparison with exact automata-based elimination shows complementary scaling.

papers.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.

papers.title: Integer electron-count cuts in variational second-order reduced-density-matrix theory. I. Molecular dissociation with fixed real-space and orbital partitions
papers.abstract: Van Aggelen et al. [Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys. 11, 5558 (2009)] showed that variational second-order reduced-density-matrix (2-RDM) calculations with the standard two-index conditions dissociate diatomic molecules into fractionally charged atoms with energies far below the exact limit, a drastic violation of size consistency; the proposed subsystem constraints require auxiliary calculations with the physical fragment Hamiltonians. We show that two long-known ingredients, combined, remove most of this failure without such calculations: the requirement that the number of electrons in a part of the molecule be an integer, imposed as linear conditions on the 2-RDM, and a chemically motivated partition of the molecule into atomic regions bounded at the bond critical point of the Hartree-Fock density. In a minimal basis, compared with full configuration interaction, a single such condition reduces the energy errors of NO$^+$ and CN$^-$ at 6 Å from 108.9 and 80.7 m$E_\mathrm{h}$ to less than 0.02 m$E_\mathrm{h}$. In N$_2^+$, whose fragments have the correct mean population but too small a fluctuation, the region and three-index conditions act complementarily, reducing the error at 4 Å from 138.0 to 1.6 m$E_\mathrm{h}$. At the separated-atom limit, the region cuts make the $P$, $Q$, $G$ energy additive over the fragments to within 0.2 m$E_\mathrm{h}$ in 7 of 10 systems, 3 already nearly additive without cuts; adding the $T_1$ and $T_2$ conditions also makes CO nearly additive, while a nonadditive error remains for N$_2^+$ and CO$^+$. Effective partitions are those whose condition is nearly saturated by the exact state.

papers.title: Risk measures for infinite-server queues driven by a Cox-BESQ process
papers.abstract: This paper analyses infinite-server queues driven by a Cox process whose stochastic arrival intensity follows a squared Bessel (BESQ) process. Exploiting the affine structure of the model and previously derived transform representations for infinite-server queue variables, we derive the joint moment-generating function (MGF) of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the time integral of the queue length at two or more dates. This enables a detailed analysis of the temporal evolution of infinite-server queues driven by a Cox-BESQ process. The availability of these explicit MGFs enables the development of risk measures for these variables, such as the joint moments of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the integral of the number of customers in the system over a time interval, conditional on one of these variables exceeding a critical threshold. These risk measures can be determined at one or two dates. They rely essentially on the explicit form of the MGF of the state variables and on Fourier representations of the risk measures. Numerical experiments demonstrate the practical implementation of the proposed methodology and highlight the relevance of the theoretical results.

papers.title: Probabilistic Causal Panel Analysis
papers.abstract: Many causal panel estimators construct counterfactuals using weights or latent structure estimated directly from observed outcomes, making their estimates sensitive to observation noise. Bayesian hierarchical models can account for this noise and pool information across related observations. Existing Bayesian approaches to causal panel analysis, however, typically specify counterfactual imputation within the probabilistic model, so changing estimators may require a new formulation. We develop a framework that learns the latent untreated panel with a probabilistic model and applies established causal estimators to its posterior draws. The model accommodates non-Gaussian observations and structured pooling, while re-estimation across draws propagates uncertainty through counterfactual imputation. We establish conditions for posterior consistency and characterize how pooling affects imputation risk. Under correct posterior specification, we show that the excess Bayes risk of our approach is bounded by the causal estimator's expected squared imputation error when given the true latent outcomes in observed untreated cells. We also develop a fast cross-validation approach for model selection and calibration of predictive uncertainty for treatment effects. We use simulations to examine when pooling helps or harms imputation and cross-validation to assess whether probabilistic modeling improves accuracy in multiple empirical applications.

papers.title: Does the Escape Fraction Prescription Shape Reionization History and Morphology?
papers.abstract: The escape fraction of ionizing photons, $f_{\rm esc}$, is among the least constrained quantities of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), and intergalactic opacity prevents its direct measurement at high redshifts. We constrain three power-law parameterizations, $f_{\rm esc}(z)$, $f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h})$, and $f_{\rm esc}(z, M_{\rm h})$, against JWST UV luminosity functions and EoR observables (ionizing emissivity, neutral hydrogen fraction, and Thomson optical depth) using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, with priors allowing $f_{\rm esc}$ to increase or decrease with redshift and halo mass. We propagate the best-fit models into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 and compare their ionization morphology and 21 cm power spectra with a constant-$f_{\rm esc}$ model. All models reproduce the observations with nearly identical global reionization histories. The data favor $f_{\rm esc}$ decreasing with redshift, from $\approx 0.8$ at $z = 5$ to $\approx 0.35$ at $z = 15$. The halo-mass-only model prefers $f_{\rm esc}$ increasing with halo mass, but this trend is a proxy for redshift evolution. When both dependencies vary jointly, the data prefer a mass-independent $f_{\rm esc}$. At matched global neutral fraction, all four prescriptions yield similar ionization morphology, and the 21 cm power spectra agree to within $\approx 10\%$. Thus, once calibrated against the same observations, the details of the $f_{\rm esc}$ prescription, set by interstellar medium physics, largely average out in both global observables and the 21 cm power spectrum. Distinguishing them may require statistics beyond the power spectrum, such as Ly$α$ and 21 cm forest sightline statistics, or forecasts that exploit their small differences in reionization timing.

papers.title: Holographic Approaches to Hadron Structure
papers.abstract: We give an introduction to and an overview of holographic approaches to QCD and hadron structure. After an introduction to the string-theoretic foundations of holographic QCD, we review the predictions of top-down and bottom-up models for the phenomenology of mesons, baryons, and glueballs. We focus on the top-down model following from probe flavor branes in the Witten model of low-energy Yang-Mills theory and, in the more phenomenological approach of bottom-up models, mostly on minimal models based on five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, which also implement global symmetries and their anomalies consistently, but allow the high-energy behavior to better match real QCD.

papers.title: How Tuning, Reference Preview, Actuator Modeling, and Fallback Policies Change Quadrotor Controller Comparisons: A Reproducible Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. Matched tuning changed the mean-RMSE ordering of the fixed baseline settings, mainly by moving BL-SMC from last to first. The ordering recurred on fresh realizations and did not change with 48 candidates, although BL-SMC's lead there depends on a wider search range for one of its gains. Reference preview reduced MPC tracking error and removed fallback activity on the figure-eight task. In single abrupt-step runs, completion depended jointly on fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in these profiles. We propose a reporting checklist that adds tuning effort, failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing to tracking accuracy.

papers.title: Learning to Remember: Advances in Memory Mechanisms for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation. By aligning conceptual motivations, computational memory mechanisms, benchmarks, and deployment concerns, the survey provides a structured roadmap for designing memory-augmented LLM agents that are persistent, adaptive, auditable, and safe to update over time.

papers.title: Results for distinct covering systems with a prime minimum modulus $q \ge 11$
papers.abstract: We prove that if the smallest modulus of a covering system is a prime $q \ge 11$, then the sum of the reciprocals of the moduli is at least $1+10^{-33}$. This improves on a previous more general bound of the first two authors in this particular case. We also show that it is impossible to construct a covering system using distinct multiples of $q$ as moduli. Finally, we show as a corollary that it is impossible to construct $10$ distinct covering systems with the property that no modulus is used in more than one of the covering systems.

papers.title: Minimum Extension Degrees for Reed-Solomon Codes:Exact Values and a Quadratic Transition
papers.abstract: We study the minimum extension degree of Reed-Solomon codes admitting exact linear repair of every failed coordinate from any $d$ surviving coordinates at the cut-set bound. Write $s=d-k+1$, and let $Q_s(n)$ be the minimum product of $n$ pairwise coprime integers, each at least $s$. We locate the transition for the formula $sQ_s(n)$ near $n=d^2$: for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$ and sufficiently large $d$, the formula is exact up to $(1-\varepsilon)d^2$, whereas strict improvement is possible at every length at least $(1+\varepsilon)d^2$, uniformly over the base field and code dimension. The lower bound follows from an inequality for the cost of residual prime powers; the upper bound follows from an existing affine-plane construction. We also show that the full-helper coordinate-count bound is attained over sufficiently large base fields. Finally, nonlinear repair at cut-set equality induces linear repair over the prime field. Thus the degree bounds over that field remain valid, and the same transition holds when the repair base field is prime.

papers.title: Yb/Sr optical clock comparison at 2.08E-18 uncertainty over a 1350-km fiber link
papers.abstract: Redefining the International system of Units (SI) second requires independent frequency-ratio measurements between clocks based on different laboratories, with an overall uncertainty below 5E-18, to validate individual clock evaluations through consistency checks. Reaching this uncertainty over long distances has remained challenging. So far, comparisons at this level have been achieved only a few times, between co-located clocks, and their results disagree markedly. Previous high-precision comparisons have therefore been limited to local or kilometre-scale links. Here we compare a ytterbium optical lattice clock in Wuhan with a strontium optical lattice clock in Shanghai over a phase-stabilized fiber link spanning 1350 km, and determine the Yb/Sr frequency ratio to be 1.207 507 039 343 337 716 0(26), with a Bayesian statistical uncertainty of 1.14E-18 and a total uncertainty of 2.18E-18. To our knowledge, this is the first intercity long distance frequency-ratio measurement, whose total uncertainty reaches the level required by the redefinition roadmap. The measured ratio exhibits a significant correlation with Earth tides and its response agree with the model within the statistical uncertainty. At intercity scale, this comparison demonstrates the capability of an optical-clock network for frequency comparison and Earths gravitational-potential sensing, a key step toward a wide-area optical-clock network.

papers.title: Symplectic capacities and Weyl laws from Abelian Higgs min max theory
papers.abstract: For a Hermitian line bundle $E\to Y$ over a Riemannian manifold $(Y^n,g)$, the self-dual Abelian-Higgs energy is defined by $\mathcal{E}^Y_{\varepsilon,g}(u,a)=\frac{1}{2π}\int_Y \left(|\nabla_a u|_g^2+\varepsilon^2|F_a|_g^2+ \frac{(1-|u|^2)^2}{4\varepsilon^2}\right)dV_g$, where $u$ is a smooth section of $E$, $a$ is a unitary connection, and $F_a$ is its curvature. Pigati and Stern studied the energy as a codimension-two analogue of the Allen-Cahn energy to study minimal submanifolds in a Riemannian manifold. In this paper, we use this functional to define a nondecreasing sequence of symplectic capacities $\{c_k^{\mathrm{AH}}\}_{k\ge1}$ in dimension four by a min-max construction. In particular, we prove that $c_1^{\mathrm{AH}}$ is normalized on the ball and the cylinder. For the upper bound on the cylinder, we combine Gromov's theory of families of $J$-holomorphic spheres with Taubes's planar vortex. For the lower bound on the ball, we use the properties of the Abelian-Higgs theory developed by Pigati-Stern, together with a geometric estimate on smooth approximations to the double of the ball and an equivariant deformation of low energy sublevels. These estimates give the normalization without Seiberg-Witten theory. We then use Seiberg-Witten moduli spaces on $\mathbb{CP}^2$ and $S^2\times S^2$ to prove an upper bound on the higher capacities of balls and the formula $c_k^{\mathrm{AH}}(Z^4(a),ω_0)=ka$. We also prove Weyl laws for domains in $\mathbb{R}^4$, both for the capacity sequence and for the min-max sequence with the standard Euclidean metric. For these results, we construct AH sweepouts from moduli spaces of the solutions to the perturbed Seiberg-Witten equations.

papers.title: Extrinsic Curvature Estimation by Closest Point Projection of Rays
papers.abstract: We propose a parametrization-free method that estimates the principal curvatures and principal directions of a submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^d$ from the closest point projections of a few random rays, without coordinate charts or local fitting. The projection of a ray induces a curve on the submanifold, which is a geodesic only in special cases, so its curvature is in general not a curvature of the submanifold. The velocities of these curves, however, relate to the derivative of the closest point projection, whose eigenpairs carry the information of the principal curvatures and directions. Finite differences along $d$ rays can estimate them without relying on the normal information at a cost of $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$ besides the projections, and we provide error bounds. The method extends to submanifolds of any codimension and to point clouds, and experiments confirm the predicted rates in up to $128$ dimensions.

papers.title: LegoSR: A Unified Framework for Self-Improving Agent-Guided Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: Discovering equations from data provides governing laws, constitutive relations and closure models for scientific understanding and prediction. Yet a method that succeeds on one system may fail on another or on noisy data, so discovery depends on expert trial and error. Unsuccessful searches can still reveal useful parts of an equation, but these clues must be recognized and combined. We present LegoSR, a unified framework for agent-guided equation discovery built on composable discovery and cumulative experience. Seven complementary equation discovery methods and shared computational modules form reusable building blocks, connected through a common equation representation. Researchers can launch discovery with one command and guide it with partially known equations. LegoSR Agent selects methods, revises searches using feedback and combines partial findings into new hypotheses. Its Experience Library consolidates graded outcomes into lessons that guide later tasks across equation families. Evaluation covers 134 algebraic regression problems, 40 ordinary differential equation targets and 25 partial differential equation problems at several noise levels, together with three case studies. On noisy PDEs, LegoSR Agent recovers more equations than seven expert-tuned methods combined and stays close to them on ODEs. It also exceeds a generic agent with the same model, tools and budget by up to 28 percentage points, with 63-73% shorter median wall-clock time on PDE problems.

papers.title: The Cost of an Unknown Horizon for the Last Iterate of Clipped SGD under Heavy-Tailed Noise
papers.abstract: When training stops at a data-dependent time, a guarantee for the returned model must hold at all times simultaneously. We study the last iterate of clipped SGD on smooth convex objectives under heavy-tailed stochastic gradients with a bounded central $p$th moment, $1<p\le2$. With a known horizon $T$, clipped SGD reaches the optimal last-iterate rate $O(T^{-α_p})$, where $α_p=(p-1)/p$ (Liu, 2026; Jiang et al., 2026). Without a known horizon, Chezhegov et al. (ICLR 2026) obtained the time-uniform rate $\tilde O(t^{-2(p-1)/(3p)})$ and conjectured that a better schedule reaches the optimal rate. We show that for clipped SGD, and more generally for every rule whose iterate does not advance on rounds without new gradient information, the optimal time-uniform rate is $\tilde O(t^{-β_p})$, where $β_p=2(p-1)/(3p-1)$. Our deterministic schedule for clipped SGD uses neither a horizon nor a confidence input and attains $\tilde O(t^{-β_p})$ at all times simultaneously, and hence almost surely. Conversely, no such rule attains $\tilde O(t^{-r})$ at all times for any $r>β_p$; for clipped SGD, this holds even with adaptive, randomized step sizes and clipping thresholds. Under finite variance, the known-horizon, optimal time-uniform, and previous time-uniform exponents are $1/2$, $2/5$, and $1/3$. Since $β_p<α_p$, the conjecture, which holds with a known horizon, fails without one. By contrast, an update that queries gradients at the running average can advance the iterate on rounds without new gradient information and attains $\tilde O(t^{-α_p})$ at all times. Memory alone does not suffice: heavy-ball momentum with geometric forgetting and polynomially bounded step sizes cannot improve on the exponent $β_p$.

papers.title: Maximizing Measures for Subadditive and Almost-Additive Potentials on Countable-Alphabet Subshifts
papers.abstract: We prove the existence of maximizing measures for subadditive and almost-additive families of upper semicontinuous, bounded-above potentials $\mathcal F=\{f_n\}_{n\geq1}$ on closed subshifts over countable alphabets. Under a coercivity condition on $f_1$, we prove that every maximizing sequence, that is, $\{μ_k\}_{k\geq1}\subset\mathcal M_σ(X)$ satisfying $\bar{\mathcal F}(μ_k)\toβ(\mathcal F)$, is uniformly tight, preventing mass from escaping to arbitrarily large symbols. As a consequence, a maximizing measure exists. We apply these results to matrix cocycles, establishing the existence of invariant measures that realize the joint spectral radius for countable families of matrices.

papers.title: Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design
papers.abstract: De novo protein design campaigns remain bottlenecked by the inference compute time required to generate and rank candidates, limiting wider functional exploration. Here, we introduce and evaluate an epitope excision approach that truncates targets to local interface windows to accelerate both backbone diffusion and structure prediction. Across 15 targets and 3,666 designs, excised windows closely reproduced full-target binding interfaces (median CαRMSD of 0.37 Å) and made it practical to design binders against the 719-residue extracellular domain of fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) by cutting RFdiffusion and AlphaFold3 GPU time by ~ 88% in one of the epitopes. Pairing this workflow with an agentic optimization loop allowed the system to autonomously identify catalytic-site targeting strategies. Under a fixed compute budget, a human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflow raised the computational hit rate from 5.06% to 9.33% while further cutting GPU hours by ~ 42%. We also found that omitting target multiple sequence alignments during refolding roughly substantially increased the apparent yield. Wet-lab validation with yeast display identified nanomolar binders from the generated designs with the HITL and the fully autonomous agent (human-out-of-the-loop, HOOTL) arms recovering more enriched designs than the PI-alone baseline. Together, target excision and agent-guided search offer a practical way to scale de novo binder design to large, therapeutically relevant proteins.

papers.title: Communicating with the Entire Population: Machine Translation of Emergency Alerts and Warnings
papers.abstract: It is essential that we communicate with the entirety of an affected population during a crisis, including those who do not speak a region's dominant language(s). Commercial Translation tools offer a tempting solution to broaden access and can provide a lifeline when no other resources are available. However, Emergency response managers often operate in the dark regarding the quality and adequacy of these automated outputs. In this paper, we conduct a nationwide survey of emergency managers to understand their current workflows, perspectives, and operational challenges. We then evaluate commercial translation tools against these needs, shedding light on their utility and offering practical guidance on how and when these tools can be safely used in emergency response.

papers.title: Corner Regularity and Asymptotics for the Two-Dimensional Radiation Transport Equation
papers.abstract: The regularity of solutions to the two-dimensional radiation transport equation plays a central role in understanding the behavior of scalar flux near geometric corners. In a previous study of Kaper's corner singularity problem, the physical transport kernel was decomposed into its principal inverse-distance singularity and a lower-order remainder, reducing the corner asymptotic analysis to the question of whether the scalar flux possesses sufficient continuity to justify differentiation of the associated singular potential. The required regularity, however, remained unresolved. In this paper, we establish a sharp modulus-of-continuity estimate for the scalar flux generated by the physical transport kernel and prove the estimate $ω_ϕ(h)=O\!\left(h\log(D/h)\right)$, which implies Dini continuity. This estimate yields absolute convergence of the fluctuation term arising in the differentiated principal potential and permits a rigorous differentiation formula for transport solutions. Using this regularity framework, we derive the fixed-angle asymptotic behavior of the scalar flux and its first derivatives near a rectangular corner. For every fixed interior ray, the gradient exhibits logarithmic growth, while the scalar flux admits an $r\log(1/r)$ correction with an explicitly identified coefficient determined by the corner values of the flux and source. The analysis shows that a rectangular corner does not generate a singularity stronger than the logarithmic first-derivative singularity already present in smooth-boundary transport theory. Numerical calculations on benchmark problems are consistent with the theoretical predictions. These results provide a rigorous resolution of the regularity issue underlying Kaper's corner singularity problem and establish a mathematical framework for corner asymptotics in two-dimensional radiation transport.

papers.title: Hyperparameter-Free Boundary-Interior t-vMF Dice Loss for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Class imbalance and errors near anatomical boundaries remain challenges in medical image segmentation, motivating loss functions that account for these difficulties. Adaptive t-vMF Dice Loss adjusts the similarity function during training but requires hyperparameter tuning. We propose Self-Tuned Boundary-Aware t-vMF Dice Loss (STB-tvMF Dice), which adapts the function separately for boundary and interior regions without tuning shape-adaptation parameters. Each region's shape parameter of t-vMF function is determined from its mean prediction-target cosine similarity in the preceding epoch and remains fixed throughout the current epoch. This rule maximizes the slope of the similarity function at the observed mean similarity, providing a principled basis for adaptation without validation-based parameter selection. Experiments on three datasets and architectures demonstrated its effectiveness. On Synapse with U-Net, STB-tvMF Dice achieved a mean DSC of 70.75%, compared with 63.03% for Adaptive t-vMF Dice Loss. Our code will be available soon.

papers.title: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
papers.abstract: Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool did. We saw such misrepresentations in a production RAG research system used by the Pilsudski Institute in New York, where tool output formatters misled an agent into giving wrong or incomplete information to users. Each tool did its job correctly, but its output omitted search limits, result caps, or identifier namespaces. Within this same production system, we studied whether faulty formatters mislead agents and verifiers and how much repaired wording helps. We fed tool results to agents using two formatter versions: one with key omissions and one with all missing details clearly stated. That difference alone changed what the agents claimed and what the verifiers accepted. Unsupported agent claims dropped substantially for three of the four failure types. In one test, verifiers went from accepting incorrect answers 90 out of 90 times to rejecting them 90 out of 90 times. A control showed the verifiers could catch the errors once they were given the missing facts and asked to judge correctness. We include the audit prompt we used with Codex and Claude Code in an exploratory demonstration, written with prior knowledge of our own system's defects. When pointed at an old version of our own system, it rediscovered the defects that were still live and surfaced twelve more we had not catalogued. When pointed at OpenClaw and Hermes, two of the best-known open-source agentic systems, it found warped formatters in both. We opened PRs to fix both, and the OpenClaw fix has already been merged. Practitioners can run the same prompt on their own systems today.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) approximations of capillary menisci in polygonal channels
papers.abstract: A capillary interface must satisfy both its curvature equation and the contact angle at the container walls. We study how strong-form physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) approximate these conditions when the prescribed equilibrium is geometrically incompatible. In zero gravity, the Concus-Finn critical contact angles for spanning graphs in square and equilateral-triangular cross-sections are respectively 45 degrees and 60 degrees. Below these angles, classical subdomain flux balance yields a certified lower bound on the continuous combined interior and wall residual loss, retaining the sampling densities and wall weight. The subdomain bounds and their sums over disjoint regions tend uniformly to zero as the contact angle approaches the threshold from below at fixed wall weight. The computed PINNs return smooth graphs with finite axial extent in the nonexistence regime: small interior residuals coexist with corner wall-flux deficits, where the adjoining contact-angle conditions demand more flux than a finite-slope graph can supply. At the default wall weight, several degrees into this regime, neural losses computed by quadrature are 1.6-1.8 times the bound from one cut per corner, with higher ratios occurring near the critical angle. Polynomial least-squares comparisons support the same geometric interpretation in a second smooth trial family. The bound supplies a physical scale for the residual compromise and explains why residual assessment must include wall flux and continuum compatibility.

papers.title: Conditional Reset-Enhanced Dissipative Quantum Metrology
papers.abstract: Open quantum sensors work either in a transient regime with finely timed readout or in a steady-state regime with robust but weaker sensitivity. To overcome this trade-off, we ask whether repeatedly resetting a probe to a fixed state, even a suboptimal one, can outperform the optimal single-shot transient protocol. We prove that blind resets, triggered by an external clock, cannot do so even with memory. Conditional resets, triggered by the probe's own state, break this no-go result by capturing parameter-dependent quantum jumps or by recycling heralded losses, for parameters encoded in dissipative rates and Hamiltonians alike. A three-level thermometer capturing thermal excitations outperforms the optimal no-reset protocol in both transient and steady-state regimes, even with a $40\%$ preparation error. Conditional resets can even saturate the ultimate bound of nonequilibrium thermometry with a single readout. Heralded recycling enables steady-state frequency estimation to outperform optimal transient Ramsey interferometry. The advantages extend to interacting probes and to elapsed-time estimation, and both mechanisms can be realized using established experimental techniques.

papers.title: DeXplicit: Making Physical State Explicit in Dexterous Manipulation World Models
papers.abstract: Before acting on an object, a robot needs to anticipate how its hand motion will change the physical world and what the resulting scene will look like. Existing approaches typically entangle action-conditioned dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis within a video generation model, or represent dynamics as point trajectories without explicit object structure. We introduce DeXplicit, a dexterous manipulation world model that predicts how the world evolves explicitly in metric 3D before rendering its visual consequences. Given an initial scene and a future hand trajectory, a lightweight 3D dynamics network predicts object-centric motion and deformation, providing structured and geometrically grounded future world states. These predictions guide video generation through appearance transport and geometric projection, allowing the renderer to focus on uncertain and newly visible content rather than implicitly learning object dynamics from pixels. To retain these controls in an efficient autoregressive generator, we develop a two-stage causal adaptation procedure: alignment of the transferred geometry, hand, and appearance conditions to a frozen few-step backbone, followed by on-policy distillation with a conditional video critic. The resulting model generates four-frame latent blocks with two denoising steps while conditioning on its generated history. Across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, DeXplicit reduces moved-point error by 27-40% relative to PointWorld and improves object IoU+ by 47% on HOT3D under a shared renderer. Causal-DeXplicit retains an object IoU+ of 0.490 while accelerating video synthesis by 57 times relative to our 14B bidirectional configuration.

papers.title: Thouless Pumping of One-Dimensional Dark Solitons and Domain Walls
papers.abstract: We predict that quantized transport of dark solitons and domain walls can be observed in mutually sliding optical lattices in both focusing and defocusing nonlinear materials. Two different classes of underlying periodic backgrounds are considered here -- unstaggered and staggered -- which are accurately represented, respectively, by the in-phase and out-of-phase trains of Wannier functions. The nonlinear excitations formed on top of these backgrounds -- dark solitons and domain walls -- are sustained by defocusing or focusing Kerr nonlinearities of the optical medium. Despite non-zero asymptotics, dark solitons and domain walls can still undergo quantized topological transport in dynamically changing refractive index landscape when they and background on which they are constructed are dynamically stable. The extended intervals of propagation constants (and, correspondingly, of the background amplitude) and lattice depths, where stable quantized transport occurs, are identified for both dark solitons and domain walls. Outside these intervals, the quantized transport regime is found to be unstable. Our results extend the concept of nonlinear topological transport from bright to dark soliton states.

papers.title: Resonant-pair energy return beyond the early Green-Kubo plateau in a quartic chain
papers.abstract: The Green-Kubo formula gives the thermal conductivity as the long-time limit of the running Green-Kubo integral, the time integral of the equilibrium heat-current autocorrelation function. In simulations, this integral often approaches a plateau at finite time. We study how it evolves after such an early plateau in a weakly coupled chain of quartic oscillators, where the plateau value is close to the rate at which independent neighboring cells exchange energy. Two neighboring cells with nearly equal frequencies form a resonant pair: their relative phase oscillates like a pendulum, and energy that has crossed the bond between them flows back. We show that, at weak coupling, the running integral of such a pair follows the pendulum trapping response of nonlinear Landau damping. For the quartic potential, the small-oscillation period of this pendulum, $T_{\rm lib}\propto\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ with intercell coupling $\varepsilon$, does not depend on energy, so all resonant pairs share one time scale. Without fitted parameters, the theory predicts that the running integral of an isolated pair falls to a negative first minimum of $-0.74$ times the plateau value at $0.952\,T_{\rm lib}$. Simulations of isolated pairs approach this prediction as the coupling decreases. In chains, the first minimum occurs on the same time scale but is shallower, and a small positive value can remain much later. Chains of strongly chaotic cells show no comparable decrease, and energy-conserving noise much faster than $1/T_{\rm lib}$ largely removes the decrease. The pair response provides a quantitative finite-time reference for interpreting early Green-Kubo plateaus in such chains.

papers.title: Sparse-grid discretizations of BGG sequences
papers.abstract: For Bernstein--Gelfand--Gelfand (BGG) complexes, we develop the first sparse-grid finite element discretizations, for dramatically reducing the number of degrees of freedom used in tensor-product finite elements. Alpert wavelets and their first and second primitives yield compatible hierarchies of discontinuous, continuous, and continuously differentiable piecewise polynomials, that serve as one-dimensional ingredients of BGG sparse-grid finite elements. For the three-dimensional Hessian, elasticity, and div-div complexes, we construct a bounded commuting sparse-grid projection that yields stable discrete potentials, exactness and uniform inf-sup stability of associated mixed methods. Under mixed Sobolev regularity, we also prove sparse-grid approximation estimates with dimension-independent algebraic convergence rates in the number of degrees of freedom. Experiments for a three-dimensional incompatibility problem and a two-dimensional biharmonic problem on an annulus illustrate the efficiency of sparse grids relative to tensor-product finite elements.

papers.title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
papers.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

papers.title: AI Security Literacy: Ecosystem-Based Competency Framework and K-12 Learning Platform
papers.abstract: Adoption of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI-literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. We propose an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, ground its technical dimensions in public AI-safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi-seed adversarial evaluation, and ground its attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro-data from U.S. teachers and adults. Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy, and teachers see their own AI use as easing their work but students' use as complicating it; on the technical side, a reported robustness figure depends as much on the attack and the particular trained model as on the system evaluated. NeuralFortify, a browser-based K-12 platform built on real AI models, is presented as an illustrative operationalization.

papers.title: CRAFT-ε: A Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for the Static Relative Permittivity of Pure Organic Liquids
papers.abstract: The static relative permittivity is an important property in thermodynamic modeling, electrochemistry, and solvent design, but predicting it directly from molecular structure remains challenging because both electronic polarization and molecular dipole orientation contribute to the measured response. Here, we introduce CRAFT-ε (Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for ε), a conformer-resolved molecular descriptor model for predicting the static relative permittivity of neutral pure liquids. Conformer free energies, molecular dipoles, and atom-resolved polarizabilities are obtained from a GFN2-xTB/ALPB 10 workflow. The molecular dipole is decomposed into chemically defined polar-fragment vectors, allowing fitted corrections to retain both the magnitude and relative orientation of local dipolar contributions. Electronic and orientational polarization are combined with a group-contribution molar volume in the Onsager-Kirkwood-Fröhlich relation. A staged parameterization with 41 parameters is applied to nonpolar, polar, and hydrogen-bonding compounds. For 1393 liquids with permittivities between 1.5 and 183, CRAFT-ε reaches a five-fold cross-validated average absolute deviation of 2.40 ({R^2} = 0.93). Conformational averaging 15 is essential for liquids with several polar groups. Compared with an established fragment-based model with 139 parameters, it reaches a similar cross-validated RMSE (3.65 versus 3.41) with about a quarter of the parameters and applies to every liquid of the dataset. The resulting framework provides a computationally inexpensive route from molecular structure to liquid dielectric response and forms a basis for later application to solvent mixtures and electrolyte systems.

papers.title: Lower Bounds for Smooth Nonconvex Zeroth-Order Optimization: The Price of Determinism under Low Curvature Trace
papers.abstract: Low curvature trace, an effective rank condition, is a common explanation for why randomized zeroth-order methods scale to language model fine-tuning. Can deterministic methods achieve the same savings? We study finding an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of an $L$-smooth nonconvex function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ from exact function values when, on the set where $f$ is below its initial value $f(0)$, the Hessian is dominated by a fixed matrix of trace at most $LE$. For an initial gap $Δ$, let $T=LΔ/\varepsilon^2$. We show that the Gaussian two-point method used in fine-tuning needs only $O(ET)$ calls if it accepts only the steps that decrease $f$, and we prove that every randomized method requires at least $Ω(ET)$ calls when $ET\le d$, so this cost is optimal up to constants. In that range, every deterministic method requires at least $\widetildeΩ(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$ calls, and adaptive subspace search attains $O(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$ calls. A deterministic method pays about $d$ calls for each direction it discovers, and the trace budget allows about $\sqrt{ET}$ directions. Determinism therefore multiplies the cost by a factor of order $d/(E+\sqrt{ET})$, up to logarithmic factors. Once $E$ exceeds $T$ by a logarithmic factor, deterministic methods require $Ω(dT)$ calls, just as they do without any trace budget. Our lower bounds hold for $C^\infty$ functions that satisfy the matrix bound on all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, even when each call also returns projections of the gradient, charged by their rank.

papers.title: Graphexon Mean Field Games on Large Network Limits
papers.abstract: This paper analyzes graphexon mean field games (GXMFG) on large network limits. By considering edge distributions of a sequence of finite graphs, we define the empirical graphexon measures and study their subsequential weak limits in a graphexon space consisting of all symmetric probability measures on $[0,1]^{2d}$. This concept of network limits extends graphon theory to general, not necessarily dense, networks. To formulate the game using the graphexon limit, we exploit a useful property that a probability measure on a product space is the product of a probability kernel and a marginal distribution. Based on such graph limits and the probability kernel of the associated graphexon measure, we derive the GXMFG equations, and present a detailed analysis for the linear-quadratic case. For linear-quadratic models with finite populations residing over large networks, we use the GXMFG equations to construct decentralized strategies, for which an $ε$-Nash equilibrium property is established.

papers.title: Latent Projection for Latent Planning
papers.abstract: Latent world models let an agent plan in latent space. The planner searches for an action sequence that minimizes a cost, and that cost is often the $\ell_2$ distance between the predicted terminal latent and the goal latent. The latent, however, is partly noise: the regularizer that prevents collapse during world model training promotes variance in the directions carrying no signal. We show that the same regularizer also supplies the structure to prune that noise in the latent. SIGReg drives the latent marginal to a standard Gaussian at every step, and assuming further that the latent sequence is a Gauss-Markov process, the transition is linear with its covariance pinned by the map itself, $z' \mid z \sim N(Az,\, I - AA^\top)$. Fitting the state dynamics $A$ therefore yields the covariance at no additional cost, and in its eigenbasis each latent direction carries its own uncertainty. Furthermore, constraining $A$ to be a normal matrix fixes that basis across timesteps, so one eigenbasis measures the uncertainty over an arbitrary number of steps and serves as a stable basis to compute the planning cost on. We then restrict the $\ell_2$ cost to the $k$-dimensional subspace the state dynamics carry forward with the least uncertainty. The correction is post hoc: the encoder, the predictor, the rollout, and the planner are all left untouched, and only a single constrained matrix, $A$, is fit. We evaluate across six environments and show large gains on the 2D navigation tasks, TwoRoom and PointMaze, raising success rate over the plain $\ell_2$ cost by up to $+54.7$ points under a harder planning setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yjang43/lp2.

papers.title: Mutually touching cylinders: Littlewood's seven, and at most ten in general
papers.abstract: We give a computer-assisted proof that at most seven congruent infinite circular cylinders in $\mathbb{R}^3$ can touch pairwise. This answers a question of Littlewood from 1968. For cylinders of arbitrary radii we prove the upper bound ten. Whether ten can be attained remains open.

papers.title: An Inverse Problem for the Moore Gibson Thompson Equation: Injectivity and Stability
papers.abstract: We study an inverse problem for the variable coefficient Moore Gibson Thompson (MGT) equation in a bounded domain, where the objective is to recover an unknown initial acceleration from boundary measurements of the acoustic field. We establish both injectivity and stability of the associated measurement operator. Injectivity is established through a unique continuation property by applying a theorem of Tataru for analytically principally normal operators. The argument relies on a factorization of the third order operator into wave type components, combined with Carleman estimates and propagation techniques in the spirit of Tataru. Stability is derived through a microlocal analysis of the forward operator, based on the construction of geometric optics approximate solutions and the identification of an elliptic pseudodifferential operator arising from microlocal back propagation of the data. These results connect the MGT inverse problem with the classical theory of hyperbolic inverse problems, such as photoacoustic tomography, while highlighting new features induced by the third order dynamics and damping.

papers.title: Capacitated Line Aggregation with Maximum Delay
papers.abstract: We study capacitated line aggregation with per-batch maximum delay. Requests arrive over time at locations on a rooted half-line and are served in instantaneous batches of at most $g$ requests. Each batch pays the distance to its farthest request plus the waiting time of its oldest request. The objective is to minimize the total cost. We give a deterministic online algorithm with competitive ratio $36+12\sqrt3$. The algorithm uses a Next Fit idea along paths of nested time intervals: it assigns a new group to an existing batch when a path-load test permits, and opens a new batch otherwise. The path load controls both capacity and the cost of opening new batches. Randomizing the common scale improves the expected competitive ratio to $(18+6\sqrt3)/\ln2$ against an oblivious adversary. Both guarantees extend to arbitrary indivisible request sizes. We also study capacitated LAD in the learning-augmented model. Advice revealed at its service times allows $(1+ε)$-consistency against every complete feasible advice schedule and $O(ε^{-2})$-robustness. The analysis charges repeated switches to successive decreases in the remaining advice cost. Controlled synthetic experiments with 9,180 exact-rational monitor runs illustrate both the benefit of optimal advice and the delayed fallback caused by the stated conservative constants. We provide all inputs, outcomes, and reproducibility code; the experiments do not claim performance on learned predictions or large-scale demand traces.

papers.title: Interior caustics and rigidity near noncircular ellipses
papers.abstract: We prove local rigidity near every fixed noncircular ellipse from integrable rational caustics in an arbitrary nonempty open interval $I\subset(0,1/2)$ of rotation numbers. For each fixed $r>11/2$ and bound on the $H^r$ norm of the elliptic graph displacement, every sufficiently $C^1$-small positively curved perturbation admitting such caustics at all rational rotation numbers in $I$ is an ellipse. It suffices to assume these caustics at a suitably chosen family of rotation numbers in $I$ with any prescribed rational point of $I$ as its unique accumulation point. The key linear result classifies real $L^2$ displacements with phase-independent orbit sums at every rational rotation number in $I$ as infinitesimal ellipse deformations.

papers.title: Commutative exact superalgebras and super-modular tensor categories
papers.abstract: We consider the theory of commutative exact algebras in braided finite tensor categories to superalgebras, motivated by extensions of vertex operator (super)algebras. For a braided category $\C$ let $\B=\C^{\gr}$ be the category of $\mathbb Z/2$-graded objects with the Koszul-signed braiding. Its even-morphism part is the underlying category of the supercategory of Creutzig-Kanade-McRae. A supercommutative superalgebra $A=A_0\oplus A_1$ in $\C$ is the same as a commutative algebra $\bA$ in $\B$, and super-local modules are the local $\bA$-modules. Hence, rigidity, pivotality and ribbon statements are instances of the ordinary theorems of Shimizu-Yadav, with the ribbon condition $θ_{A_0}=\id$, $θ_{A_1}=\varepsilon\,\id$, where $\varepsilon=\pm1$ is fixed by the statistics of the odd part. For $\C$ non-degenerate and $\bA$ haploid and exact we prove that the category of super-local modules is a braided finite tensor category whose Müger center is $\mathsf{sVect}$. It is the centralizer of a fermion in a non-degenerate category obtained by condensing in $\C\boxtimes(\text{toric code})$. If $\C$ is ribbon and $\bA$ is symmetric Frobenius it is ribbon. We give a self-contained treatment of graded simple current algebras and of the free fermion (Ising) example. We compare our formulation with Creutzig-Kanade-McRae and Creutzig-McRae-Shimizu-Yadav.

papers.title: Who Plans, Who Edits? Verified, Cost-Aware Division of Labor for LLM-Driven Analog Layout Repair
papers.abstract: Language-model agents can repair analog layouts when sign-off tools check every edit, but which model should plan a repair, which should edit it, and at what cost remain open questions. In our tool-grounded repair agent, models only choose bounded layout operators; sign-off tools rerun each task's contract checks after every edit, so failing layouts are never accepted. On layout-versus-schematic (LVS), design-rule checking (DRC), and post-layout repairs of three designs (a production high-voltage digital-to-analog converter (DAC), a 5-V oscillator, and a SKY130 operational transconductance amplifier (OTA)) with six tier-matched models from two vendors, 182 blind runs show that cheap models execute plans but rarely succeed alone (the cheapest model: 1 of 11 runs alone, 16 of 17 under a flagship planner; p < 0.001), cheap planners fail more often, and no fixed assignment is cheapest on every task. We propose a learning controller that selects models for each role and the escalation order from the first tool evaluation and updates Bayesian estimates after every attempt. With rules and initial estimates frozen before testing, the controller fixed 7 of 8 episodes on four sealed held-out tasks, matching the OpenAI flagship alone, at 15-40% of the flagship's spend per fix on three tasks but 8% higher spend overall. The cheapest mid-tier model alone fixed 6 of 8 at the lowest overall spend per fix but missed the hardest task. All 32 extracted DAC repairs match the human-guided LVS repair's integral nonlinearity (INL) within 0.005 least significant bits (LSB) at every code.

papers.title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
papers.abstract: When the process behind a time series changes on an announced date, like Australia's switch to five minute electricity settlement on October 1, 2021, intervals calibrated before it can stop covering at their stated level. Whether a forecaster needs the next interval to cover or a finished period's share of misses on target decides the restart. We recompute the next conformal interval from post-break forecast errors, and for n independent ones from the same continuous law, its expected coverage error is $O(n^{-1/2})$, the optimal order in a fixed class among methods told the date. For a finished period's share of misses to match its target, we restart adaptive conformal inference (ACI), which on bounded errors brings that share within $O(n^{-1})$ of target if its corrections at a lower limit stay bounded in total, for that period only. After a simulated mean jump of 5.0 standard deviations, recomputed 90% intervals lie an expected 3.5 percentage points from target at the 50th forecast, a third closer than the 5.2 of the best of five adaptive methods. Of 9 announced changes in Texas, Australian and PJM power markets and a Federal Reserve decision, only Australia's switch moves the errors enough for a 5% test at 80% power to resolve a gain from restarting ACI, and dates help restarted ACI only after large changes.

papers.title: Holographic two-point functions across a PT symmetry-breaking transition
papers.abstract: In parity-time (PT)-symmetric non-Hermitian systems, an exceptional point, where eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce, typically separates a real spectrum from complex-conjugate eigenvalues. In logarithmic conformal field theories (LCFTs), such an exceptional point appears in the spectrum of scaling dimensions. Holographic models of LCFTs, such as the dipole model, are built exactly at this point. Here, we deform the holographic dipole model so that its two coalescing scaling dimensions split into either two real ones or a complex-conjugate pair. We obtain the renormalized two-point functions in closed form. They change continuously from a linear combination of two power laws, through the logarithmic form of the LCFT at the exceptional point, to log-periodic oscillations. For any pair of scalar primary operators with real mixing under dilatations, the conformal Ward identities fix this form up to two normalization constants, which the holographic dictionary determines. In PT-symmetric theories with such a dilatation operator, real and complex-conjugate scaling dimensions correspond to the PT-unbroken and PT-broken phases. In the BTZ black hole at finite temperature, the difference between the quasinormal frequencies associated with the two scaling dimensions changes from purely imaginary to purely real across the real-to-complex spectral transition. Correspondingly, the linear response changes from overdamped to underdamped, with critical damping at the exceptional point. Direct experimental observation of the two-point functions across the exceptional point could be achieved in two hyperbolic electric circuits with a non-reciprocal coupling, through the voltage response between their edge nodes.

papers.title: SimpleVLN: Towards Simple and Frontier Vision-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to ground language in visual observations and make long-horizon decisions. Existing methods often address these demands through task-specific architectures. As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly capable, an important question remains: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? We present SimpleVLN, an architecture-preserving framework developed through studies of navigation formulation, data construction, and optimization. At the formulation level, SimpleVLN combines single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global-local memory to efficiently use navigation history without unbounded context growth, while action chunks enable efficient output of multiple primitive actions per model invocation. For data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent DAgger experience and develop a scalable synthesis pipeline that generates large-scale tasks for reinforcement learning. At the optimization level, a progressive IL-DAgger-RL pipeline advances from action imitation to task-level outcome optimization. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these three aspects. We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple MLLM backbones and model sizes, demonstrating its generality. SimpleVLN achieves 76.7% and 80.1% success rates on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE splits, respectively, substantially outperforming existing methods. These results show that the navigation capabilities of native MLLMs can be effectively unlocked without task-specific architectural designs.

papers.title: Four colours are needed for closed-neighbourhood conflict-free colouring of planar graphs
papers.abstract: A colouring of the vertices of a graph is conflict-free with respect to closed neighbourhoods if every closed neighbourhood contains a colour that appears on exactly one of its vertices. The colouring need not be proper. Every planar graph has such a colouring with four colours. Fabrici, Lužar, Rindošová and Soták [Proper conflict-free and unique-maximum colorings of planar graphs with respect to neighborhoods, \emph{Discrete Appl.\ Math.}\ \textbf{324} (2023) 80--92] conjectured that three colours always suffice. We disprove this conjecture. We give a simple gadget construction that turns every planar graph of chromatic number four into a planar graph with no conflict-free colouring with three colours. This also shows that it is NP-complete to decide whether three colours suffice for a planar graph. We also give a critical planar graph on $25$ vertices and $51$ edges that needs four colours, with a proof that can be checked by hand. Finally, we give an infinite family of plane triangulations that need four colours, and an infinite family of critical examples.

papers.title: On the location of mass concentration for attractive Bose-Einstein condensates with a ring-shaped potential in bounded domains
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the ground states of attractive Bose-Einstein condensates in a bounded domain $Ω\subset \mathbb R^2$ under the ring-shaped trapping potential $$ V(x)=(|x|-1)^2. $$ Letting $Γ=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ be the ring of global minima of $V(x)$, we focus on a unified geometric setting $Γ\cap Ω\not=\emptyset$, which allows $Γ\subset Ω$ or $Γ\cap\partialΩ\neq\emptyset$. In this setting, we determine the precise location of mass concentration for ground states as the interaction strength approaches the critical value. More precisely, we prove that the mass concentrates at a point $x_0\inΓ\cap Ω$ that has maximal distance from $\partialΩ$. Our method relies on exponential upper and lower bounds on the difference between the minimal energies in the bounded domain and whole space. The essential lower bound follows from a uniform quadratic-growth estimate near the ground state manifold of the whole space problem, which is established by combining the nondegeneracy of the optimizer for the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality with a Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction.

papers.title: Cooperation Dynamics with Environmental Feedback: Steady States and Transitions
papers.abstract: Cooperative behavior and its regulatory mechanisms are central to complex systems and evolutionary game theory. In natural populations, strategy updates and endogenous payoff environments interact bidirectionally, shaping cooperation. We propose a strategy-payoff environmental-feedback model for four canonical games: Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag-Hunt, and Harmony. Mathematical derivation reduces the high-dimensional coupled system to an analytically equivalent canonical replicator equation. Bifurcation diagrams, phase portraits, and simulations show how initial cooperation, temptation to defect, and punishment jointly regulate cooperation. Stag-Hunt and Harmony display bistability and initial-state dependence; Prisoner's Dilemma exhibits robust dynamics with stable mixed equilibria. Temptation and punishment drive sequential cross-type game transitions at critical thresholds. Sufficient punishment suppresses defection, shifts bifurcation thresholds, delays destabilization of cooperative steady states, and reshapes these transitions. Numerical tests confirm equivalence and stability switching. Spatial lattice simulations agree with theoretical predictions, supporting robustness. This work reveals regulatory mechanisms from endogenous payoff feedback and initial-condition sensitivity, providing a basis for understanding and optimizing collective prosocial behavior.

papers.title: Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts, but generating complete rollouts and computing per-token teacher feedback are computationally expensive. Existing truncation methods save computation by stopping rollouts early. However, they do not compensate for truncated token gradients, which biases the gradient estimates and changes Vanilla OPD's original training objective. Furthermore, their truncation decisions rely on assumptions about supervision quality or criteria that may not generalize across settings. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.

papers.title: Brezis--Nirenberg-type results for coupled critical elliptic systems with sign-changing perturbations
papers.abstract: We establish Brezis--Nirenberg-type existence results for elliptic systems with symmetric linear coupling, a radial critical nonlinearity and a subcritical potential. For any dimension $N\ge3$, the potential may change sign, with its negative part bounded by a subquadratic power for some exponent $q_1\in(1,2)$ and no smallness restriction on the coefficient. Under coercivity and suitable near-zero and subcritical growth assumptions, we obtain a nontrivial weak solution if the largest eigenvalue of the coupling matrix is positive when $N\ge4$, or exceeds a positive constant depending on the domain when $N=3$. No homogeneity, convexity or monotonicity along rays is required of the perturbation potential, and either sign of the linear coupling is allowed. The proof combines a variational criterion below the critical Sobolev energy level with estimates showing that the negative part of the potential contributes less than the linear energy decrease. On star-shaped domains, we also obtain a Pohozaev nonexistence criterion.

papers.title: Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes
papers.abstract: Surrogate models approximate the solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) for given geometries and boundary conditions. Conventional Transformer-based approaches typically employ a common feature-mixing mechanism across the solution domain, despite the presence of spatial variations at different scales. In this paper, we propose a mixture of transformer experts that combines a routing mechanism with multiscale supervision. Specifically, the individual experts are routed through a controller that utilizes learnable Laplacian matrices to compute weights, used to define a weighted sum of the experts for the output feature vectors at each point of the domain. Subsequently, a decoder receives the weighted sum of the experts output and predicts the solution fields. During training, the reference fields are decomposed into components at different spatial scales by repeated smoothing with a mesh Laplacian. We evaluate our approach on the official AirFRANS dataset using remeshed solution domains leading to unstructured triangular meshes of $4.9$k vertices. The experimental outcomes reveal lower mean relative $L_2$ error and interior mean squared errors among the compared models of this study. Code and data are publicly available in https://github.com/snousias/hodge-moe-pde

papers.title: Large-Tiny Spin-Stripe SDW Order in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ via $^{139}$La-NQR Spectroscopy: Reconsideration Based on the $Am2m$ Structure
papers.abstract: The lower-symmetry $Am2m$ structure was recently proposed as the intrinsic ambient-pressure phase of La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ based on synchrotron x-ray diffraction, whereas earlier studies investigated its properties assuming the commonly accepted $Amam$ structure. Here, we reexamine the crystal structure in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ and the spin configuration of spin-density-wave (SDW) state via $^{139}$La nuclear quadrupole resonance (NQR). The observation of two distinct La(2) sites in the NQR spectra is naturally accounted for by the $Am2m$ structure without any special assumptions, whereas it cannot be reconciled within the $Amam$ framework. Within the $Am2m$ framework, we reanalyze the spin configuration of the SDW phase and identify it as a large-tiny spin-stripe structure, arising naturally from two inequivalent Ni sites with large and tiny magnetic moments. These results establish the itinerant nature of the SDW order at ambient pressure in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$, providing a basis for understanding its relationship to the emergence of high-$T_c$ superconductivity under high pressure.

papers.title: Adiabatic particle production in a time-dependent accelerated frame
papers.abstract: We study a massive scalar field in flat spacetime written in a time-dependent accelerated frame whose fixed-coordinate observers have maximal proper acceleration at $t=0$ and become asymptotically inertial without forming a horizon. The Klein-Gordon equation separates into a modified Mathieu equation in time and a confining Schrödinger problem in space with a discrete spectrum. We impose an adiabatic vacuum at the instant of maximal acceleration and compute the particle number in the inertial future. For the zeroth-order adiabatic state it falls as the inverse eighth power of the initial mode frequency, and raising the adiabatic order cancels successive terms of the endpoint expansion, in analogy with the switching transients of finite-time detectors. Analytic continuation of the spatial eigenfunctions gives the out modes in closed form and an exact expression for the particle number, which is entirely the mismatch at $t=0$ between the initial state and the out vacuum. The spectrum is algebraic rather than Planckian.

papers.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
papers.abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass.
