Since Pauli rotations are periodic, so Euclidean rounding may produce wrong codeword near a chart boundary; error due to coordinates alone cannot measure how much the final state was changed. Herein we define a metric, Quantum Shock, for Pure State it is defined as the average of the square of the Fubini-Study distance (over all inputs) between the pre-deployment and deployed states. This value is limited by constant multipliers of the mean of infidelity and provides upper limits on displacement when observing bounded quantities and margin based predictive stability. Extensions to the analytical Bures-angle for mixed-states were derived, along with a finite shot stability bound. The proposed Train-Time Constrained Quantization allows a delay in applying a penalty for selecting a codeword aligned with periodicity until after task only optimizations. Three small binary tasks were evaluated on a four qubit, two layer classifier using ten matched seeds, K = 4, 8, 16 and exact expectation values from simulation under noiseless conditions and state vector simulations. On our primary evaluation, T-CQ exhibited smaller average local quantum shock compared to circular post-training quantization for each task and code-book size tested. The re-execution on the x86-64 platform using K=8 preserved the direction of the mean-shock comparison but had varying magnitudes.

papers.title: Local gluing classification and bulk-locked clock rings for $\mathbb{Z}_N$ models on a Klein bottle
papers.abstract: We classify local reflection gluings of the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ plaquette model on lattice Klein bottles and solve the obstructed literal seam. Within the monomial far-corner ansatz, all commuting gluings form a family labelled by a unit $u$ of $\mathbb{Z}_N$. They exist for every $N$ at even seam length and, at odd length, exactly when $-1$ is a square modulo $N$. We determine the anyon transport, including exchange seams with $P^2=C$ for charge conjugation $C$, and the relation phases that distinguish an unfrustrated code from a commuting but frustrated Hamiltonian. For the literal gluing, the $2L_x$ noncommuting plaquettes form self-dual clock rings whose sectors are locked by the bulk. This gives an exact reduction of the spectrum to clock-ring spectra, closed-form ring ground energies for $N=2,4$, and a closed-form ground-state degeneracy. We further determine twisted-coefficient homology on the stated surface domains and compare it with logical modules on registered lattice grids; composite dimensions need not give squares of cyclic groups. Dressed-isometry gates and monodromy are reported with their finite-grid scope. Finally, the qudit Gottesman--Knill theorem bounds the computational interpretation: Clifford deformations and Weyl measurements with stabilizer inputs and no external magic states cannot supply a non-stabilizer resource. Charge-conjugation measurements that do supply such states lie outside this operation model. The new results concern explicit seam classification, phase-sensitive consistency and bulk-locked spectra, not a new general no-go theorem or a universal computing architecture.

papers.title: Improved Closed-Form Identification of the Air-Gap Permeance in Magnetic Equivalent Circuits of Rotor-Eccentric Electric Motors
papers.abstract: Fast and accurate simulation of electric motors is essential for their design, fault diagnosis and control. Magnetic equivalent circuits (MECs) offer a computationally efficient alternative to the finite element method (FEM), yet their flux tube representation poorly captures the air-gap field. This creates a challenge, as the air gap stores most of the magnetic energy and governs the electromagnetic torque and, in rotor-eccentric motors, the unbalanced magnetic pull (UMP). Existing air-gap permeance expressions vary widely in their results for torque ripple and UMP and account for tooth-normal eccentricity only. This paper proposes the dual-term air-gap permeance (DTAP) model, a closed-form expression for the air-gap permeance between a stator and a rotor tooth that accounts for tooth-normal and tooth-tangential eccentricity, with and without rotor skew. Its parameters are identified from a FEM model of the air gap and the complete set of tooth heads, which includes the shielding by the neighbouring teeth. For three motors, DTAP reproduces the FEM air-gap permeance with a 2.8-4.8 times smaller error than the state of the art, at a comparable computational cost. Implemented in the MEC of an eccentric induction motor, it reproduces the torque ripple within 1.6% and the peak UMP within 1.3% of the reference, i.e., with 2.8 and 27 times smaller deviations than the state of the art. DTAP thereby enables MEC to predict the torque pulsations and bearing loads of eccentric motors more accurately without sacrificing computational speed.

papers.title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(http://cai.1688.com/), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.

papers.title: An accelerated multiobjective gradient flow with implicit Hessian-driven damping
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose an accelerated multiobjective gradient flow with implicit Hessian-driven damping for unconstrained convex multiobjective optimization problems in a real Hilbert space. The continuous flow is formulated as a system of two first-order equations involving only a single multiobjective projection operator and suitable time-scaling factors. Formally, it can also be expressed as a second-order system with explicit multiobjective Hessian-driven damping, which corresponds to the usual Hessian-driven damping introduced by Alvarez et al. [J. Math. Pures Appl., 81(8):747--779, 2002]. The first-order formulation, however, involves no Hessian term and can be regarded as an extension of the Hessian-driven Nesterov accelerated gradient flow by Chen and Luo [arXiv:1912.09276, 2019]. Assuming that the objective gradients are Lipschitz continuous on bounded sets and that the common lower level sets are bounded, we establish global existence in finite dimensions under suitable time-scaling conditions. An a priori energy estimate confines the solutions to a fixed bounded set, and a Lyapunov argument yields fast decay of a merit function and the KKT residual. Under an additional bound on the time-scaling factors, the trajectory of every global solution converges weakly to a weak Pareto point. Numerical tests illustrate the rapid residual decay and reduced oscillations.

papers.title: Closed formulas for the permanents of structured matrices
papers.abstract: We give finite formulas for permanents of structured matrices and prove polynomial bounds for their evaluation. Over any field, the permanent of a matrix of bounded rank-width can be computed from the matrix alone, answering a question of Lyaudet. In characteristic $p>0$, the bound is $p^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}$, where $k$ is the rank-width. In characteristic zero, a determinant formula treats Cauchy matrices with an added polynomial of fixed degrees in the row and column nodes. This includes polynomial perturbations of Hilbert matrices and dense Toeplitz and Hankel families. For ordered cuts we give a single determinant; in positive characteristic, rational diagonal sequences give a fixed rational generating function for the Toeplitz permanents. We also give formulas for cycle weights and hook immanants. For translation matrices we obtain signed determinant formulas and classify the supports for which the permanent is the coefficientwise absolute value of the determinant. Further formulas cover cyclic block matrices, residue supports, and bands bounded on one side.

papers.title: AI Reviews Are Biased Towards the Appendix
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by reviewers to highlight weaknesses during the reviewing process, and their outputs often shape the reviews that humans submit. Prior work studies how LLM reviews align with human ones, yet we know little about which parts of a paper these models actually criticize. In this work, we investigate 2,000 papers from ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR, and show that the latest GPT and Claude models draw about 50% or more of their review weaknesses from the appendix. This behavior holds across the API, coding-agent, and web access methods for using LLMs to review a paper. In contrast, we find that humans draw only 8.4% of their weaknesses from the appendix, and these weaknesses primarily revolve around a paper's presentation and content related to its core idea. Meanwhile, LLMs draw weaknesses from deep in the appendix that concern fine-grained technical details not central to the paper's contributions. We anticipate that our analysis will contribute to the scholarly discourse on AI reviews. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/cincynlp/review_appendix.

papers.title: Phases of deformed sine dilaton gravity and JT limit
papers.abstract: We study the implications of marginal deformation in sine dilaton gravity (sDG). We investigate the thermodynamic properties of deformed sine dilaton gravity (dsDG) and examine the phase stability of black holes in two space-time dimensions. We found that the deformation parameter ($λ$) sets a critical temperature threshold ($T_0$). Below this critical value ($T<T_0$), the system enters an unphysical phase characterized by a fractional density of states and a negative Wald entropy. Above the critical temperature ($T>T_0$), we obtain a physical black hole phase with positive entropy and negative free energy. Furthermore, we evaluate the Komar integral, derive the Casimir function for dsDG, and establish the first law of black hole thermodynamics. Finally, we explore the infrared (IR) limit of dsDG which we identify as Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity accompanied by marginal deformation. We also perform a detailed analysis of various thermodynamic entities pertinent to this deformed JT solution.

papers.title: No universal LOCC entanglement purification
papers.abstract: Entanglement purification aims to obtain high-fidelity entangled states from noisy entangled states. This task becomes particularly challenging when the available input states are finite in number, only partially characterized, and may not be identical. Whether there exists a universal purification protocol applicable to such inputs has therefore been a longstanding question. This motivates the study of universal $n$-to-$1$ entanglement purification. Although no such LOCC protocol exists for the full set of two-qubit entangled states, it has remained open whether this no-go result extends to higher-dimensional bipartite states and multipartite states. In this work, we resolve this question by proving that, for any fixed finite local dimensions, no $n$-to-$1$ LOCC protocol is universal for all bipartite entangled states or all multipartite entangled states. We further show that the bipartite and multipartite no-go results persist under several natural extensions and establish an analogous no-go theorem for coherence purification under strictly incoherent operations.

papers.title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_α$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.

papers.title: Squeezing Drives Southward Magnetic Field Enhancement During 10 May 2024 CME-CME Interaction
papers.abstract: The southward magnetic field carried by coronal mass ejections (CMEs) is a key driver of space weather events, yet how interacting CMEs amplify this field remains debated. The 10 May 2024 event, which produced the strongest geomagnetic storm since 2003, offers an ideal testbed for this question. Combining multi-spacecraft observations with high-resolution controlled numerical experiments, we track the CMEs continuously from their origin near the solar surface to beyond Earth, and find that inherent squeezing during CME-CME interactions generates the sustained enhancement of the southward field, exceeding 60 nT in magnitude near Earth. First driven by the dynamic pressure of the trailing CME and later maintained by magnetic and thermal pressures at the CME-CME interface, squeezing transforms the preceding CME from a bulky cloud into a flattened "pancake" structure, prevents expansion-induced field decay, and maintains an amplified southward field over long distances. The strength of this enhancement scales with the intensity of the squeezing. Our findings establish a direct link between CME-CME interaction and strong southward fields, laying a physics-based foundation for understanding and forecasting the geoeffectiveness of interacting CMEs.

papers.title: Can Agents Keep Up with Time? An Empirical Analysis of Temporal Adaptation After a Conversational Hiatus
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents increasingly serve as persistent personal assistants across modern web platforms, managing schedules, applications, and multi-step plans over weeks or months. Users often return to an ongoing conversation after a long conversational hiatus, while earlier bookings and preparation notes stay on record. During this hiatus, scheduled dates may pass even though the retained records remain unchanged and event outcomes go unrecorded. Existing evaluations of long-horizon agents focus on fact retention and explicit state updates. Whether agents perceive the passage of time and adapt their advice accordingly therefore remains unknown. We frame this ability as temporal state perception and use, which means perceiving the current time and applying it when interpreting dated records. To study it, we design session-rekindling tasks that keep the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and the way temporal information reaches the agent. Experiments across five model routes and five temporal-information conditions show that agents can obtain the current time but often fail to use it. They reliably query the clock and even note in their reasoning that the scheduled date has passed, yet many still tell users to prepare for the expired event. Supplying explicit temporal context reduces this error, and providing the computed date relation removes it entirely. Keeping up with time therefore depends on turning perceived time into updated plans. Based on these findings, we design a session-rekindling benchmark that provides temporal-awareness guidance for designing long-horizon agents. The code can be found at https://github.com/Adoreu2/session-rekindling-benchmark.

papers.title: Periodic Modulation of Linear Polarization Fraction in Repeating FRB 20240114A
papers.abstract: Long-term polarization changes in repeating fast radio bursts (FRBs) can probe their emission geometry and propagation environment. We searched for periodic variation in the degree of linear polarization (DOL) of FRB~20240114A using the polarization catalog from the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope. The sample contains 6,099 bursts detected on 95 observing days over $\sim 488$ days. The daily mean DOL series was analyzed using phase distance correlation and Lomb--Scargle periodograms over trial periods of 10--240 days. The strongest peaks occur at $119.91^{+2.67}_{-2.04}$ and $122.31^{+2.63}_{-2.82}$ days, respectively. The quoted ranges correspond to the period intervals above the global $3σ$ thresholds. Global false-alarm probabilities were estimated from \(10^7\) random permutations of the daily values among the fixed observing dates, with the full period search repeated for each permutation. The resulting probabilities are \(9.98\times10^{-4}\) and \(8.95\times10^{-4}\), corresponding to equivalent Gaussian significances of \(3.09σ\) and \(3.12σ\), respectively. As a supplementary check, the same analysis using daily median DOL yielded similar peaks near 120 days. A descriptive sinusoidal fit to all 95 daily mean DOL measurements at a fixed period of 119.91 days has a semi-amplitude of 3.23\%. Possible explanations include precession-driven changes in viewing geometry and variations in propagation conditions within a binary system.

papers.title: Tight Quantum Query Bounds for Collision Finding over Arbitrary Bounded Types
papers.abstract: We determine the bounded-error quantum query complexity of finding one $r$-collision in an $N$-input function of prescribed type, which specifies all equality-class sizes. For every fixed maximum class size and collision order, we give a tight bound as the maximum of scales determined by the numbers of classes of size at least $2,\ldots,r$. The lower bound holds for a uniformly random function of that type, and a matching algorithm succeeds on every such function. No intermediate class size is required to occur, and every feasible output alphabet is allowed. The characterization connects the abundant-collision regime associated with set equality to the sparse-target regime of $k$-distinctness. In particular, finding the unique $(k+1)$-collision in type $(k^n,k+1)$ has complexity $Θ_k(N^{3/4-1/[4(2^{k+1}-1)]})$, where $N=kn+k+1$, resolving an open problem of Belovs. For the lower bound, we introduce a filtered compressed permutation oracle that projects onto a harmonic database subspace after each complete function query. Its $O(T/N)$ comparison error over $T$ queries overcomes the square-root limitation of the unfiltered process. Hidden capacity extensions and moment estimates retain the populations at each intermediate collision order. Matching upper bounds use sampled collision lists and colored adaptive learning graphs, with a coherent decision-to-search conversion that avoids logarithmic overhead. We also give an alternative nested quantum-walk algorithm for three-collision search, matching the bound up to polylogarithmic factors.

papers.title: Resource Management and Trajectory Optimization for UAV-IRS Assisted Maritime Edge Computing Networks
papers.abstract: With the exponential growth of maritime wireless devices and the rapid development of maritime applications, traditional maritime communication networks encounter communication and computation limitations in supporting computation-intensive and latency-critical tasks. Edge computing and Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) have emerged as promising techniques to improve communication and computation services for maritime devices with limited computation capabilities and battery capacity. This paper studies an IRS Mounted on Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UIRS) assisted maritime edge computing network, in which the UIRS is deployed to assist the transmission from Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs) to the edge server via Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) protocol. We propose a resource management and trajectory optimization scheme by jointly optimizing subslot duration, offloading ratios, transmit power, edge computation capability allocation, UIRS phase shifts and UIRS trajectory, aiming at minimizing the overall energy consumption. Since the non-convex nature of the optimization problem, we propose a two-layered method by decomposing the original problem into two subproblems. The top-layered subproblem is solved by the Semi-Definite Relaxation (SDR) method and the underlying-layered subproblem is solved by the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm. Numerical results demonstrate that our proposed scheme can effectively and efficiently reduce overall energy consumption.

papers.title: Multimodal Person Concept Model for Person Identification under Varying Observation Conditions
papers.abstract: Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content. To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions. The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA). We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination. Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88). We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot. These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. The project page and demonstration video are available at https://okitamisan01.github.io/person_concept/.

papers.title: Novel observables for exploring jet quenching effects in individual jets
papers.abstract: We introduce event-shape observables in the jet frame to characterize intra-jet shapes and study medium modifications in heavy-ion collisions. Using the JEWEL model, we investigate jet constituent angular and transverse momentum distributions, together with two representative event-shape observables, transverse thrust $τ_\perp$ and transverse sphericity $S_\perp$, in $p$+$p$ and 0--10% central Pb+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}} = 5.02\,\mathrm{TeV}$. These observables are evaluated after transforming the jet constituent momenta into the jet frame. The intra-jet shape distributions in Pb+Pb collisions shift toward larger values relative to those in $p$+$p$ collisions, indicating more isotropic distributions of constituent transverse momenta. Comparisons between calculations with and without recoil, along with the dependence on the constituent transverse momentum threshold, indicate that medium response plays an important role in these modifications. These results suggest that jet-frame event-shape observables provide sensitive probes of medium response in jet quenching, complementary to single-particle angular and transverse momentum distributions.

papers.title: Emerging understanding of the rare kaon decay $K^+\toπ^+\ell^+\ell^-$ from lattice QCD
papers.abstract: Rare kaon decays provide sensitive probes of the Standard Model and potential new physics. For $K^+\toπ^+\ell^+\ell^-$, the experimental decay rate determines only the squared vector form factor $|V(z)|^2$, leaving its sign undetermined. Previous lattice QCD calculations have either used unphysical pion masses or suffered from uncertainties too large to resolve this sign. Here we present a first-principles calculation using two domain-wall fermion ensembles with near-physical pion masses. We develop a computational strategy that establishes the ultraviolet finiteness and continuum equivalence of local and conserved vector currents, substantially simplifying the calculation of nonlocal matrix elements. Four independent subtraction schemes provide nontrivial consistency checks, while the one-end trick reduces noise from quark-self-loop contributions. We determine $V(z)$ at six spacelike and timelike momentum transfers. Fits consistently yield $V(0)<0$, with a statistical significance of $5.8σ$--$7.9σ$ at $M_{η_c}=1.1,\mathrm{GeV}$. After extrapolation to the physical charm-quark mass, the negative sign persists across all fit forms, with a significance of $2.0σ$--$3.4σ$. Our results provide direct first-principles evidence favoring the negative-sign solution and establish a framework for more precise lattice QCD determinations.

papers.title: Localization for Lipschitz monotone quasi-periodic operators with power-law hopping
papers.abstract: We prove spectral and dynamical localization for quasi-periodic operators on $\mathbb Z^d$ with Lipschitz monotone potentials and power-law hopping. For sufficiently small coupling, localization holds at every allowed phase whenever the hopping decay exponent $r$ exceeds the Diophantine exponent $τ$. The proof is based on multiscale analysis with exponentially growing scales. We use homotopy in the coupling constant to select the local eigenvalue branches and Schur complement estimates to control the successive elimination of coordinates.

papers.title: Elasticy: A Runtime-Reconfigurable Architecture for Dynamic Streams
papers.abstract: Reconfigurable Dataflow Accelerators (RDAs) have demonstrated high performance and energy efficiency for dense, regular tensor applications. However, conventional RDAs with static configurations show dramatically reduced performance and efficiency on irregular tensor workloads with data-dependent, non-uniform, dynamic tensor shapes. We propose Elasticy, a dynamically reconfigurable dataflow accelerator that employs streaming and tile abstractions to minimize the overhead of dynamic support. By encoding dynamic shapes into streams using rank-variable expressions, Elasticy exploits data-dependent tensor shape dynamism to minimize off-chip data traffic and wasted compute cycles. Elasticy employs stream-embedded reconfiguration information to trigger fine-grained runtime scheduling decisions. Elasticy also introduces a novel distributed linked streaming memory (DLSM) that more effectively uses on-chip memory to minimize off-chip data traffic and support dynamically sized tensors. Both reconfiguration and shape dynamism incur minimal overhead in Elasticy: reconfiguration occurs infrequently at the granularity of a stream of tiles, while rank-variable expressions enable lightweight handling of dynamic dimensions. On a Llama 3-8B decode layer, Elasticy achieves 92.6% of its roofline performance, compared to 69.7% on an H100. On evaluated GEMMs, the DLSM reduces total off-chip traffic by up to 61.4% relative to the best evaluated cache configuration, with no additional burden of programmer-managed memory. Elasticy's distributed runtime scheduler overlaps dependent kernels, speeding up kernel pairs by up to 1.42x. Programs can also run in both space and time: each phase of a layer's graph is pipelined spatially, while phases fold onto the same fabric over time. Compared to a traditional spatial accelerator, Elasticy achieves a 6.34x-31.67x improved area delay product on full layers.

papers.title: Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding
papers.abstract: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. However, this architectural coupling introduces a fundamental bottleneck. Agent performance remains strictly bounded by internal perceptual limitations. Furthermore, text-only agents lack native perception. Without specialized tools, they cannot perform visual reasoning. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm. Prior visual tool-use merely manipulates images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read. In contrast, VaaT reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities. As a result, text-only agents can completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Meanwhile, vision-capable agents can dynamically augment their native perception on demand. We instantiate this paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. We comprehensively evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents. These findings highlight that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems.

papers.title: Robustness Evaluation of GPU Cloud Pricing Benchmarks under Incomplete Observations: A Controlled Missingness Study
papers.abstract: Daily GPU rental-price benchmarks can fail when marketplace quotes are missing. This article stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms and four benchmark-level recovery methods. Across 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations in 27 scenarios on 190 held-out days, whole-source outages reduce publication coverage to 0.77 while preserving zero conditional error on published dates; composition-changing loss retains 0.86 coverage but produces 7.74 log points of error. A separate past-only stratum-level ablation reduces error by 4.15 to 6.70 log points in five composition-changing cases, using a richer information set. An observable-signal withholding rule improves the primary error-coverage criterion in 0 of 10 cases. Results concern observed asking-price measurements, not transaction prices or identified real-world missingness mechanisms.

papers.title: Striatal Optogenetic Modulation Shifts Seizure Onset Timing: A Survival-Analysis Reanalysis with Effect Sizes, Permutation Validation, and Sensitivity Analysis
papers.abstract: We present a worked methods vignette, not a novel biological claim: a reanalysis of the public dataset accompanying Hyder and colleagues' report that optogenetic activation and inhibition of the dorsal striatum bidirectionally control seizures, applying a time-to-event framework to the pilocarpine-induced status epilepticus (SE) arm, the only arm with genuine per-animal event-level data rather than aggregate statistics. The original study compared latencies with a Mann-Whitney U test (ChR2 vs GFP: p = 0.0125; ArchT vs GFP: p = 0.0025). We first directly replicate that test on the same data (p = 0.0151 and p = 0.0025), confirming we analyze the same numbers, then designate the log-rank test as this reanalysis's pre-specified primary comparison, with a Cox model, a label-permutation test, a bootstrap confidence interval, and a leave-one-out analysis serving as validation checks rather than co-equal findings. ChR2 activation delays SE onset relative to its paired GFP control (hazard ratio 0.338, 95% CI 0.128-0.895; log-rank p = 0.023), and ArchT inhibition accelerates it (hazard ratio 9.18, 95% CI 1.91-44.09; log-rank p = 0.0011); a Schoenfeld-residual check found no significant proportional-hazards violation, though this check has limited power at n = 8-11 per group. Both results are confirmed by a 2,000-shuffle permutation test and survive leave-one-out, though the ChR2 comparison loses significance in 2 of 20 leave-one-out iterations, a fragility we report rather than omit. We do not claim this demonstrates anything the field did not already believe; its value is methodological, a reusable survival-analysis template with a Cox-derived effect size and documented sensitivity, extending naturally to future datasets with genuine censoring, which this one does not have.

papers.title: Federated Physics-Informed Thermal Field Prediction Across Unseen Geometries in Distributed Additive Manufacturing
papers.abstract: In additive manufacturing (AM), each change in part geometry requires a new thermal simulation, which makes design evaluation over many candidates costly. Geometry-aware models reduce this cost by predicting thermal fields on unseen parts with a single learned model, but they assume that diverse geometries are available centrally. This assumption is restrictive when each manufacturing site holds only a limited set of proprietary part designs that it cannot share. We propose Fed-PIGANO, a federated framework that trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator (PI-GANO) models at individual sites and aggregates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without sharing part geometries. We evaluate the framework on a 2D steady-state thermal benchmark for metal AM, with geometries from five polygonal families distributed across three sites under four scenarios that range from identical to strongly different family compositions. Over seven replications, Fed-PIGANO achieves mean relative L2 errors of 1.83% to 2.04% across all 12 scenario-site cases, compared with up to 20.46% for local-only training, and consistently yields lower PDE residuals. Its prediction accuracy is comparable to that of a centralized model trained on the pooled geometries of all sites. These results demonstrate that federated learning lets manufacturing sites benefit from each other's geometries without sharing them, enabling rapid thermal prediction on new part designs for tasks such as shape optimization, inverse design, and uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals
papers.abstract: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.

papers.title: The Dirichlet Problem for Quaternionic $k$-Hessian Equations
papers.abstract: We study the Dirichlet problem for quaternionic $k$-Hessian equations on smooth bounded domains. For a smooth positive density $f(q,z)$ satisfying $f_z\ge0$, we prove existence and uniqueness of a smooth admissible solution whenever a smooth admissible subsolution with the prescribed boundary values exists. The proof extends the quaternionic Monge--Ampère subsolution method to $2\le k<n$ through boundary second derivative estimates. We also construct subsolutions on strictly quaternionic $(k-1)$-convex domains and characterize smooth solvability for constant boundary values.

papers.title: Domains of attraction of quasi-stationary distributions for an absorbed random walk
papers.abstract: We study a continuous-time random walk on the positive integers, killed at zero, where the downward rate $a$ and upward rate $b$ satisfy $a>b>0$. Its quasi-stationary distributions form a one-parameter family. We show that if the initial distribution $(m_n)_{n\geq 1}$ is strictly positive and satisfies $m_{n+1}/m_n\to r$, where $(b/a)^{1/2}<r<1$, then its conditional distribution given survival converges in total variation to the corresponding nonminimal quasi-stationary distribution. We obtain asymptotic equivalents for the joint probabilities of position and survival, and for the survival probability itself. We also give a moment condition under which the minimal quasi-stationary distribution is selected. Finally, we construct an initial distribution whose successive-term ratios do not converge but whose conditional distribution nevertheless converges to a nonminimal quasi-stationary distribution. Thus the ratio condition is sufficient but not necessary.

papers.title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

papers.title: Can Large Language Models Optimize Pretrained Neural Network Weights? A Multi-Phase Empirical Evaluation of Gradient-Free Editing in YOLO26 Object Detection
papers.abstract: Direct weight editing offers a gradient-free alternative to fine-tuning pretrained detectors, but its generalization and the value of large language model (LLM) guidance remain uncertain. We evaluate five experimental phases using YOLO26 models and MS COCO, comparing deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, CMA-ES, structured interventions, real local-LLM proposals, failure-aware guidance, and hybrid LLM-CMA-ES against a matched random-policy control. Optimization uses native Ultralytics mAP50-95 on 1,000 COCO Val2017 images; selected candidates are assessed on a disjoint, previously examined 1,500-image subset, with COCO API AP50-95 reported separately where available. Increasing the CMA-ES budget from 8 to 250 evaluations raised development gains from +0.11 to +0.28 percentage points, while selection changes remained negative (-0.03 to -0.12 points); the 250-evaluation result uses one seed. The hybrid LLM approach showed no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance (p = 0.612, 0.369, and 0.694 at budgets 8, 25, and 50). Five-seed YOLO26m replication yielded a COCO API AP difference of +0.004 points (95% CI: -0.026 to +0.034). Of 225 archived LLM proposals, 53 satisfy the final strict schema; early tensor-level execution cannot be fully verified. Genuine LLM-mediated weight editing is feasible, but the tested approaches did not demonstrate consistent transfer beyond the development subset or a measurable LLM advantage.

papers.title: RAG-FGO: Dynamic Optimization of Query-Rewriting Agents for Generative RAG
papers.abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), query rewriting serves as a core interface that aligns user intent with external knowledge bases, and its effectiveness directly determines overall system performance. However, generative retrieval faces three critical challenges in real-world deployment: noisy retrieval feedback, the difficulty of jointly optimizing discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding-control parameters, and the limited generalization of static rewriting strategies under semantically complex scenarios. To address these issues, we propose RAG-FGO, a dynamic optimization framework for generative retrieval strategies. RAG-FGO formulates query rewriting as a non-differentiable black-box optimization problem in a mixed discrete-continuous space, and represents prompt templates and decoding parameters as adaptively optimizable query-rewriting agents. The framework performs global search to enable semantic jumps and structural reorganization that escape local optima, while applying local perturbations for fine-grained alignment and precise refinement. In addition, RAG-FGO introduces an elite-preserving memory pool that accumulates high-quality strategies across iterations, thereby mitigating the impact of stochasticity and noisy feedback on optimization stability. Experimental results on a diverse suite of benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method, supporting its applicability to complex semantic retrieval tasks.

papers.title: Spin asymmetry in vacuum pair production under polarized electric fields
papers.abstract: We study spin-resolved electron--positron pair production from the quantum vacuum in spatially homogeneous, time-dependent electric fields with linear, elliptical, and circular polarizations. The equal-time Dirac--Heisenberg--Wigner formalism is employed to compute the final momentum distributions in two distinct frequency regimes, for both unchirped and chirped field configurations. In the high-frequency regime, characterized by a reference Keldysh parameter, linearly polarized fields yield identical particle yields for the two spin projections considered, whereas elliptical and circular polarizations generate pronounced spin-resolved population imbalances near the dominant multiphoton resonance. Frequency chirping broadens the resonant spectral structures and extends the momentum range over which a sizable normalized spin difference persists. In the low-frequency regime, the pair-production spectra are governed by quantum tunneling and temporal interference effects. Although the peak spin asymmetry in this regime is substantially weaker than in the high-frequency case, the normalized differential spectra still exhibit sign-changing interference fringes. We find that the spin-asymmetry degree exceeds 90$\%$ for circular polarization in the high-frequency regime, while it saturates at approximately 20$\%$ in the low-frequency regime. Given the purely electric background field, we interpret these results in terms of spin-projected Wigner components and the handed time dependence of rotating electric fields, while clearly distinguishing normalized spectral differences from local or integrated polarization observables.

papers.title: Towards Seconds-level Video Representation: Quadratically Gated Feature Grid with Adaptive, Prediction-free Sampling
papers.abstract: Implicit neural video representations are notoriously slow to build, which does not cross the basic practical threshold for most industrial applications. Here, we present Q-GAS, a coordinate-queryable video representation that couples multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids with a compact SwiGLU-style quadratic-gating (QG) decoder and an error-aware, prediction-free sampler. The explicit grids avoid hash-collision coefficient sharing at the cost of modestly higher storage yet greatly boost the expressive capacity; the QG decoder introduces low-rank local second-order interactions to improve the nonlinear feature response. During fitting, a global error map periodically refreshes a high-error pool, and each batch mixes pool samples with uniform samples, which is free from the auxiliary model to predict difficult samples, thereby further escalating the efficiency. On UVG Beauty/Bosphorus/Jockey, Q-GAS fits and quantizes under 50 s on one RTX PRO 6000, decodes at over 370 FPS with mixed precision and about 146 FPS in FP32. In our PyTorch implementation, Q-GAS trains and quantizes 5.5-7.2 times faster than the evaluated Instant-NGP baseline and 19-28 times faster than RNeRV. Under a 90 s budget, it improves PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS over the evaluated NeRV-family pipelines at comparable BPP over the measured overlap. We have shared our code at https://github.com/MillenRosen/Q-GAS for readers' free use.

papers.title: CHARMING: Parallel Edge AI Acceleration Across Tensor Processing and In-Memory Computation
papers.abstract: Edge AI increasingly relies on specialized accelerators for low-latency inference under tight resource and energy constraints, yet their efficiency remains limited by data movement. Prior work, CHARM, mitigates this overhead by overlapping data movement with computation. We observe that in-memory computing can further supplement tensor processing as a parallel accelerator while eliminating certain data movements entirely. We present CHARMING, a heterogeneous edge AI architecture that uses accuracy- and quantization-aware partitioning to distribute and concurrently execute inference workloads across tensor processing and in-memory computation. CHARMING partitions attention heads between an AIE array and an in-DRAM compute unit, balancing execution according to model architecture, sequence length, and precision while selecting heads to minimize accuracy degradation. CHARMING also integrates quantization into the AIE projection stage to further reduce data movement. We validate CHARMING end-to-end in hardware on AMD Versal VCK5000 and Alveo U200 platforms and evaluate LLM and video-generation models across multiple precisions using measured hardware results and simulation of the latest in-memory compute hardware. CHARMING improves prefill performance by up to 23.6 percent and decode performance by up to 44 percent over AIE-only acceleration. With int4 x int4 fixed-point in-memory computation, CHARMING reduces per-layer energy by up to 7.6 percent and improves energy-delay product by up to 24.7 percent, while maintaining accuracy similar to a 32-bit floating-point baseline.

papers.title: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning.

papers.title: Entire curves in surface bundles over tori
papers.abstract: Cattalani recently initiated the study of Ahlfors currents in symplectic topology. We combine these with the symplectic pairs of Bande-Kotschick to show that some non-trivial surface bundles over tori have pseudoholomorphic entire curves. In particular the Kodaira-Thurston manifold has an entire curve for every $J$ tamed by an invariant form.

papers.title: Exceptional sequences of line bundles on $\mathrm{Fl}(1,\ell;\ell+1)$
papers.abstract: Let $X_\ell=\mathrm{Fl}(1,\ell;\ell+1)\subset\mathbb{P}^\ell\times(\mathbb{P}^\ell)^\vee$ be the incidence variety of points and hyperplanes in $\mathbb{P}^\ell$. We prove that for every $\ell\ge 3$, every exceptional sequence of line bundles on $X_\ell$ of maximal length $\ell(\ell+1)=\operatorname{rk} K_0(X_\ell)$ is full. Together with the case $\ell=2$, due to Altmann, Hochenegger and Witt, this shows that for all $\ell\ge2$ an exceptional sequence of line bundles on $X_\ell$ is full if and only if it has maximal length. The proof translates exceptionality into a combinatorial condition on lattice points of $\operatorname{Pic}(X_\ell)\cong\mathbb{Z}^2$ and reduces fullness to sequences containing a non-orthogonal descent. A capacity count for admissibly ordered subsets rules out all but one family of descents; for that family we classify the possible configurations and verify generation using Euler sequences and Koszul complexes.

papers.title: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go
papers.abstract: When a Go model predicts a move different from the expert's, coordinate distance measures how far the prediction lands from the reference. We introduce Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to compare how the two moves change a board-state embedding. Both moves are executed from the same position under the game rules, and TReC is the cosine similarity between the two resulting representation changes. In experiments with a frozen KataGo network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the highest and lowest candidate per position has a median of 0.01 to 0.08 for the direct successor-state cosine and 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC, depending on the evaluator layer. TReC follows coordinate distance only weakly: the rank correlation between a candidate's distance to the reference and its TReC, computed within each position, has a median of -0.19 over these positions.

papers.title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: https://github.com/IAMIbrahimmemon/luthorsql

papers.title: Mobile Edge Deployment and Resource Management for Maritime Wireless Networks
papers.abstract: Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) has been envisioned as one of the key technologies for supplying computation and storage resources in Internet of Vessels (IoV) networks. Due to its flexible deployment, low cost and agile maneuverability, Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) has emerged as a promising solution, to provide communication and computation services for maritime users. In this paper, we study mobile edge deployment and resource management for MEC-assisted maritime wireless networks where USVs with diverse computation resources are deployed to provide edge computing services that complement the cloud-based services. To this end, we formulate an optimization problem to minimize the expected response time by jointly optimizing the deployment of mobile USVs and computation offloading decisions. To solve the mixed-integer nonlinear program problem, we propose a Dual-Layer Reinforcement Learning (DLRL) framework to attain a near-optimal solution. Specifically, a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm is designed to obtain the best USV deployment in the outer layer learning, and a Q-learning algorithm is designed to determine the best computation offloading decisions in the inner layer learning. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed solution outperforms some literature algorithms by effectively handling both continuous and discrete variables.

papers.title: A Consistent Bayesian Adaptive Quotient Graph Framework for Graph-Informed Random Partition Models
papers.abstract: Bayesian graph-informed random partition models are widely used to model heterogeneity in structured data. A prominent approach assigns a prior directly on the space of contiguous partitions of a pre-determined graph G; however, such models are not data-adaptive and can be computationally infeasible for large graphs. To address these limitations, we propose a Bayesian adaptive quotient graph framework that induces partitions through a two-level hierarchical prior: a prior is first imposed on quotient graphs of G, followed by a conditional prior on a reduced contiguous partition space induced by each quotient graph. We develop high-level assumptions that guide the construction of the two-level prior such that the reduced space retains desirable partitions. We further establish high-level assumptions for posterior concentration on desirable quotient graphs and partitions. The framework can be readily embedded into many existing Bayesian hierarchical models with latent cluster structures as a contiguous random partition prior. As a specific example, we apply the proposed framework to the spatial random partition model proposed in Huang and Sang (2026). The resulting model adapts to the unknown number of clusters, achieves a faster clustering-consistency contraction rate, and yields substantially lower partition error and computation time in simulations. Finally, we apply the resulting model to a large spatial transcriptomics dataset to demonstrate its practical utility.

papers.title: Active turbulent flows of dense persistent particles driven at constant velocity
papers.abstract: We study dense assemblies of self-propelled particles with infinitely persistent active forces, driven at a constant average velocity $V$ along their propulsion directions. Because the velocity $V$ introduces a finite timescale, it plays a role analogous to the shear rate in globally-deformed amorphous solids, and the system approaches a transition analogous to a yielding transition as $V \to 0$. We construct a force-velocity flow curve which is of the Herschel-Bulkley type, with a finite force threshold for flow. As $V$ decreases, the instantaneous velocity field becomes increasingly dominated by rare, localized plastic events, which produce fat tails in the velocity distribution and coexist with a slow, spatially correlated flow of streams and vortices. Many such events must accumulate throughout the system to fully relax its structure, so that the flow patterns reorganize after particles have been driven over a few particle diameters. The spatial extent of these correlated flows grows rapidly as $V$ decreases, and becomes only limited by the finite system size in our simulations. The kinetic energy spectrum displays a robust $k^{-1/2}$ regime also found in self-propelled particles at large but finite persistence times. Approaching the flow threshold thus leads to the same active turbulent state as increasing the persistence time in dense active matter, while displaying both analogies and differences with the yielding transition in sheared glassy materials.

papers.title: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents
papers.abstract: The Thomson problem asks for N unit charges on a sphere with minimum Coulomb energy; for large N the best configurations known are curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database, whose largest-N entries were set in October 2026. We report configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730 and 0.0614033 below the database values, certified by exact integer arithmetic. All three are numerically strict local minima modulo rotations and keep the defect inventory and scar compositions of the database configurations; the database value for N = 912 had been reached by two different methods. Our search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations, with a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling by geometry, and gradient-only polishing; replica-exchange basin hopping alone found the N = 912 and 1382 configurations, the former in one of five runs. We built and ran it with large language model agents (Claude, through a chat interface and the Claude Code agent), and we report every search, including those that failed. Two findings matter for others who search the database. Polishing alone lowers two entries by more than the threshold at which our pipeline reports a candidate, which produced two spurious records until candidates were compared with the polished database energies (the polished baseline). A local-relaxation speed-up passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within 15 minutes. We distil three practices for computational discovery with large language model agents: calibrate the search code and verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare candidates with the polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.

papers.title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models
papers.abstract: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.

papers.title: Estimand-specific bootstrap confidence intervals after optimism correction for prediction models
papers.abstract: Confidence intervals after bootstrap optimism correction are often reported for prediction models, but what they cover depends on the estimand. We distinguish two estimands: the target-population performance of the final model developed from the observed sample, $θ_{\mathrm{FM},n}$, and the average performance over repeated model development, $θ_{\mathrm{proc},n}$. Using first-order expansions of the estimation errors, we identify the bootstrap root that matches the error for $θ_{\mathrm{FM},n}$. We use this root in the nested error bootstrap (NEB) as a new reference method, and we show that the optimism error bootstrap (OEB), which needs no inner bootstrap, approximates NEB. We also show that the conventional two-stage bootstrap (TSB) and location-shifted bootstrap (LSB) reproduce the first-order variation for $θ_{\mathrm{proc},n}$. In simulations, NEB generally achieved coverage closer to the nominal level than TSB and LSB for the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, Brier score, and log loss. OEB was close to NEB at moderate to high events per variable (EPV) but could give narrower intervals at low EPV. The distinction is particularly clear for calibration measures: first-order effects of perturbing the training and evaluation distributions cancel in the TSB root, yielding a degenerate first-order limit. In contrast, the NEB root has a nondegenerate first-order limit and yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals for $θ_{\mathrm{FM},n}$ under regularity conditions. Consistent with theory, TSB showed substantial undercoverage for calibration even at larger sample sizes. Our findings emphasize the need to construct confidence intervals for a specified estimand and performance measure.

papers.title: Compatible by Construction: Bottom-Up Nonlinear Model Reduction without Interface Bases
papers.abstract: Nonlinear manifolds can provide compact representations of solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs), but generating training data and learning these representations on large domains remain costly. We present a bottom-up framework that reuses local nonlinear representations learned on a small training domain to solve larger PDE systems. A shared nonlinear decoder represents the full set of degrees of freedom owned by each subdomain, without separate interior and interface models. Each global degree of freedom has a unique owner, and local residuals directly use decoded state values from the corresponding neighboring subdomains. The resulting discrete state is single-valued by construction, eliminating the need for independent interface copies and additional interface compatibility constraints. Physical coupling is retained through the original time-discrete PDE residual. With the decoder held fixed, the subdomain-specific reduced coordinates are determined jointly by minimizing this residual, and the Gauss--Newton system is assembled from local contributions. Experiments on parameterized viscous Burgers and incompressible Navier--Stokes problems demonstrate reuse on larger domains without retraining. Comparisons with local proper orthogonal decomposition models under the same coupling construction show favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-offs in the tested regimes.

papers.title: Antidistillation is Cheap: Lightweight Distillation-Resistance via Stylistic Corruption
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective paradigm for transferring capabilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller, more specialized student models. In commercial deployment where frontier models are restricted behind black-box APIs, sequence-level distillation remains a potent vector for competitors to clone proprietary capabilities at a fraction of the development cost. Existing defenses mostly rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which increases computational overhead and real-time inference latency. In this work, we propose a lightweight defense that dynamically injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations upon malicious queries. This framework offers exceptional flexibility, allowing hosts to customize target defensive styles and dynamically blend them to maximize stylistic variance. Crucially, this inference-time intervention preserves semantic utility and fluency during malicious queries, misleading adversaries into believing that they are extracting pristine teacher outputs, while standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework successfully disrupts student learning, achieving substantial anti-distillation performance while incurring negligible overhead and preserving text naturalness. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/distill-resist-38C6/.

papers.title: Interpretable confidence regions for causal discovery
papers.abstract: Most work in causal discovery focuses on point estimation of the underlying causal graph, while uncertainty in the learned structure has received substantially less attention. We develop confidence regions for the completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG) identified from observational data. Our approach builds on perturbed PC (Chang et al., 2026), which generates plausible CPDAGs by perturbing the conditional independence tests underlying the widely used PC algorithm. The threshold used in these tests controls how perturbations translate into variation across the resulting CPDAGs. We propose a new thresholding strategy that suppresses spurious variation across runs while preserving asymptotic coverage, producing a substantially tighter collection of plausible CPDAGs. This collection is summarized through confidence balls and model confidence intervals constructed from the partially ordered set of CPDAGs under model inclusion. We also develop new theory and algorithms for the exact computation of these regions. Simulations show that our confidence regions attain good coverage while being substantially smaller and more interpretable than the original perturbed PC collections.

papers.title: Bridge: Database-Grounded Interactive Disambiguation for Text-to-SQL
papers.abstract: Ambiguity remains a persistent challenge in text-to-SQL, where an underspecified natural-language question may admit multiple plausible SQL interpretations. Recent work attempts to recover the user's intended interpretation through iterative clarification, but typically relies heavily on LLM parametric knowledge for ad hoc reasoning, leading to limited ambiguity-resolution effectiveness and high LLM cost. We further observe that many ambiguity errors stem from ambiguous column grounding, which remains poorly handled. Therefore, we propose Bridge, a database-grounded disambiguation framework built on an existing iterative protocol. Bridge supplies the LLM's ambiguity detection with offline-distilled knowledge about potential ambiguity relations among columns in the target database. Offline, Bridge constructs a Column Ambiguity Graph by first identifying potentially ambiguous column pairs using complementary database-grounded signals, followed by LLM-based verification. Online, columns and values mentioned in a previous incorrect SQL prediction are used as anchors to retrieve alternatives from the Column Ambiguity Graph and an offline-constructed value similarity index, respectively. The results are integrated for further pruning and consolidated for subsequent ambiguity detection. Extensive experiments on BIRD-dev without the benchmark-provided evidence show that, at comparable LLM cost, Bridge outperforms the strongest baseline by 11.60% in execution accuracy and improves the recall and precision of column usage in the final SQL by 5.25% and 12.37%, respectively.

papers.title: Uncertainty evaluation of length measurement by spectral domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing
papers.abstract: In this study, we evaluate the measurement uncertainty of spectral domain interferometry with super-Gaussian windowing, which has significant potential for interferometer-based dimensional calibration services owing to its simple configuration and nanometer-level precision. A super-luminescent diode (SLD) with a broadband spectrum was used as the light source for high-precision length measurement, and a frequency-calibrated spectrometer captured the spectral interference signal. The length measurement results were compared with a laser displacement interferometer. To evaluate the measurement uncertainty, numerical simulations were performed by considering the intensity-noise level of the CCD in the spectrometer and the frequency-axis uncertainty of the spectrometer. Through a comprehensive uncertainty analysis supported by numerical simulations, the combined standard uncertainty of the measured length was evaluated as sqrt((10 nm)^2 + (9.7x10^(-6)xL)^2). The resulting uncertainty budget provides a metrological basis for extending SLD-based SDI with super-Gaussian windowing toward interferometric dimensional calibration tasks over the millimeter-scale range.

papers.title: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon
papers.abstract: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long periods of incoherent rumination. We employ methods from activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method we introduce, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the model's digressions over long stretches of generation. The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.

papers.title: Learning Anisotropic Prediction Targets for Flow Models
papers.abstract: Flow-based generative models are trained on a hand-chosen prediction target, such as the velocity, the noise, or the clean data. This choice strongly affects training and sample quality. We introduce Anisotropic Flow Models (AnisoFlow), which replaces a fixed prediction target with a fully learnable one. AnisoFlow learns to scale the noise component of the target anisotropically, assigning a separate nonnegative weight to each direction in a jointly learned basis. A closed-form map recovers the velocity from the network's prediction, leaving the architecture, flow-matching loss, and sampler unchanged. Since recovery is exact, training optimizes the target purely to make it easier for the network to predict. We theoretically analyze the resulting prediction error and predict that the preferred noise weight in each direction scales near-linearly with data variance, in agreement with the weights learned empirically in pixel space. AnisoFlow improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the JiT baseline on ImageNet 256$\times$256, by learning only the prediction target, without representation alignment or architectural changes. In pixel-space text-to-image generation, AnisoFlow improves image quality and, through better-conditioned velocity recovery, largely removes patch-seam artifacts under reduced-precision inference.

papers.title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
papers.abstract: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.

papers.title: Toward the Minimal Set of Information Inequalities in Regenerating Codes: An Algebraic Approach
papers.abstract: Information-theoretic outer bounds for exact-repair regenerating codes can be formulated as linear programs, but the associated Shannon-type systems contain many implicit equalities and redundant inequalities. We directly specify a reduced system for the $(n,n-1,n-1)$ exact-repair model using the closure structure induced by its repair dependencies. Nonempty closed sets index the reduced joint-entropy coordinates, and inseparable edges determine the defining inequalities. We prove equivalence with the initial system by characterizing its implicit equalities and establishing sufficient redundancy criteria. We also give an algorithm that constructs the directly defined system for any $n$, count its entropy coordinates, and derive an explicitly computable upper bound on its number of inequalities. For every $n\ge2$, we prove that the reduced system has no implicit equalities and that each distinct defining inequality is nonredundant and defines a facet in the nonempty closed-set coordinate space. Exact enumerations for $n\in\{2,3,4,5\}$ verify the reported system sizes.

papers.title: Rational lines on pairs of quadrics and cubic hypersurfaces
papers.abstract: We study rational lines on smooth intersections of two quadrics and on smooth cubic hypersurfaces over number fields. For an intersection of two quadrics in $n$ variables, we prove the Hasse principle and weak approximation for the variety of lines when $n\geq 11$, and more generally for the variety of $r$-planes when $n\geq 3r+8$. In this range an $r$-plane exists over the ground field if and only if one exists over every real completion. For the variety of lines, we also prove the Hasse principle and weak approximation when $n\geq 8$, conditional on the finiteness of certain Tate-Shafarevich groups. For a smooth cubic hypersurface in $n$ variables, we prove that a line exists over the ground field when $n\geq 23$.

papers.title: Knowledge After Collapse: Context and Wording Shape Factual Accessibility in Language Models
papers.abstract: When a language model accepts a false correction in a factual discussion, its next answer can depend on how the conversation continues. We introduce Knowledge Answer Divergence (KAD), an event-conditioned evaluation protocol that distinguishes initial false-answer adoption from subsequent persistence, recovery, and abstention. KAD freezes the conversation at the first explicit adoption of a designated false target and branches independent probes from that exact history. This enables matched comparisons of post-adoption behavior and history-management interventions that a single susceptibility score cannot capture. We evaluate eight local checkpoint conditions and six hosted endpoints, alongside an audited 300-question rerun. In corrected Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B controls, a neutral-history branch yields 42/46 correct responses, compared with 16/46 under full history. A matched cue-placement control changes false adoption by 27.3 percentage points in Qwen 3.5 4B. Twelve independently authored pressure templates demonstrate substantial sensitivity to wording. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of KAD for evaluating factual reliability beyond initial susceptibility, enabling systematic comparisons of false-answer persistence, recovery conditions and conversational interventions.

papers.title: Creative Product Design under Brand Image Constraints
